title: A Data-Informed Analysis of Scalable Supervision for Safety in Autonomous Vehicle Fleets
evidence: Sec. V: "a merging AV must be supervised if there is any possibility over some time horizon h of collision with a vehicle on the lane to which it is merging"; Sec. VI sets h=5 s because "more than 80% of the 520 mean times for human takeover of vehicular control from an automated system were below five seconds".
method: DISCES couples historical traffic reconstruction with microsimulation of 1,097 freeway merges; kinematic reachability flags merges needing a remote operator; an M/M/k queueing model sizes supervisor teams.
evaluation: 27 day-long settings (3 counties x 3 penetration rates x unconnected/connected/cooperative AVs), 1 s granularity; vs in-vehicle supervision (>99% fewer); supervisors needed, reliability nines (+3.67 CCAV), speed.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; latency/jitter aware; time-to-irreversibility; human handoff
contribution: Quantifies how many remote supervisors a county-scale AV fleet needs, showing that reachability-triggered handoff plus cooperative connectivity and task pooling buys orders of magnitude of supervision reliability.
flag: Deferral is modelled, not implemented: the measured outcome is supervisor demand and queue reliability rather than collisions or violations, and takeover latency enters only through the 5 s reachability horizon. Strong fit for RQ2/RQ3 nonetheless.

title: A Distributed Multi-Agent Control Strategy for Agricultural Row Following
evidence: Sec. III (Prop. III.1): 'the pose of the follower agent i converges asymptotically to the desired pose... while keeping the safety distance from the next agent in the line'; Sec. IV reports only convergence plots.
method: Fully distributed row-following control law for heterogeneous agricultural agents: each follower regulates lateral distance and orientation to the crop row and longitudinal spacing to its predecessor without communication.
evaluation: ROS/Gazebo vineyard simulation, one 3-agent and one 4-agent run (one leader simulating a human operator); distance, orientation and velocity convergence plots; no baseline, ablation or hazard metric.
contribution: Distributed row-following controller keeps agricultural robots and human operators at safe lateral and longitudinal distances in vineyards without inter-agent communication or central coordination.
flag: Formation/coordination controller rather than a safety mechanism: no runtime override, no baseline and no hazard metric, so exclude-E2 applies too; the human operator appears only as an independently moving leader agent, not a handoff.

title: A Distributed Multi-Agent Framework for Real-Time Privacy Monitoring and Compliance in Enterprise AI Systems
evidence: Sec. III: 'Prompt/Completion Interception: SDK-level hooks capture all user inputs and model outputs before they reach the agent or user respectively'; graduated actions in Sec. IV: 'High (0.6-0.8): Block output, alert security team / Critical (0.8-1.0): Quarantine agent', and Level 4 data where 'Complete blocking prevents agent access entirely'.
method: Distributed Monitor/Detection/Reporter agents instrument prompts, tool calls, memory and egress; behavioural entropy, KL drift, LSH hallucination similarity and multi-turn attack graphs drive redact/block/quarantine enforcement.
evaluation: 50-node Kubernetes simulation, 500 GPT-4/Llama-2 agents, 50k interactions and 2.5k adversarial cases; baselines Symantec DLP, Splunk SIEM, Microsoft Purview; 94.7% detection accuracy, false positives 4.9% vs 18.4%, 0.8ms redaction, +0.5% latency.
contribution: Distributed privacy sub-agents intercept enterprise LLM-agent prompts, tool calls and outputs, blocking or redacting violations at sub-millisecond cost with far fewer false positives than DLP and SIEM baselines.
flag: Industrial paper: every number is self-reported from a synthetic enterprise simulation, with no code, seeds or variance. 'Multi-agent' means 500 monitored agents plus monitor agents, not interacting agents. Human escalation exists (approver-gated token reversal, security-team alerts) but is never evaluated, so (e) is not claimed.

title: A Game-Theoretic Model of Trust in Human–Robot Teaming: Guiding Human Observation Strategy for Monitoring Robot Behavior
evidence: Sec. IV cost model: 'Inconvenience to the human if the human observes the execution of an unsafe plan and it has to intervene ... to stop the robot from executing the plan pi_pr'; Study II monitors execution step by step, 'if they monitor the robot long enough, the robot will do safe behavior'.
method: Bayesian game between a supervisor's probabilistic observation strategy and a robot choosing a safe or probably-risky plan; a mixed-strategy 'trust boundary' makes the safe plan the robot's best response.
evaluation: Two IRB-approved human studies (n=32 strategy elicitation; n=26 between-subject treatment vs control interface); metrics monitoring steps/time, utility, deviation from optimal strategy; t-tests, TOST equivalence, survival analysis.
contribution: Trust-boundary analysis that tells a human supervisor the minimum probabilistic monitoring effort keeping a robot on its safe plan, validated in two human studies against unaided supervision.
flag: Safety is measured indirectly (utility and whether the chosen strategy lands in the trust region), not as a violation rate; single human-robot dyad so no multi-agent hazard; the human's stop action is modelled as a cost, not implemented.

title: A Heterogeneous System of Systems Framework for Proactive Path Planning of a UAV-assisted UGV in Uncertain Environments
evidence: Sec. V: the UAV predicts the UGV's reachable states using 'a set of virtual particles representing simulated instances of the UGV'; in Sec. VI 'since multiple particles drive into the hazard, the UAV determines that this path is unsafe for the UGV and adjusts the waypoints'.
method: System-of-systems UAV scout predicts UGV reachable states by particle sampling; self- and event-triggered rendezvous delivers MPPI-adjusted replacement waypoints when the current UGV plan is inefficient or unsafe.
evaluation: 20 simulated environments, four scenarios (Proposed, UGV Alone, Ideal, UAV Explore); metric mission completion time with hazard entry counted as failure; lab trials with ROSbot and Crazyflie (37% time saving).
contribution: A UAV scout predicts a ground robot's reachable trajectories and proactively reroutes it around hazards and blocked paths, treating the heterogeneous pair as one system of systems.
flag: Mechanism is a proactive replanner handing over new waypoints, not a runtime interceptor; hazards are environmental rather than multi-agent and the primary metric is completion time, so (c) fails the primacy test.

title: A Hybrid RL-GNN Approach for Precise Pedestrian Trajectory Prediction in Autonomous Navigation
evidence: Sec. 3.2: 'the node is denoted as the pedestrian agent and the edges are represented as connection between the spatial distance and movement patters. The links between pedestrians are dynamically updated to depict changing interactions'; reward eq. (2) R_t = -(alpha*ADE + beta*CR) where 'the collision penalty discourages dangerous forecasts'.
method: GNN over a dynamically updated pedestrian interaction graph produces trajectory predictions that an RL policy refines online with a reward combining displacement error and a collision penalty.
evaluation: ETH, UCY and nuScenes; Table 3 gives ranges (ADE 0.6-0.8m, FDE 1.2-1.8m) against unnamed 'machine learning based' and 'transformer based' models, with collision-rate reduction 'up to 50%'. No hardware, seeds, ablation or per-dataset numbers.
contribution: Hybrid GNN-RL pedestrian trajectory prediction models interaction graphs and refines forecasts online, reporting lower displacement error and collision rate than machine-learning and transformer predictors.
flag: Reported results restate the pre-declared target column of Table 2 ('>50% reduction' in CR, '>10%' ADE), baselines are unnamed model classes, all values are ranges, no ablation. (c) also fails primacy since ADE/FDE is the headline. Paper itself states the model 'makes real-time inference on low-power edge devices challenging'.

title: A Mori-Zwanzig Formalism Based Estimation Approach for Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance
evidence: Abstract/Sec. V-B: the method 'enables an ego robot to predict the trajectory of a dynamic obstacle that is outside its sensing range, solely by observing the historical trajectory of an ally robot', and implementing it gives 'a substantial reduction in the collision rate to 22.1%' from 59.1% without it.
method: Mori-Zwanzig formalism justifies feeding an ally robot's trajectory and control history to an LSTM that estimates an unseen obstacle's position; the estimate drives the ego robot's potential field.
evaluation: 5000 randomized simulation trials, 3 agents: collision rate 22.1% (M-Z, window 10) vs 59.1% without prediction and 13.7% omniscient; ablation over window lengths 5/10/30; proved prediction-error bound; noise-free dynamics.
contribution: Mori-Zwanzig-justified LSTM estimator that infers an out-of-sensing-range obstacle's position from an ally robot's avoidance behaviour, cutting ego collision rate from 59% to 22% with a proved error bound.
flag: The prediction feeds an APF controller, so there is no execution-time veto (runtime_interceptor no); idealised noise-free 3-agent simulation, and even the omniscient baseline collides 13.7% of the time, which weakens the comparison.

title: A Multi-Agent Driving Simulation Approach for Evaluating the Safety Benefits of Connected Vehicles
evidence: Abstract: 'the result of analyzing crash potential index (CPI) showed that the greatest safety benefits were obtained with the CV-CV case... Approximately 45% of CPI reduction was achievable' - the mechanism is a warning shown to a human driver, nothing that overrides or defers.
method: Two synchronised driving simulators (multi-agent driving simulation) run four CV/RV vehicle-pair scenarios on a four-lane freeway blocked by a crash, with in-vehicle hazard warnings for CV drivers.
evaluation: 54 participants, each driving all four pair scenarios; indicators ANI, relative-speed variation, lane-change likelihood and crash potential index tested by repeated-measures ANOVA; RV-RV is the no-warning baseline.
contribution: A paired driving-simulator study quantifies crash-potential reduction of roughly 45% for connected-connected vehicle pairs receiving in-vehicle hazard warnings, and the resulting interaction behaviour.
flag: 'Multi-agent' here means two coupled human-driven simulators, and the intervention is a driver warning rather than deferral, interception or autonomous hazard detection; criterion (c) covers safety evaluation only for LLM/tool-calling agents. The CPI-versus-no-warning result could still be cited as RQ3/RQ5 background on human warning benefit.

title: A Multi-Agent Framework for Step-Level Tool-Call Safety Evaluation in Industrial Control Systems
evidence: Sec. IV: the dataset supports 'guardrail models that can screen each proposed tool call before execution'; Sec. VI-C: decisions are 'made online at each step, which better matches real-world industrial requirements where a single unsafe action must be intercepted immediately'.
method: Multi-agent pipeline generates a step-level industrial tool-call safety dataset (benign, injected-benign, malicious) with deterministic PLC-constraint labels; LoRA fine-tunes Qwen2.5-7B into a guardrail labelling each proposed call safe/borderline/unsafe.
evaluation: Benchmark split of six unseen industrial domains, 1619 steps; baselines GPT-4o mini and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; strict-mode accuracy/precision/recall/F1 (overall F1 0.807 vs 0.449 and 0.189); no latency or hardware.
contribution: A step-level benchmark and fine-tuned guardrail for industrial LLM tool calls, showing instruction-tuned models miss contextually injected unsafe actions (recall 0.9-34%) that a trained screener catches at 85%.
flag: 'Multi-agent' describes the data-generation pipeline; the guardrail itself is a sequential single-agent tool-call gate, so (c) rests on the 'safety evaluation of LLM/tool-calling agents' clause rather than on an inter-agent hazard. The six industrial-process domains are all one domain type, so this is not cross-domain evaluation in the protocol sense. Real-time interception is motivated but never timed.

title: A Privacy-Preserving On-Device Multi-Agent Architecture for AI PC (POMA) Workflow Automation
evidence: Sec. V and Fig. 2: 'a runtime Policy Verifier that mediates high-impact actions' which 'checks intent alignment, destination trust, and sensitive-data exposure, computes a risk score, and applies least-privilege gating. High-risk actions trigger escalation to human oversight, unsafe actions are denied'.
method: On-device multi-agent desktop automation: SLM drafting agent, compact VLM+OCR perception, sandboxed computer-use agent under a local orchestrator and a runtime Policy Verifier doing risk scoring, least-privilege gating, escalation and audit.
evaluation: No results: defines a workflow task suite, adversarial injection battery, metrics (task completion, latency, policy overhead, confirmation burden, leakage) and a no-verifier baseline; only third-party AI-PC latencies are tabulated.
contribution: Architecture for on-device enterprise workflow agents in which a runtime Policy Verifier gates, denies or escalates high-impact computer-use actions, plus a proposed utility, privacy and safety evaluation battery.
flag: Design/position paper. (a), (d) and (e) are all squarely addressed and its stated baseline (CUA without verifier gating) with policy-overhead and confirmation-burden metrics is exactly the RQ5 comparison this review wants - but nothing is measured (Table 1 is cited vendor benchmark data). Keep as a design reference and watch for a follow-up with results.

title: A Probability-Based Approach for Multi-Robot Collision Avoidance
evidence: Abstract: 'When a potential collision is detected, robots generate candidate velocity strategies and evaluate their success probabilities ... and select the velocity combination with the highest combined success probability through distributed consensus'; risk is detected by 'geometric safety distance and future trajectory comparison' (Sec. III).
method: Decentralized fixed-path framework: linear trajectory prediction, geometric collision-risk detection, Bayesian-network success-probability scoring of accelerate/decelerate candidates, distributed consensus on the highest joint probability, then nominal-velocity restoration.
evaluation: Gazebo 11.10.2, two two-robot intersection scenarios (OmniBot, MecaBot); reports Bayesian success probabilities, velocity profiles and completion without collision; no baseline, no collision rate, no latency or compute figures.
contribution: A decentralized velocity-consensus scheme that keeps planned paths fixed and uses Bayesian success probabilities to decide which robot yields at an intersection, demonstrated in two Gazebo scenarios.
flag: Qualitative demonstration only: two scenarios, two robots, no baseline or ablation and no measured collision rate, so the v1.5 evaluation floor fails. It also fails the (c) primacy measured-outcome test and reads as a coordination planner balancing passing order and efficiency, so exclude-E1 is a defensible alternative ground. The velocity override of nominal commands is never framed or structured as a safety filter, hence runtime_interceptor=no.

title: A Real Time Simulation Optimization Framework for Vessel Collision Avoidance and the Case of Singapore Strait
evidence: Sec. V: 'Table II summarizes the average number of conflicts computed over 100 macro-replications of 3-hours intervals with (refer to the S2TA column) and without (refer to the w/o S2TA column) the conflict avoidance procedure ... the safety increases by orders of magnitude.'
method: Mines AIS data to cluster vessel-captain behaviour patterns, embeds them in an agent-based simulator of surrounding vessels, and runs metamodel-based (eTSSO) simulation-optimization over course/speed to minimise conflict probability and deviation from the intended path.
evaluation: Singapore Strait; 8 AIS scenarios (24 h, ~50000 points, >100 vessels), 15-min look-ahead, 10 replications per candidate, 100 macro-replications; with vs without S2TA; metric average detected conflicts (two orders of magnitude lower); no computation times reported.
contribution: Couples an AIS-learned agent-based model of vessel behaviour with fast surrogate-based optimization to recommend real-time collision-avoidance manoeuvres, cutting detected conflicts in the Singapore Strait by two orders of magnitude.
flag: Advisory decision support for the captain, not an execution-time veto, and conflict probability is an objective inside the trajectory optimiser, so (a) fails the strict runtime test; 'real time' is claimed but no computation time or latency figure is given anywhere.

title: A Reputation-Based Distributed Controller Reconfiguration Algorithm for Misbehaving Agents in Networked Control Systems
evidence: Sec. IV: when the 'reputation value becomes less than a certain amount... the corresponding agent is recognized as not behaving normally and will be isolated', and a trust parameter 'can act as a switch to reconfigure' that agent's control loop and steer it to a predefined safe location.
method: Distributed reputation and trust algorithm over neighbour measurement residuals detects misbehaving agents, isolates them from the consensus, and switches their control loop to drive them to a safe state.
evaluation: MATLAB simulation, leader-follower platoon of four robots, DoS and replay attacks on agent 2; proposed versus conventional reputation algorithm as position plots; detection after 0.7 s and 1.5 s.
contribution: A distributed reputation algorithm isolates cyber-attacked agents from consensus and reconfigures their controller to drive them to a safe state, preserving leader-follower formation.
flag: Criteria (a) and (c) are met and the trust switch is a genuine execution-time override, but the comparison against the conventional reputation algorithm is figure-based only: detection/isolation times (0.7 s DoS, 1.5-2.3 s replay) are the only numbers, collision reduction is asserted as 'obvious' from the plots, and no violation, collision or formation-error metric is tabulated, so the v1.5 floor fails. Closest paper in this batch to the review's reflex mechanism - maintainer may want to look for a journal extension.

title: A Robust Machine Learning Method for Safe and Efficient UAS Integration
evidence: Sec. IV: r-GCBF+ 'maintains high safety rates as well as high goal-reaching rates' where GCBF+ degrades, over 32 trajectories at 8/16/32/64 agents; Sec. V-C: in 13 Crazyflie trials 'the non robust version of the controller experienced 4 collisions while the robust version... only experienced 1'.
method: GNN-based graph control barrier function plus distributed controller trained self-supervised with look-ahead labelling; an adversarial uncertainty estimator learns worst-case sensor and process perturbations used for robust retraining.
evaluation: Double-integrator sims, 8-64 agents, 32 trajectories each: safety and goal-reaching rate vs GCBF+ under 30-50% acceleration and velocity noise; 13 two-Crazyflie hardware trials counting collisions.
contribution: Adversarial training of a GNN graph-CBF controller surfaces worst-case sensor and process uncertainty, holding multi-agent safety and goal-reaching rates where the non-robust model degrades.
flag: Strict (a) borderline: the learned controller takes the nominal command as input and modifies it at execution time, but the GCBF condition is enforced through a self-supervised training loss, not a runtime QP, so the row is scored on (c); hardware results are single trials the authors call 'not conclusive'.

title: A Safety Filter for Realizing Safe Robot Navigation in Crowds
evidence: Abstract/Sec. IV: the safety filter 'provides safety guarantees by verifying whether the optimal action recommended by an unsafe method is safe and, if not, corrects the action'.
method: One-step-ahead QP safety filter adding time-varying safe-set state constraints and discrete-time generalized velocity-obstacle action constraints to any base navigation policy, with heuristic soft-constraint fallback when infeasible.
evaluation: CrowdNav simulation, 500 episodes, three configuration groups; ORCA/CADRL/LSTM-RL/SARL with and without filter; collision, danger, success rates, navigation time; real-world mr1000 LiDAR robot.
contribution: A one-step predictive safety filter that corrects unsafe actions of reaction- and learning-based crowd navigation policies, lowering collision and danger rates in simulation and on a real robot.
flag: No computation-time or hardware latency numbers, so (d) not met; crowd humans are uncontrolled agents rather than a coordinated multi-agent system.

title: A Simulation-Based Framework for Generating Alerts for Human-Supervised Multi-Robot Teams in Challenging Environments
evidence: "Our models and simulations of mission outcomes must be accurate enough to predict the possibility of unwanted events, while the determination to issue alerts to human supervisors must be sufficiently fast in order to be actionable" (Sec. I); alerts fire when a situation "may occur with a probability greater (or less) than a human-specified value" (Sec. IV).
method: Monte-Carlo discrete-event forward simulation of a multi-robot mission with adaptive time-step size, robot grouping and consequential-interval selection; alerts trigger when a predicted hazard probability crosses a human-set threshold.
evaluation: Three 10-robot missions; baseline 20,000 high-fidelity runs; four hazard-alert probabilities estimated within 95% CI from 250 runs; 5-21 s compute, 1.44-2.28x faster than fixed step.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; latency/jitter aware; human handoff
contribution: Adaptive discrete-event Monte-Carlo simulation estimates multi-robot mission hazard probabilities accurately enough to raise supervisor alerts within seconds, creating opportunities for human retasking before failures occur.
flag: Advisory alerts only - nothing overrides or halts the robots, so (a) is not met. (c) is borderline: the measured outcome is hazard-probability estimation accuracy against a high-fidelity baseline rather than a hazard rate, and no false-alert rate is reported. The human-subject evidence for alert value sits in the authors' prior work [5], not here.

title: A Superellipse-Like Barrier Design for Multi-Robot Obstacle Avoidance in Formation Motion
evidence: Sec. 3.2: 'When P <= Q, the CBF controller's input u = 0, hence the PID controller uh can directly control the robots. As the robots approach the unsafe zone (when P > Q), the PID input uh will be counteracted by the CBF controller u, ensuring that the robots remain within the safe zone at all times.'
method: Superellipse-like CBF covers arbitrarily shaped obstacles; a CBF controller counteracts the PID formation-tracking input only near obstacles, steering along the barrier's minimum-gradient direction.
evaluation: Simulation only, three formation robots, one- and four-obstacle scenes; baselines circular CBF and A*; sole metric traversal time (20%/10% faster); safety shown qualitatively by positive barrier plots.
contribution: A superellipse-shaped control barrier function filters a PID formation controller so multi-robot formations skirt arbitrarily shaped obstacles, passing obstacle regions faster than circular-CBF and A* alternatives.
flag: Genuine runtime CBF filter over a nominal PID controller, so (a) is met, but the only quantitative comparison against the circular-CBF and A* baselines is traversal time; safety is a qualitative barrier-value plot, which is the v1.5 E2 floor. Hazard is static obstacles, not inter-agent. Text file is extracted with a corrupted font encoding (garbled but decodable); quotes above are decoded, not byte-literal.

title: A Two-Stage Approach to Path Planning and Collision Avoidance of Multibridge Machining Systems
evidence: Sec. V/VI: 'the supervisors can monitor the bridges and prevent two neighbouring bridges from colocating in their shared workspace', including collisions newly caused by faults, fault treatment or human intervention in runtime.
method: Two-stage: PBIL with 2-opt solves serial-coloured TSP path planning offline; a Petri-net P-invariant supervisor then blocks or delays bridges entering shared workspaces at runtime.
evaluation: Tribridge waterjet cutting case study; PBIL+2-opt vs PBIL vs greedy on route length (44262 vs 66265 vs 48756 mm); supervisor validated only by Tina Petri-net simulation.
contribution: Combines offline coloured-TSP scheduling with a Petri-net supervisor that blocks neighbouring machining bridges from co-occupying shared workspaces at runtime, tolerating faults and human intervention.
flag: Criterion (a) genuinely met (supervisory control can hold execution), but the safety layer is only demonstrated in one Tina simulation; all quantitative results (route length, computing time) are planning metrics against planning baselines, with no collision or violation rate. 2017, no learning component.

title: AIDR-Cloud: An Agentic AI—Driven Incident Response Framework for Cloud Failures
evidence: 'Before any plan proceeds to execution, the Critic or Governance Agent reviews it... It decides whether the plan can be executed autonomously, whether it should be partially automated subject to human approval for selected steps, or whether it should be downgraded to an advisory plan' (Sec. III).
method: Three-layer agentic incident response: telemetry perception, multi-agent LLM cognition (Detector/Hypothesis/Validator/Planner/Critic) over a Neo4j cloud dependency knowledge graph, guarded action layer with canary, auto-rollback and approval gates.
evaluation: Chaos-Mesh fault injection on multi-region Kubernetes/Kafka plus multi-week production deployment; baseline experienced SREs with runbooks; MTTR -63%, escalations -65%, 70% correct remediations, 0 unsafe actions, ~$0.08 LLM cost/incident.
contribution: Agentic incident-response framework whose governance agent gates LLM remediation plans before execution, cutting MTTR and human escalations on injected and real cloud failures without unsafe actions.
flag: Borderline on the evaluation floor: headline outcome is MTTR/RCA latency (efficiency), not a hazard rate; 'no unsafe actions' is reported as zero with no baseline count. Results prose gives no per-scenario numbers ('on the order of tens of minutes', 'large majority of runs') and the statistics section is written prospectively ('can be reported in tabular form'); only Table III (MTTD/MTTR p90) and the conclusion carry figures. Multi-agent = the LLM agent team, not hazards among agents, so (c) fails primacy.

title: Action Selection via Reinforcement Learning in Supervisory-Controlled Multi-Robot Construction
evidence: Sec. III: "the RL agent operates within an MDP where the supervisor has already eliminated all forbidden actions and unsafe states", with the supervisor evaluating enabled events at each step; but Table II reports only transitions (41 versus 100.58 greedy, 382.08 random) and a 100% success rate for all three policies.
method: Monolithic SCT supervisor (28,552 states, 127,528 transitions) for two-robot TERMES-style 3D block construction mapped to a deterministic MDP; Q-learning selects among supervisor-enabled events to minimise transitions.
evaluation: Simulated two-robot 3D construction, 50 test episodes; baselines SCT+greedy, SCT+random and a BFS optimum of 36 transitions; metrics transitions, reward per transition, task success; no safety metric, no timing.
contribution: Combining a correct-by-construction supervisor with Q-learning action selection cuts a two-robot 3D construction task from 100.6 to 41 transitions while keeping formal collision and deadlock guarantees.
flag: Interception is genuine (the supervisor vetoes events every step) but safety is guaranteed by construction and never measured: there is no unshielded baseline and all three policies reach 100% success, so the safeguard's incremental safety value is unquantified. Metrics are efficiency only; two robots; synthesis cost reported but no runtime latency.

title: Adaptation for Validation of Consolidated Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec. IV: 'We control robots i in Anc \ Ancnr using a C-CBF based decentralized controller of the form (21) with constituent functions hc, hs, hr, an LQR based nominal control input', where (21) is 'arg min ||ui - u0i||^2' subject to the consolidated-CBF constraint; Sec. I notes CBFs succeed 'in rectifying some unsafe legacy controller'.
method: Smoothly synthesises arbitrarily many candidate CBFs into one consolidated C-CBF, with a weight-adaptation law proved to certify validity for nonlinear control-affine multi-agent systems inside a QP filter.
evaluation: Warehouse simulation (speed, corridor, inter-robot constraints, non-responsive agents) plus AION R1 rover lab study among static and dynamic rovers under Vicon; no baseline; barrier/gain/input traces only.
contribution: Consolidating many candidate CBFs into one adaptively weighted barrier certifies joint satisfaction of several multi-agent safety constraints inside a single QP filter over a nominal controller.
flag: Runtime QP filter over an LQR nominal controller with hardware validation, so (a) is met, but there is no baseline, no ablation and no quantitative safety rate - only barrier-value traces - so it falls below the v1.5 floor. The consolidation of arbitrarily many constraints is the part relevant to RQ4 (hazard combinations) if the maintainer overrides.

title: Adaptive Centralized State Prediction for Multi-Agent Systems via Sliding-Window Dynamic Mode Decomposition
evidence: Sec. V: 'the centralized sliding-window DMDc (solid blue) effectively prevents cumulative drift, severely outperforming the individual DMDc', validating open-loop prediction of the aggregated multi-agent swarm state.
method: Sliding-window Dynamic Mode Decomposition with control identifies a time-varying linear surrogate of the aggregated swarm state, intended as the prediction engine of a centralised MPC (closed loop not implemented).
evaluation: Three Elisa-3 wheeled robots, overhead-camera tracking, 402 samples, window 100, rank 8; centralised vs per-agent DMDc baseline; relative position error 1-2% versus spikes approaching 50%.
contribution: Shows that identifying a sliding-window DMDc model of the whole swarm, rather than agent by agent, holds multi-agent open-loop prediction error at 1-2% on real wheeled robots.
flag: protocol v1.6: included as world-model/predictor evidence on a predictive-accuracy metric with a baseline or ablation; not safety evidence, RQ5 capped at 2. Criterion (b) met with a real-robot baseline comparison, but there is no safety mechanism and no safety metric (prediction error only), and the MPC is outlined with closed-loop execution deferred to future work. Same floor judgement as the CCDC STGNN paper; useful as a non-generative multi-agent predictor if the floor is relaxed for (b).

title: Adaptive Safe Control for Bounded Rational Human--Robot Interaction Based on Reinforcement Learning and Reachability Analysis
evidence: 'we develop an online low-conservative adaptive safety monitor based on backward reachability analysis'; Average Switching Number is 'the average number of times the controlled vehicle switches to the conservative safe control in each round' (Sec. I, Sec. V).
method: Cognitive-hierarchy game model of bounded-rational opponents with RL-computed level policies, plus an online backward-reachable-tube safety monitor that prunes the opponent action space using inferred rationality level and switches to conservative safe control.
evaluation: Four-lane highway, 50 vehicles at 20 Hz; collision rate and average switching number vs full-BRT, SAC, PS-SAC (8.7-16.8%) and IRL (>35%, ->14% with monitor); NGSIM US-101 prediction accuracy 81.5% vs level-k 62.4% and PS-SAC 67.5%.
contribution: Bounded-rationality game model with an adaptive backward-reachability safety monitor that cuts conservatism over 70% and safety-control switches while keeping collision risk essentially unchanged in dense highway interaction.
flag: Strong fit for (a) and for RQ5 (ASN = false-halt proxy, average speed = throughput). BRT horizon Tp = 3 s with 0.5 s sampling is the closest thing to a time-to-irreversibility signal. No measured solve time, so (d) not claimed despite the 20 Hz action rate; simulation plus logged NGSIM data only, no hardware. Humans appear as interacting opponents, not as a handoff recipient.

title: AgentFuzz: Trace-Level Fuzzing for Prompt Spillover in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: "SPC-Lite signs source-agent identifiers and rejects provenance-inconsistent messages" and SPC-Full "cross-checks upstream factual claims against the executor's state representation", cutting ASR from 35.2% to 20.4% and 8.7% (Sec. V-A, RQ4); "inter-agent communication amplifies unsafe behavior by 5.8x" (RQ1).
method: AgentFuzz: bandit-selected MAS-native mutation operators (role laundering, structural encapsulation, context insertion) driven by a trace-level composite reward over inter-agent traces; plus a source-preserving-communication runtime defense.
evaluation: AutoSafe-MAS, 300 safety-critical missions, five-agent MAS, three backbones, three topologies, five channels, B=40 queries, 8xH100; vs PromptFuzz 26.8% and LLM-Fuzzer 23.1%; ASR 35.2%, defense 8.7%, clean success 90.6%.
contribution: Trace-level fuzzing shows prompt spillover is a communication-layer vulnerability amplified 5.8x by inter-agent messaging, while provenance-preserving message filtering cuts attack success 75% for under three points of clean performance.
flag: The primary contribution is the attack search; the runtime interceptor is the SPC defense, evaluated only in RQ4. The benchmark's hazards (restricted zones, obstacle collision, human zones, battery) are simulated planning missions, not a physical deployment, so cross-domain does not apply. Two compound hazard classes exist in the benchmark but no per-class results are reported - worth asking the authors for that breakdown given RQ4.

title: AgentPay: A Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Autonomous Payment Orchestration with Formal Compliance Guarantees
evidence: Sec. II-C and III-A: 'an SMT check is a hard precondition, and the LLM can only narrow, never widen, what the solver permits', with CVL: Action -> {permit, deny, escalate} and Theorem 2 guaranteeing 'uncertain actions always reach human oversight'.
method: Five-role payment agent system over typed message passing; neuro-symbolic Compliance Verification Layer pairs Z3 SMT checking of PCI-DSS/PSD2/AML rules with a confidence-scored classifier; SBAM sets per-agent escalation thresholds.
evaluation: 15,000 synthetic AgentPayBench transactions; ablations rule-only and single-LLM; false negatives 0.62% vs 75.6%, escalation 30.9% vs 32.4% oracle-worthy; Z3 gate 0.88ms mean, 0.73ms median, 2.1ms p95, 'within payment-rail timeouts'.
contribution: A verified SMT compliance gate acting as a hard precondition on autonomous payment actions, with risk-scored escalation to human review, clearing 69% of traffic symbolically in under a millisecond.
flag: Evidence is internal consistency, not generalisation: the neural stage is 'a calibrated stand-in' rather than a real LLM, the labelling oracle shares the gate's own rule encoding (so 100% is 'faithful realization of the encoding at scale'), and the paper flags that p95 and throughput 'use stand-in neural latency, so they are projections' while only Z3 latency is measured. Cite for RQ1 (sub-ms symbolic gate under an explicit rail-timeout constraint) and RQ3 (permit/deny fast path vs escalate).

title: AgentShield: A Lightweight Sentinel Framework for Mitigating Hallucination Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
evidence: Sec. III-B/III-D: 'A sentinel Sj intercepts message mi transmitted from Ai to Ai+1 and performs anomaly detection before forwarding'; on alarm 'the flagged message is quarantined' and the upstream agent regenerates, reducing propagation depth by over 55% and raising success by 36.7 points over the undefended pipeline.
method: Non-participating sentinel agents on each communication edge run cross-entropy jump detection over a moving-average context baseline; on a threshold breach they quarantine the message and trigger bounded rollback-and-regenerate (Rmax = 2).
evaluation: HumanEval code generation (164 problems, MetaGPT) and literature-review synthesis (50 topics, AutoGen), GPT-4o agents with GPT-4o-mini sentinels, injection at 5/15/30%, 5 runs; baselines No Defense, Majority Vote, LLM-as-Judge; propagation depth, success, detection F1 80.5%, 8.6% false alarms, 8-22% latency and 72% token overhead.
contribution: Embeds immune-system-inspired sentinels on inter-agent links that detect hallucinations by cross-entropy jumps and confine them through rollback-and-regenerate at a fraction of judge-based cost.
flag: Strong RQ5 material: explicit detection-threshold sweep trading recall against false alarms (recall 91.3% with 18.7% false alarms at tau = 0.15 versus 68.5% recall with 4.2% at tau = 0.35) plus latency and token overhead against Majority Vote and LLM-as-Judge. Run on real LLMs, unlike the other cascade papers in this batch. Hallucinations are synthetically injected and the literature-review score is itself LLM-as-judge (validated against 20 manual scores, r = 0.82).

title: Agentic AI in Cybersecurity:Threat Modeling and Containment Strategies for Autonomous LLM Agents
evidence: Sec. IV-D: the middleware 'intercepts and mediates all communications between the orchestrator, tools, and sub-agents'; Sec. IV-C: below a similarity of 0.40 'the agent's execution is paused entirely, and a human review is requested'.
method: Three-layer containment middleware for LLM agents: RoBERTa injection classifier and boundary enforcer on all ingress, risk-tiered tool sandbox with call-graph anomaly detection, embedding-based goal-drift auditor with reanchor and pause thresholds.
evaluation: 47 red-team scenarios across AutoGPT, LangChain, CrewAI; attack success 76.8% to 20.6% vs unprotected baseline; full 2^3 ablation (p<0.001); 91.2% utility on 60 GAIA tasks; 47ms/tool call, 12ms/planning step.
contribution: A framework-agnostic three-layer middleware that sanitizes agent ingress, sandboxes tool calls by risk tier and halts goal drift for human review, cutting red-team attack success 73% at 3.8% added latency.
flag: Closest batch match for RQ3: explicit dual-threshold design, soft goal reanchor at 0.62 and hard pause plus human review at 0.40. Multi-agent exposure is only AV-5 cross-agent trust escalation (6 of 47 scenarios, CrewAI only), so (c) rests mainly on tool-calling agent safety. Per-decision latency is reported (12-47ms) but no budget is stated, so (d) not credited. Scenarios were authored and reviewed by the same small security team.

title: An interval approach to multiple unmanned aerial vehicle collision avoidance
evidence: Sec. IV: 'Where no obstacle collisions are likely to occur (i.e. tau < 0 is true for all obstacles) the agent is guided towards a designated target heading' - otherwise the interval avoidance manoeuvre overrides waypoint guidance; the abstract reports 'successful avoidance rates of 88%, 96% and 91%'.
method: Interval-geometric Sense, Detect and Avoid: sensor uncertainty carried as intervals on obstacle radius and proximity, a collision-time interval test per obstacle, and a 3D escape heading derived from interval geometry, extended to multiple obstacles and UAV formations.
evaluation: Three simulated conflict scenarios (crossing flight paths, head-on, 3-agent concentric), 100 Monte-Carlo runs each with perturbed position/velocity/heading; metrics collisions (12/4/9) and waypoints attained (90.5-99.5%); mean computation time 13.2/13.6/24.6 ms; no baseline method.
contribution: Interval-geometric sense-detect-avoid algorithm that propagates sensor uncertainty into 3D escape trajectories, avoiding 88-96% of collisions across two-agent and three-agent UAV conflict scenarios in Monte-Carlo trials.
flag: Has a quantitative hazard metric (collision counts over 100 Monte-Carlo runs per scenario) but no baseline or ablation, so it fails both the v1.5 floor and the (c) primacy test; the reported mean decision time of 13.2-24.6 ms is directly RQ1-relevant if the maintainer overrides.

title: Analysis of Group Effect in Group Emergency Stopping Behavior of Autonomous Multi-Robot Systems with Uncertain Sensing Delay
evidence: Abstract: 'Simulation results indicates that Group Emergency Stopping Behavior contributes to reduce the opportunity of rear-end collision due to the sensing delay'; Sec. III-C and Table 1 report rear-end collision numbers for single-interaction, single-lane group and multi-lane group stopping modes.
method: Lane-based sub-group emergency stop: on an urgent event a robot enters Emergency Stopping Mode driven by brake force, selected inter-robot emergency forces and a delay-decayed attention force.
evaluation: Simulation, two lanes of 10 robots, Gamma sensing delay (mu=0.57), 100 stops and 1800 distances per mode at 1.67/2.00 m/s; modes compared on rear-end collisions and stopped-distance variance.
contribution: A lane-based group emergency stopping behaviour whose inter-robot and delay-weighted attention interactions shrink the variance of stopped inter-robot distances and reach zero rear-end collisions under uncertain sensing delay.
flag: Simulation only (no hardware, prior work used robots); the stop is a reflex control law rather than a filter over a nominal command, so (a) is borderline; the delay studied is sensing delay, not inference latency, so (d) is not claimed although the paper is squarely delay-aware.

title: Application of Supervisory Control to Arbitration for Multi-Robot Systems with Learning Robots
evidence: Fig. 3 arbitration mechanism: 'If action pattern pi_0 = (sigma_1,0, ..., sigma_N,0) is included in control pattern gamma, pi <- pi_0 and exit. If pi_0 not in gamma, action pattern pi is determined by the following optimization problem' over the permitted actions.
method: Discrete-event supervisory control computes the permitted control pattern from forbidden states; an arbitrator picks the action tuple maximising weighted learned Q-values inside it, replacing unsafe DQN choices.
evaluation: Three DQN robots in a grid with collision-avoidance forbidden states; authors 'confirmed that each robot learns an optimal policy without collisions during learning'; no numbers, baselines or ablations.
contribution: Supervisory-control shield plus value-based arbitrator that keeps independently learning multi-robot DQN policies inside a collision-free joint action set and reduces joint-learning complexity.
flag: Ideal mechanism fit (shield over multi-agent RL decisions at execution time) but a 2-page GCCE abstract with a purely qualitative 3-robot grid demonstration: no metrics, baseline or ablation. Worth looking for an extended version by the same authors.

title: Architectural Resilience in AI-Driven Decision Systems under Adversarial Conditions
evidence: Sec. III-A: when inference paths disagree 'the system does not accept either extreme without override logic'; the control layer's 'policy enforcement components implement resilience principles including preventing dangerous actions during attack stages' and can 'trigger system lockdowns'.
method: Four-layer resilience architecture for one AI decision pipeline: input sanitisation, redundant inference paths with semantic checkpointing and rollback, trust-weighted cross-path consistency override, and a supervisory control layer with isolation zones.
evaluation: TensorFlow/IBM ART simulations (fraud detection poisoning, navigation spoofing) vs an undescribed baseline; recovery latency 412 to 128ms and 536 to 149ms, decision integrity +29-32pp, availability +14-16pp; figures labelled 'conceptual'.
contribution: A four-layer resilience architecture that isolates adversarial faults in AI decision pipelines and overrides inconsistent inference paths, cutting recovery latency about 70% in two adversarial simulations.
flag: Multi-agent only nominally: 'empirical validation across 20 cooperative agents' and 'cross-agent failure propagation' appear in the abstract but nowhere in the body, which evaluates one perception-inference-decision-control pipeline; Semantic Checkpointing is described but Quarantine Isolation and Adaptive Consensus Reset are abstract-only, and the abstract also carries future-work text. The baseline is never specified and figures are 'conceptual graphs', so exclude-E2 is an alternative ground. Only datum of possible interest: recovery-latency jitter (baseline oscillating 380-550ms vs a stable 120-160ms).

title: Attention-Enhanced Feedback Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Network for Multi-Agent Formation State Prediction
evidence: Abstract and Sec. III: 'an Attention-Enhanced Feedback Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Network (AF-STGNN) ... to achieve high-precision multi-agent state prediction', forecasting UAV formation positions and velocities over the inter-agent graph.
method: Spatio-temporal graph convolution over the UAV formation graph with spatial and temporal attention plus an explicit prediction-residual feedback channel inside the graph-convolution cell to suppress long-horizon error accumulation.
evaluation: MATLAB urban-canyon UAV formation dataset (2000x18); ablation ST/FST/AFST and SVR, LSTM baselines; trajectory RMSE 0.33 vs 1.34 at T=1; RTX 4060 laptop GPU; no latency reported.
contribution: Attention-enhanced spatio-temporal GNN with prediction-residual feedback forecasts multi-agent formation state, cutting trajectory RMSE about 40% against a feedback-only variant and 75% against a plain STGNN.
flag: protocol v1.6: included as world-model/predictor evidence on a predictive-accuracy metric with a baseline or ablation; not safety evidence, RQ5 capped at 2. Criterion (b) is squarely met with a clean ablation plus two baselines, but every metric is prediction error (RMSE/MAE/MAPE/accuracy) and no safety metric is reported, so the v1.5 floor as written excludes it. Maintainer may wish to override: a pure world-model paper can have no hazard rate. No latency, no edge hardware.

title: Bayesian Fusion of Multiview Human Crowd Detections for Autonomous UAV Fleet Safety
evidence: "during flight, an area is marked as crowded (therefore, a no-fly zone) if all, or most, UAV-mounted visual detectors have recently and confidently indicated crowd existence on it" (Abstract); the annotations "may be exploited by a path planner to form safe UAV trajectories" (Sec. I).
method: CNN crowd heatmaps from several UAV cameras are back-projected by raycasting onto a 3D Octomap and fused by a Bayesian linear-opinion-pool filter that favours newer observations, annotating no-fly voxels.
evaluation: Synthetic Unreal Engine 4 multiview UAV sequences of outdoor crowds; baseline the no-fusion OR-accumulation method [11]; mean IoU of projected crowd regions only; no safety, hazard or latency metric.
contribution: Bayesian linear-opinion-pool fusion of multiview UAV crowd heatmaps raises 3D no-fly-zone localisation accuracy over unfused accumulation, supporting regulation-compliant crowd avoidance by a drone fleet.
flag: Detection IoU against a no-fusion baseline is the only outcome - no hazard, violation or no-fly-breach rate - so the evaluation floor fails and (c) also fails the primacy test; the maintainer may prefer E1. The fused map only feeds a planner, with no runtime veto, and no onboard timing is reported despite the embedded-CNN framing.

title: Behavioral Verification of Fault and Delay Prone Multirobot System for Sim-to-Real Applications
evidence: Sec. V-B: "A safety violation is flagged whenever the actual separation between any pair of robots falls below the specified safety threshold"; violations between leader and F1 occur 140 times in simulation and 479 times in the TurtleBot 4 experiment (Sec. V-C).
method: LTL specifications for controller, consensus and follower components of a leader-follower multirobot system under faults and delays, verified compositionally and then checked trace-by-trace at runtime in MATLAB and ROS 2.
evaluation: Three-robot MATLAB simulation plus two TurtleBot 4 robots with injected faults, 9-20 ms time-varying delay and 20 percent packet loss; safety-distance violation counts, ISE/IAE/RMSE; no baseline or ablation.
contribution: Compositional LTL specification and trace-based runtime verification of a fault- and delay-prone leader-follower multirobot system, counting inter-robot safety-distance violations in simulation and on TurtleBot hardware.
flag: Quantitative violation counts exist but there is no baseline and no ablation - a single-configuration case study - so it fails the v1.5 evaluation floor. The monitor only detects deviations and never overrides or halts, so (a) also fails. The explicit jitter model (9-20 ms sinusoidal plus Gaussian delay, Bernoulli loss with burst outage, verified delay bound psi = 2 timesteps) on real hardware may still be worth citing as background for RQ2.

title: Bounds of Neglect Benevolence in Input Timing for Human Interaction with Robotic Swarms
evidence: Sec. 6: "it may be important to allow the human to intervene in response to 'out of band' information or other anomalies... the possibility of manual control may be an important element for preventing out-of-the-loop effects or complacency and enabling the operator to effectively monitor the system for failures or abnormal behavior"; the task studies "comprehension of the swarm's state" and the timing of the operator's single diverting input.
method: Human-swarm interaction reference task: operators time a single goal-change input to an LTI consensus swarm; Gestalt-augmented display draws robot-to-target lines; optimal input time computed offline for comparison.
evaluation: 44 participants (22 aided, 22 unaided), 36 test trials, simulated swarm; metrics input-time deviation from optimal and convergence time; aided significantly closer to optimum (z=-2.164, p=.03). No safety metric.
contribution: Human-swarm benchmark showing operators learn near-optimal intervention timing and that displays exposing the consensus variable improve it, but performance, not safety, is the measured outcome.
flag: Methodologically strong human-subjects study (44 participants, aided vs unaided control group, ANOVA plus Mann-Whitney) but every dependent variable is performance: input-time deviation and convergence time. No collision, violation or hazard metric anywhere, so the protocol v1.5 safety-metric floor fails and the human input is operator-initiated rather than automation deferring. Still worth keeping as a cited background reference for RQ3/RQ2: it quantifies asymmetric cost of early vs late intervention and a deadline past which the swarm cannot converge within the trial (Fig.1, ~33 s).

title: CBF-QP Based Collision-Constrained Shared Control for Multi-Agent Robot Swarms
evidence: Sec. V-C / VI-A: human supervisory commands are 'treated as a nominal input rather than a hard constraint... unsafe human inputs are automatically projected onto the closest admissible control action', and 'the proposed CBF-QP framework achieved zero robot-robot and robot-obstacle collisions' across all Monte Carlo trials.
method: Per-robot CBF-QP safety filter minimising deviation from a blended human supervisory velocity command and swarm cohesion term, subject to pairwise inter-agent, obstacle and actuator-limit constraints.
evaluation: Simulation only, N = 5/10/20/50 single-integrator (plus unicycle) robots at 20 Hz, 100 Monte Carlo trials per condition, cooperative and adversarial human commands; baselines unfiltered shared control, potential fields, velocity obstacles; collision rate, minimum distance, command deviation, time-to-goal.
contribution: Enforces formal inter-agent collision constraints directly on human supervisory swarm commands through a CBF-QP filter that intervenes minimally and preserves operator intent.
flag: Authority flows the other way from criterion (e): the filter overrides the human rather than deferring to one, so (e) is not credited and the 'human handoff' gap cell is granted only for human-automation authority arbitration. No human participants - the operator is a modelled global velocity command, including adversarial ones. Real-time execution at 20 Hz is asserted but no solve times are measured, so (d) is not met; simulation only, no hardware.

title: CBF-inspired Weighted Buffered Voronoi Cells for Distributed Multi-agent Collision Avoidance
evidence: Sec. IV-A: 'We ran 3 trials with randomly assigned pairwise counterparts for agents to swap positions. It is observed that no safety violation happens during the whole process'; Algorithm 1 projects the nominal goal onto the cell boundary at runtime.
method: Risk-aware weighted buffered Voronoi tessellation whose cell weights are updated at runtime from CBF-inspired accumulated pairwise collision risk; nominal goals are projected into each agent's own cell.
evaluation: Simulated position-swapping games with 6 and 16 unicycle agents; 3 trials reported with no safety violations; static qualitative comparison of cells against traditional Voronoi tessellation.
contribution: CBF-inspired risk weighting biases buffered Voronoi cells towards agents facing higher interaction risk, giving controller-agnostic distributed collision avoidance without requiring a CBF-based controller.
flag: Fails the v1.5 evaluation floor: 3 trials with no collision or violation rate against a baseline or ablation; the Voronoi comparison is a static qualitative figure. Topically relevant if the maintainer wants it as background.

title: COSTAR: Cloud-Observed Safety and Trust-Aware Agentic Reasoning for Enterprise Workflows
evidence: Sec. III-B Execution Loop: 'A policy-enforced executor manages tool calls via Amazon Bedrock Agents. Each proposed action undergoes validation against signed policies, risk budget constraints, and data governance rules before execution approval'; Sec. III-E: 'Actions exceeding established risk thresholds are automatically rejected or undergo revision'.
method: Dual-loop LLM orchestration: a deliberation loop plans and self-critiques; an execution loop validates every proposed tool call against Cedar/OPA policies and risk budgets, rejecting or rolling back actions.
evaluation: GAIA, SWE-bench Verified and enterprise workflows vs single-loop-reflection and AutoGen multi-agent baselines; 40-60% fewer policy violations, success within 2-5%, 15-25% latency overhead, Cedar checks 8-15 ms; four-component ablation.
contribution: COSTAR interposes a policy-enforced executor with risk budgets, rollback and an immutable action ledger between an LLM planner and its tool calls, cutting policy violations 40-60% versus agentic baselines.
flag: Results are called 'preliminary' and appear only in figures/prose (no result tables); multi-agent aspect nominal (one orchestrator; AutoGen is only a baseline); 8-15 ms policy-evaluation latency is quoted as a setting, not measured as a constraint, so (d) not claimed.

title: CRASH: Context-aware Recognition of Agents for Simulation of High-risk Driving
evidence: Abstract and Sec. I: "an Adversarial agent Selection Module (ASM) that models contextual interactions to probabilistically estimate each agent's likelihood of inducing a collision with the ego vehicle" using only past and present observations; Sec. V-B reports collision success rate above STRIVE, DiffScene and Safe-Sim.
method: Motion-aware masking drops near-static agents; a lightweight attention module over past and present spatio-temporal features scores each non-ego agent's collision likelihood, trained jointly with adversarial trajectory optimisation.
evaluation: nuScenes under replay and rule-based 5 Hz planners; baselines STRIVE, DiffScene, Safe-Sim; collision success rate, off-road rates, collision speed, planner solution rate; MAM/ASM ablation; RTX 3090.
contribution: First learning-based adversarial agent selection that estimates collision likelihood from past and present multi-agent context alone, raising collision-scenario generation success over future-trajectory and distance-based heuristics.
flag: Direction is inverted: this is a hazard generator for AV testing that maximises collision rate rather than preventing it, so the "safety metric" is a success rate for inducing collisions. Relevance to the review is the non-generative, past/present-only multi-agent collision-likelihood estimator; a maintainer who reads criterion (c) as prevention-side should call this exclude-E1.

title: CRDA: Content Risk Drift Assessment of Large Language Models through Adversarial Multi-Agent Interaction
evidence: Abstract/Sec. V: 'In restricted and general roles adversarial interactions, all agents of five Chinese LLMs exhibit an overall average increase of 31.5% and 16.38% in the cumulative deterioration rate respectively by the 10th round, compared to the baseline no-roles adversarial interactions.'
method: CRDA drives automatic multi-round adversarial interaction among agents that are avatars of one LLM, using role assignment plus a responses memory, and scores content risk drift by agent deterioration rate.
evaluation: Five Chinese LLMs (ChatGLM, ChatGLM2, Baichuan, Baichuan2, Qwen), four adversarial topics, eight agents, 10 rounds; no-roles baseline plus role-level and responses-memory sensitivity analyses; deterioration and cumulative deterioration rates.
contribution: CRDA measures content risk drift of an LLM by orchestrating role-played multi-round adversarial interaction among its own agents, finding restricted roles raise cumulative deterioration 31.5% over a no-roles baseline.
flag: Offline assessment harness with no runtime interception; 'multi-agent' means multiple avatars of a single LLM, so multi-agent only nominally; results are figure-based and no mitigation or safeguard is evaluated.

title: Characterizing human perception of emergent swarm behaviors
evidence: Abstract/Sec. III: 'we investigate how human operators perceive three types of common, emergent swarm behaviors: rendezvous, flocking, and dispersion ... in the presence of background noise'; the dependent measure is 'the maximum noise percentage for that behavior where recognition was still successful'.
method: Human-subject study: 72 Mechanical Turk participants viewed 24 videos of a 2,048-robot simulated swarm running rendezvous, flocking or dispersion with staircase-adapted random-motion noise, and named the behaviour.
evaluation: 72 participants, Welch t-tests and ANOVA on maximum tolerated noise and correct-answer counts; rendezvous easier than flocking (p<.001) or dispersion (p=.01); 100%-noise videos as a control. No safety metric, no system, no hardware.
contribution: An operator-perception study showing which emergent swarm behaviours survive noise in a human supervisor's reading of swarm state, with rendezvous most robustly recognised.
flag: Closest to (e) as operator situation-awareness measurement over multi-agent state, but there is no deferral, takeover or handoff event and the recognised behaviours (rendezvous, flocking, dispersion) are nominal, not hazards, so no criterion is the subject; it would also fail the E2 floor (recognition accuracy is not a safety metric, and the only control is a 100%-noise condition). Useful background for RQ3/SA measurement only.

title: Collaborative Decision-Making Using Spatiotemporal Graphs in Connected Autonomy
evidence: Approach, Sec. III-C: "Given the status embedding of the ego vehicle h'ego, we predict the action of the ego vehicle to identify if the ego vehicle should take brake action or not", from spatiotemporal graphs merged over connected vehicles; Sec. IV-B reports accident detection (AD) as the headline safety metric.
method: Connected vehicles' observation sequences encoded as spatiotemporal graphs (spatial-distance and temporal-motion edges); heterogeneous attention graph network yields a situational embedding; MLP imitation-learns the ego brake decision.
evaluation: CARLA+AutoCast, 3 scenarios, 24 trials each; baselines GAT, Collab-GAT, raw and compressed sharing, plus 3 ablations; accident detection, expert-action rate, package size; 30 ms + 3 ms, RTX 3080.
contribution: Compact spatiotemporal graph sharing between connected vehicles raises accident-prone-case detection by over 30% at 100x lower bandwidth than feature sharing, supporting graph-level multi-agent state as an interception substrate.
flag: Brake prediction IS the ego policy, not a veto over a nominal decision, so runtime criterion (a) fails; runtime reported (30 ms graph build + 3 ms forward, desktop GPU) but no latency constraint, so (d) fails; safety outcome is accident-detection ratio, not collision rate.

title: Collective Conditioned Reflex: A Bio-Inspired Fast Emergency Reaction Mechanism for Designing Safe Multi-Robot Systems
evidence: Sec. IV-B: 'applying CCR can effectively reduce the dangerous behavior frequency by 42.24%' versus the original MARL algorithms, with each robot's emergency score inferred from neighbouring robots' states (Sec. III-C).
method: A physical emergency-score model over neighbouring robots augments each agent's reward with an intrinsic term inside multi-agent RL training, yielding collective local-then-global emergency avoidance.
evaluation: Multi-Agent Particle Environment, three emergencies (turbulence, strong wind, hidden obstacle); baselines IDDPG, MADDPG, MAAC and pessimistic-penalty variants; dangerous-behaviour frequency, collisions, success rate.
contribution: Collective Conditioned Reflex adds neighbour-derived emergency rewards to multi-agent RL, cutting dangerous-behaviour frequency about 42% against MARL and pessimistic-penalty baselines in three emergency scenarios.
flag: Not a runtime interceptor: CCR is an intrinsic reward term in the MARL training loop, so (a) explicitly fails; included on (c), whose primacy test it passes (dangerous-behaviour frequency and collisions vs baselines and a lambda ablation). Particle-simulation only, no hardware, no latency; the safety/efficiency trade-off makes it useful for RQ5.

title: Collision Avoidance Control for Distributed Multi-Robot Systems Using Collision Cones and CBF-Based Constraints
evidence: Sec. III-B 'Verification of Collision Avoidance': the computed desired acceleration is checked against position-based constraints and 'in case hij becomes negative for any obstacle, we isolate the direction and adjust the magnitude of the desired acceleration'.
method: Optimization-free decentralized avoidance: collision-cone CBF constraints on heading angular velocity produce an avoidance acceleration added to waypoint PD control, followed by a position-based verification step adjusting the command.
evaluation: Realistic quadrotor-model sims, 2-32 robots, with and without moving obstacles: minimum robot-robot and robot-obstacle distances, distance travelled; six Crazyflie 2.1 flights at 0.1 s control interval; no baseline.
contribution: Collision-cone CBF constraints on heading rate plus a position-based verification step give optimization-free decentralized multi-robot avoidance, shown with up to 32 simulated robots and six Crazyflies.
flag: Authors state that comparison with existing approaches is future work: minimum-distance plots only, no baseline or ablation, so the E2 floor fails despite a genuine runtime verify-and-adjust interception step.

title: Collision Avoidance for Multiple Fixed-wing Aircrafts with 3D Voronoi Diagrams
evidence: Sec. IV-B: for the 2D buffered-Voronoi baseline "the minimal reciprocal distance among aircrafts drops drastically below the safe threshold sometime, which may induce collision", whereas the proposed 3D method stays above it.
method: Decentralized local planner partitions 3D space into Voronoi polyhedra from neighbour positions only; one-step greedy local target selection plus a target-tracking autopilot respecting fixed-wing dynamics.
evaluation: Simulated 5/10/20 fixed-wing aircraft, open and dynamic-obstacle scenes; baseline 2D buffered Voronoi cells [17]; metric minimal inter-aircraft distance versus safe threshold; per-decision-cycle time 4.1-50.7 ms, avg 8.2 ms.
contribution: Extends buffered-Voronoi collision avoidance to three dimensions with fixed-wing dynamics, keeping up to twenty aircraft above the safety threshold where a 2D baseline dips below it, at about 8 ms per decision cycle.
flag: Per-cycle decision latency reported as min/max/avg (max 50.7 ms against avg 8.2 ms) is genuinely jitter-relevant, but the mechanism itself is not latency-aware and no edge hardware is named. It is a planner over a geometric partition, not a filter over a nominal command, so (a) fails. Simulation only.

title: Collision Detection and Avoidance for Black Box Multi-Robot Navigation
evidence: Sec. II: "CODAK's design leaves full autonomy and control to the robot's internal navigation stack, and only steps in when a collision is anticipated"; Sec. III-C: when distance to the predicted collision point drops below d_th "lower-priority MRH engages the handbrake and releases it once the higher-priority robot moves away".
method: External per-robot handler reads black-box intent (pose, velocity, plan); RNN predicts Gaussian future states; thresholded pairwise collision probability makes the lower-priority robot engage its handbrake and yield.
evaluation: Gazebo (30 runs/scenario) and 5 live Jackal runs, 4 scenarios; baselines stock ROS-Nav and NH-ORCA; success rate (1/30 vs 30/30), makespan, distance; RNN vs AvgVel error.
contribution: CODAK coordinates black-box robots from outside their navigation stacks, using learned stochastic trajectory prediction and a yield-by-handbrake protocol to lift multi-robot success from near zero to 28-30/30 at modest makespan cost.
flag: Success rate conflates deadlocks and collisions (2.5% residual collisions attributed to the planner, not to prediction); no latency, jitter or compute measurement for the interception path, and no edge hardware reported.

title: Collision and Deadlock Avoidance in Multirobot Systems: A Distributed Approach
evidence: Abstract and Sec. V: 'a real-time and distributed algorithm for both collision and deadlock avoidance by repeatedly stopping and resuming robots', each robot 'checking whether its succeeding state is occupied and whether the one-step move can cause deadlocks'.
method: Robot paths discretised into labelled transition systems; a distributed one-step-lookahead rule stops or resumes each robot when its next state is occupied or would close a deadlock cycle.
evaluation: MATLAB simulation, four robots on intersecting circular paths plus a four-vehicle crossing; ablation (collision-only algorithm deadlocks) and baseline [35]: fewer stop events, zero deadlocks versus linear growth to 25 robots.
contribution: Distributed runtime policy halts and resumes robots on fixed intersecting paths, provably avoiding collisions and deadlocks, proved maximally permissive and needing fewer stops than prior zone-based control.
flag: Hazard metrics are deadlock counts and stop-event lengths rather than a collision rate; 'real-time' is asserted but no latency is measured; purely discrete-event, no learning. Borderline on the E2 floor: the quantitative safety evidence is Fig. 12/Table IV (zero deadlocks vs linear growth) plus the Alg.1-vs-Alg.3 ablation.

title: Collision-Free Trajectory Planning for Multi-Robot Systems Under Stochastic Uncertainty
evidence: Sec. 4: '8 robots exchange positions, with each method tested 10 runs'; proposed method 'consistently achieves the highest success rate as uncertainty increases' against deterministic and B-spline baselines on safety margin ratio and success.
method: Decentralized MPC planner: MINVO-basis minimal-volume polyhedra enclose predicted trajectories of neighbours and obstacles; Gaussian chance constraints are converted to deterministic mean/covariance constraints, layered on a JPS global path.
evaluation: 15x15x5 m sim, 30 obstacles, 8 and 16 robots, 10 runs per method at three noise levels; length, flight time, safety-margin ratio, success vs deterministic and B-spline baselines.
contribution: Chance-constrained decentralized MPC with MINVO polyhedral trajectory envelopes keeps multi-robot position swaps collision-free under estimation noise, improving safety margin and success rate over deterministic and B-spline formulations.
flag: Collision avoidance is a constraint inside the MPC, so strict (a) fails; inclusion rests on (c) - safety margin ratio and success rate vs two baselines, with length and flight time reported as comparable.

title: Collision/Obstacle Avoidance Cooperative Tracking Control for MASs With Network Constraints
evidence: Sec. I: the command governor is "an add-on scheme to enforce safety constraints on the system via command signals whenever necessary"; Sec. V-A: under degraded communication the prior scheme [22] shows "robots 1 and 2 collide ... the collision occurs at about 0.077 s" while the proposed governor keeps all inter-robot and robot-obstacle distances "consistently greater than the collision thresholds".
method: Distributed command governor plus barrier-Lyapunov tracking control: adjusts formation reference signals and searches artificial-potential-field-like safe commands according to measured network/communication performance.
evaluation: Four-robot simulation and three Xtark robots (Jetson Nano plus STM32, 20 Hz Wi-Fi, governor at 500 Hz); baseline scheme [22] collides; metric is inter-robot/obstacle distance versus collision threshold.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; non-generative inference; latency/jitter aware; edge deployment
methods: control-theory; networked-control; barrier-functions; quantisation; real-time-systems; reference-governor
contribution: A distributed command governor that loosens formation geometry and searches safe commands as a function of network quality, preventing collisions that a prior governor suffers at low data rates.
flag: Interception rewrites reference signals rather than vetoing or halting; safety evidence is distance plots plus one baseline collision, with no violation-rate statistics; latency enters only as communication period h, no profiling of the governor itself.

title: Collisions-Free Distributed Cooperative Tracking Control for Nonlinear MASs With Limited Data Rate
evidence: Abstract and Sec. III-B: 'The distributed command governor intelligently adjusts the reference signals of agents, which generates safe formation shapes when facing the risk of collisions'; 'the required data rate for the MAS to avoid collisions is also derived', since 'limited data rate constrains the speed at which agents make cooperative decisions, thus increasing the risk of collisions'.
method: Distributed observer over quantised limited-rate links plus a command governor with dynamical barrier functions that reshapes each agent's reference signal when inter-agent or obstacle collision risk appears, feeding an adaptive tracking controller.
evaluation: Four nonholonomic mobile robots with two obstacles, sampling period 28.8ms; at 417.38 bits/s all inter-robot and obstacle distances stay above the thresholds, at 174.71 bits/s robot 1 collides with obstacle O2 at t=25.5s; required rate mapped against obstacle-environment complexity and gain.
contribution: A distributed command governor over quantised limited-rate links reshapes formation references to keep nonlinear multi-agent tracking collision-free, and derives the data rate that collision avoidance requires.
flag: (a) borderline: the governor continuously reshapes references rather than vetoing or halting an action. Safety evidence is one four-robot simulation with a data-rate ablation rather than a competing-safeguard baseline. Still the batch's best formal link between decision rate/bandwidth and collision avoidance, which is directly relevant to the latency-aware cells.

title: Consensus Control for Multi-Agent Systems via Cooperative Game-Based Leader Trajectory Generation
evidence: Sec. III: the predictive safety index 'provides an adjustable trade-off between trajectory efficiency and environmental safety' by regulating the human/autonomy weighting inside the MPC objective, i.e. a constraint within the planner rather than an execution-time veto.
method: Cooperative-game shared control: Pareto weighting of human and autonomous inputs modulated online by a predictive safety index inside an MPC leader-trajectory generator, with RL-based consensus tracking for followers.
evaluation: One simulation run: second-order leader plus three followers, two circular obstacles, Ts=0.05 s, horizon 9; trajectory, control-input and consensus-error plots only; no baseline, ablation or safety metric.
contribution: Shared-control framework in which a predictive safety index sets the Pareto weighting between human and autonomous leader inputs inside an MPC, with RL consensus tracking for followers.
flag: Strict (a) fails: the safety index is a weighting/constraint inside the MPC cost. (e) fails too: the human injects corrective input, the automation never defers to a person. Also below the E2 floor (single simulation, no baseline, no safety metric), so exclude-E2 is equally defensible.

title: Constrained Coverage of Unknown Environment Using Safe Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Abstract: 'a safe reinforcement learning based shield method is proposed for unknown environment exploration while correcting actions of agents for safety guarantee and avoiding invalid samples into policy updating'; Sec. V-B: 'By choosing MADDPG without shield as the Baseline, we have compared their performance metrics of connectivity rate, collision rate, mean reward and step number'.
method: Distributed CBF shield corrects actions of centrally trained, distributively executed MADDPG policies for collision avoidance and connectivity, and keeps invalid samples out of policy updates; validity proved.
evaluation: Four-agent coverage of unknown target density; ablation baseline MADDPG without shield; collision and connectivity rate, coverage time, reward; 5 training runs, 100 test episodes, 3-5 agents.
contribution: A distributed CBF shield corrects MADDPG actions online, giving zero safety violations throughout multi-agent coverage training and far lower collision rates than unshielded MADDPG across 3-5 agents.
flag: Shield-plus-ablation design is the cleanest fit in this batch; note the task objective is coverage, so (c) rests on collision rate being a headline measured outcome against the no-shield baseline rather than on hazard detection being the paper's only subject. Simulation only, 4 agents, no latency or hardware.

title: Containing the Cascade: A Benchmark and Reference Mediator for Failure Propagation in Tool-Using LLM Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: Sec. V / Fig. 1: 'SENTINEL interposes on the inter-agent channel... on detection the circuit breaker halts propagation and a checkpoint rollback restores the last verified good state'; Table IV reports containment rising from 46.2% to 99.4% and task success from 31.3% to 83.7%.
method: Mediator interposed per inter-agent message: typed output contracts, then LLM-as-judge semantic anomaly gate, circuit breaker that blocks a flagged message, and checkpoint rollback converting a halt into recovery.
evaluation: CASCADE-BENCH discrete-event testbed, 1080 scenarios / 48 configurations / ~590,000 executions; baselines No Guard, Retry, Verifier, Debate plus four-way component ablation; containment rate, cascade depth, blast radius, MTTD (0.11 hops), overhead in steps.
contribution: Introduces a containment benchmark and SENTINEL, a per-message mediator whose circuit breaker and checkpoint rollback separate fail-safe containment from fail-operational task completion.
flag: Strong RQ5 candidate: the ablation isolates false-halt cost explicitly (removing checkpoint rollback keeps containment at 99.5% but collapses task success to 2.6%). Construct-validity caveat stated by the authors: results come from a calibrated discrete-event simulation, not live LLM rollouts, so absolute numbers are relative comparisons only. Overhead is in steps, not time.

title: Contamination Percolation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Measurement Framework and Benchmark
evidence: "plausible clinical misinformation propagated at up to 92% under full connectivity, and even the model that rejected nearly all nonsense control tokens propagated it at 60%" (Abstract; Sec. VI Finding 1), measured over agent-network topologies.
method: ContamPerc benchmark: 400 vignettes, 50 Tier-1 semantic markers plus nonsense canary payloads injected into LLM agent networks; Contamination Gap Diagnostic scores propagation under fully connected, chain and star topologies.
evaluation: Five model families, ~246k API calls, 100 trials per cell with Wilson CIs and bootstrap (B=10,000); isolation-control ablation, within-family size control, human-labelled detector check, MIMIC-IV real-case slice.
contribution: A benchmark and diagnostic quantifying how plausible misinformation propagates through LLM agent networks, showing topology and model scale, not refusal training, govern contamination rates up to 92%.
flag: Measurement framework only - no interception mechanism, so nothing for RQ1-RQ3. The paper's own "cross-domain validation" is healthcare/legal/financial, all logical-enterprise, so the cross-domain gap cell does not apply under the strict definition. Chain topology is offered as a mitigation but is an architecture choice, not a runtime gate.

title: Context-Driven Autonomy for Enhanced System Resilience in Emergent Operating Environments
evidence: Abstract: 'Agent-based modeling and Monte Carlo simulation are used to evaluate the incident rate and mission reliability of the proposed context-based solution against rule-based and utility-based C2 solutions, including the RTCA DO-185B standard and Dynamic A-star Lite'; Sec. VII: 'the CBA solution yielding the lowest lambda in comparison to the RBA and UBA solutions'.
method: Context-driven C2 decision engine: diagnostic/prognostic heuristics score state-of-health and situational awareness, encode each candidate action with a Resilience Impact Factor, then tabu search prohibits unsafe classes and triggers a failsafe when no action is tolerable.
evaluation: MATLAB airspace-encounter simulation, ownship vs 14 non-cooperative intruders over 10,000 sq nmi, 20 Monte Carlo simulations per uncertainty level; baselines RTCA DO-185B rule-based and D* Lite utility-based; metrics incident rate and mission reliability with paired t-tests (>10% lower incident rate).
contribution: A context-driven C2 engine that scores actions by resilience impact and prohibits the worst ones cuts air-traffic incident rates below TCAS-style rule-based and D* Lite baselines in unanticipated conditions.
flag: Borderline on (a): tabu prohibition and 'Rule 1 (Failsafe Triggering): if all C2 actions in the solution-space are prohibited, initiate a failsafe action' are constraints inside the decision engine's own action selection, not an interceptor on a separate nominal decision, so runtime_interceptor is no. Co-primary mission-reliability metric means safety is not the sole measured outcome; situational awareness is machine-side only, no human handoff.
