title: Continual Multi-Agent Interaction Behavior Prediction With Conditional Generative Memory
evidence: "we propose a multi-agent interaction behavior prediction framework with a graph-neural-network-based conditional generative memory system to mitigate catastrophic forgetting" (Abstract); the system "takes the references information and observations as input to predict the distribution of future trajectories" (Fig. 1).
method: GNN multi-agent trajectory predictor trained continually: a conditional generative memory replays synthetic interaction data for past locations, plus a small episodic buffer, when new per-scenario datasets arrive.
evaluation: INTERACTION, InD and RounD datasets presented sequentially; continual-learning baselines that exhibit forgetting plus an ablation of memory components; metrics ADE/FDE and forgetting measures; no safety metric.
contribution: First study of continual learning for multi-agent interaction prediction: a GNN conditional generative memory replays past scenarios and keeps displacement error low as datasets arrive sequentially.
flag: protocol v1.6: included as world-model/predictor evidence on a predictive-accuracy metric with a baseline or ablation; not safety evidence, RQ5 capped at 2. Journal companion of the queued ITSC paper doi:10.1109/itsc48978.2021.9564510 (shared authors and predictor) - dedupe decision needed. ADE/FDE and forgetting metrics only, no safety metric, so the evaluation floor fails.

title: Continual Multi-Agent Trajectory Prediction via Dual Knowledge Consolidation and Pseudo Data Generation
evidence: Abstract: a 'rehearsal-based dual knowledge consolidation framework, which systematically consolidates interaction patterns via intra-sample relational distillation, and retains trajectory statistics via an expandable pattern memory bank' for multi-agent trajectory prediction over the interaction graph.
method: Continual learning for multi-agent trajectory prediction: intra-sample relational distillation of interaction graphs, expandable trajectory-pattern bank with centre-feature distillation, and pseudo-data generation to diversify rehearsal.
evaluation: INTERACTION (12 areas) and Argoverse2 (6 cities) streams on FJMP vs fine-tune, EWC, ER, DER++, CTP-UGR; minADE/minFDE/SMR plus APE and forgetting; memory-size and task-order ablations.
contribution: Dual knowledge consolidation with pseudo-data rehearsal that cuts catastrophic forgetting in continual multi-agent trajectory prediction across shifting traffic domains on INTERACTION and Argoverse2.
flag: protocol v1.6: included as world-model/predictor evidence on a predictive-accuracy metric with a baseline or ablation; not safety evidence, RQ5 capped at 2. Criterion (b) is clearly met and baselines/ablations are strong, but every reported metric is prediction accuracy (minADE/minFDE/SMR) with no safety metric, no interception and no latency figure; maintainer may still want it as RQ4 background.

title: Cooperative Data-Driven Safety Control Based on Distributed Gaussian Processes
evidence: Sec. IV-C: 'Data-driven safety control and exploration in unknown environments in multi-agent systems are achieved by sequentially solving a constrained quadratic program (QP)' whose CBF constraints bound each robot's control input; Sec. V-B reports only that 'the DGP-CBF significantly reduces the computational cost compared with the standard GP-based CBF'.
method: Distributed GP-based control barrier function: a robust Bayesian committee machine fuses expert predictive distributions over partitioned datasets to synthesise the safety function, enforced by a per-robot QP on a simplified bicycle model.
evaluation: Three TurtleBot3 Burgers with LiDAR and OptiTrack in a walled field with three obstacles; 10 trials per method; the only quantitative comparison is GP computation time versus the centralised GP-based CBF. Safety shown qualitatively via trajectory snapshots and h(x) contours.
contribution: Distributes Gaussian-process regression for data-driven control barrier functions across agents via a robust Bayesian committee machine, cutting safety-function synthesis cost in multi-robot exploration.
flag: Fails the v1.5 evaluation floor: no quantitative safety metric at all - no collision count, violation rate or minimum-distance statistic - and the only baseline comparison (Fig. 3) is GP computation time, an efficiency measure. Safety evidence is a qualitative demonstration (snapshots, h(x) contours). Criterion (c) would also fail the primacy test: the paper's claim is distributed GP efficiency, and the inter-agent collision constraint is slack-relaxed with a penalty weight. Genuinely a runtime safety filter, so worth keeping on file if the floor is ever relaxed; the earlier recursive-GP CBF by the same authors (ref [12]) may be queued separately.

title: Cooperative Decision-Making for CAVs at Unsignalized Intersections: A MARL Approach With Attention and Hierarchical Game Priors
evidence: Sec. IV-D: 'The safety inspector module functions as an active conflict regulator, embodying two primary components: the Proactive Predictor of Agent Risk and the Assisted Corrector of Agent Motion'; Alg. 2 takes the policy actions A_t0 and outputs corrected actions A*_t0 that are then executed.
method: Multi-agent DDPG with attention screening of interacting vehicles, level-k game priors from attention weights, and a safety inspector that rolls out trajectories, counts conflicts and corrects actions pre-execution.
evaluation: Gym intersection and Carla/ADCU hardware-in-loop, 4 CAVs plus heterogeneous human drivers vs MADDPG and Attention-MADDPG; success 86% vs 44%/72%, PET 3.61 s vs 1.30 s; HIL 20 Hz.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; non-generative inference; latency/jitter aware; edge deployment
methods: reinforcement-learning; shielding; representation-learning; sequential-decision; real-time-systems; decision-theory
contribution: MARL intersection decision-making whose attention-derived level-k safety inspector predicts conflicts and corrects CAV actions before execution, nearly doubling passage success and running at 20 Hz on vehicle domain controllers.
flag: Closest match in this batch to RQ1, but 20 Hz (50 ms) is the only latency figure, the inspector is bundled with the game prior in the comparison (no inspector-only ablation), and it is also described as a training-time exploration aid.

title: Cooperative Event Triggered Control for Multi-Robot Systems with Collision Avoidance
evidence: Sec. 3: 'when the safety requirements are violated and the collision maybe happen, the mechanism of collision avoidance using QP will interfere the controller and give the safe control by minimal[ly modifying] the nominal controller'; 'When the safety requirements are satisfied, the mechanism of collision avoidance does not interfere the nominal controller'.
method: Event-triggered safety barrier certificates for second-order multi-robot systems: a triggering protocol on measurement error decides when a QP minimally modifies the nominal cooperative controller to enforce pairwise CBF constraints.
evaluation: One numerical simulation, four robots crossing a likely-collision area; snapshots at t=2, 5, 10 s show collision-free arrival; no metrics, baselines, ablations or inter-event-time statistics reported.
contribution: Combines event-triggered updating with safety barrier certificates so a QP intervenes on the nominal multi-robot controller only when collision is imminent, removing the need for continuous monitoring and communication.
flag: Right mechanism class (runtime QP safety filter with aperiodic triggering, which is relevant to jitter-aware interception) but the evaluation is a single four-robot qualitative simulation with no quantitative safety metric, baseline or ablation, so the v1.5 floor fails; authors themselves defer experimental validation to future work.

title: Coordinating Collision Avoidance Motions Using Distributed Guiding Vector Fields and Deadlock-Free Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec. III: "We intend to modify the nominal control quantity unom so that" the CBF constraints hold, with the controllers kept "as close as possible to their nominal controllers while satisfying the constraints of obstacle avoidance".
method: Distributed guiding vector fields supply nominal formation-navigation velocities; a CBF-QP minimally modifies them, and added "virtual obstacles" displace deadlock regions to preserve liveness.
evaluation: Ten-robot simulations over dense, dynamic and polygonal obstacles plus real-world three-wheeled omnidirectional robot trials; trajectory figures only - no quantitative metric, baseline or ablation anywhere.
contribution: Wraps distributed guiding vector fields in a CBF-QP that minimally revises nominal velocities, adding virtual obstacles that displace deadlock regions so formation navigation stays both safe and live in dense obstacle fields.
flag: Clean runtime safety filter over an explicit nominal controller, so criterion (a) is met, but the paper contains no tables and no numbers: only trajectory plots. No collision, distance or deadlock counts, no baseline, no ablation. Worth requeueing if an extended version with metrics appears.

title: Cyber-Physical GraphRAG: Safe, Real-Time, and Scalable Orchestration of Large-Scale Autonomous Fleets
evidence: "Topological Safety Firewall: A deterministic filtering mechanism that prevents unsafe agents from reaching the LLM reasoning layer" and "the graph layer ... enforces safety constraints deterministically filtering all candidates through validity-tier and policy checks before any dispatch command is issued" (Sec. I-C/I-E); sub-10 ms queries inside a <50 ms firewall budget (Sec. V-A/V-E).
method: HSK-GraphRAG: signal-weighted exponential decay over a temporal fleet knowledge graph plus a deterministic topological safety firewall gating LLM-proposed dispatch via validity-tier indexing and certification joins.
evaluation: 50 AMRs, simulated warehouse, 10 Hz telemetry; vs context-stuffing, vector RAG, Redis TTL; 0% ghost selection vs 24.5%/8.2%, 100% compliance over 200 adversarial trials, P99 7.7 ms.
contribution: A deterministic graph firewall gates LLM fleet-dispatch decisions, filtering stale, e-stopped or uncertified robots before execution at sub-10 ms query latency with zero ghost selections.
flag: Safety claims explicitly scoped to its own graph-based logical safety model; no physical collision outcome. The "world model" is a symbolic knowledge graph, not latent prediction. The 3 s staleness bound is derived from pallet-jack stopping distance - close to time-to-irreversibility reasoning but not modelled, so that gap cell was left off. No edge hardware reported.

title: Data-Driven Safety-Critical Control: Synthesizing Control Barrier Functions With Koopman Operators
evidence: Abstract: 'We propose to learn discrete-time Koopman operators of the closed-loop dynamics under a backup strategy. This approach replaces forward integration by a simple matrix multiplication'; Sec. V-A: 'Table I reports computation times ... Our approach reduced computation time by ~80%' for the online supervisory controller.
method: Learn an EDMD Koopman operator of closed-loop backup dynamics in a lifted space, with error bounds, to propagate backup trajectories and sensitivities inside a robust decentralized CBF supervisory QP.
evaluation: Robotarium robots and 3-quadrotor landing simulation; baselines ode45/CasADi forward integration plus scenario ablations; computation cut ~80%/95% per agent, zero collisions, ground impact speed 1.2 to under 0.3 m/s.
contribution: Learned Koopman operators replace online forward integration inside a backup-strategy CBF safety filter, cutting per-agent computation 80-95% and keeping multi-robot collision avoidance safe under unmodelled dynamics.
flag: Collision avoidance is demonstrated rather than rate-measured, so (c) fails the primacy test; the quantitative baselines are computation time and impact speed, which is what carries (d). Builds directly on the decentralized backup-CBF paper also in this batch (doi:10.1109/lcsys.2020.3000748) - possible overlapping-contribution pair. Table I's numeric cells did not extract from the PDF text.

title: Data-Driven Safety-Critical Flocking Control for Multi-Agent Systems With Unknown Dynamics Under Uncertain Environments
evidence: 'Comparing Figs. 3 and 6 reveals that the CBF safety filter introduces transient deviations in velocity and position during obstacle encounters'; 'average computation time per agent per time step was approximately 15 ms... well within the control frequency of 10 Hz used for the Crazyflie 2.0 UAV platform' (Sec. V-B, Remark 9).
method: DDLCBF: model-free pseudo-partial-derivative flocking controller on signed directed graphs plus Gaussian-process-learned stochastic control barrier functions, combined in a per-agent QP giving probabilistic safety without system or environment models.
evaluation: Numerical flocking simulations with three obstacles and a four-Crazyflie motion-capture testbed (500 mm clearance); comparison table against Trad. CBF, GP-CBF, MFAC-only reports only binary safety; 15 ms/agent/step on an i7 laptop.
contribution: Data-driven learning control barrier function framework that filters a model-free flocking controller for multi-agent systems with unknown dynamics, validated on a four-quadrotor indoor testbed.
flag: Table III ('Quantitative comparison of different methods') is an UNFILLED TEMPLATE - every RMSE, min-safe-distance and computation-time cell is a dash with the footnote 'to be filled after simulation with new topology'; safety is reported only as Yes/Violated, and Table IV sensitivity likewise gives binary safety. No numeric safety metric against the baselines, so the floor fails on a technicality the maintainer should verify against the final version. Flocking convergence is the primary claim, so (c) fails primacy; 15 ms is on a laptop, not edge hardware.

title: Decentralized Low-Energy Avoidance Control Framework for Multiple Mobile Agents Using Irregular Observations
evidence: Sec. IV: the self-triggering rule sets irregular observation intervals from relative distance and velocity so that an agent observes 'at least once before a collision takes place'; Sec. IV also makes the desired trajectory 'smoothly become constant when the agent is in conflict with another agent'.
method: Decentralized Lyapunov-based avoidance control with self-triggered, velocity-dependent observation intervals and detection radii; proven collision-free for arbitrarily many agents and proven free of Zeno behaviour.
evaluation: 100 random runs per team size (8-32 agents), four variants C1-C4 (C2-C4 equal prior methods); collisions (zero), completion time, path ratio, sensing-power indices; 2-3 iRobot Create 3 trials.
contribution: Self-triggered observation intervals derived from time-to-collision let agents sense neighbours as rarely as safety allows, cutting sensing power and conservatism while provably avoiding collisions.
flag: Closest batch analogue to RQ2: sampling intervals bounded by time-to-collision with a Zeno-freedom proof. But safety is proved rather than differentiated (zero collisions in all four variants) and the measured gains are energy and path efficiency; the avoidance action is an additive reactive term, not a veto gate.

title: Decentralized Robust Collision-Avoidance for Cooperative Multirobot Systems: A Gaussian Process-Based Control Barrier Function Approach
evidence: Abstract: 'a quadratic programming problem is formulated to obtain a controller that is minimally invasive to the nominal controller and satisfies the CBF and velocity constraints simultaneously'; Sec. VI: GPCCA avoids collisions in all trials 'while the nominal CBF-based approach only avoids collisions in 52% (58.2%) of the trials'.
method: Decentralized robust discrete-time CBF conditions for cooperative collision avoidance with Gaussian-process estimates of individual model uncertainty, solved per robot as a QP minimally modifying the nominal controller.
evaluation: MATLAB: 8-robot position swapping, 500 trials per nominal controller, plus formation task; vs nominal CBF and potential field: 100% collision-free vs 52%/58.2%; QP under 3.65 ms per robot-step.
contribution: A decentralized GP-robust control barrier function filter that keeps cooperative multirobot teams collision-free under learned model uncertainty where nominal CBF filters fail about half the time.
flag: (d) near-miss: per-step QP latency under 3.65 ms and average computation time are reported, but there is no explicit deadline or edge hardware.

title: Decentralized Runtime Enforcement for Robotic Swarms
evidence: Sec. 1 and 6: 'we expect to construct shields (to output actions that correct a property violation) on the two-level properties at runtime'; EXP_1 'The action of the swarm entering region C is suppressed'; Fig. 8/9 compare number of collisions for robotflocksim vs robotflocksim+RE.
method: Macro-micro runtime enforcement for robotic swarms: monitors generated from a hierarchical specification language, and D-time (discrete-time) enforcers that synthesise per-agent shields suppressing or inserting actions to restore swarm task sequence and collision-free properties.
evaluation: robotflocksim UAV swarm simulation, 80-200 UAVs at 2-12 m/s; baseline is the same platform without runtime enforcement; metric number of collisions (consistently reduced); overhead 0.01-1.21 s over 240-600 s tasks, 100 ms clock cycle, 3.1 GHz CPU.
contribution: Runtime enforcement for robotic swarms that generates agent shields from two-level specifications and corrects macro task-sequence and micro collision-free violations at runtime, measurably reducing swarm collisions.
flag: Successor to doi:10.1109/tr.2019.2923681 (same authors, cited) - treat the two as a monitoring/enforcing pair rather than independent evidence. Collision counts are only readable from Figs. 8-9 (no table), simulation only, and composed properties P1+P3+P4 are the nearest thing to a compositional test.

title: Deconfliction of Motion Paths With Traffic Inspired Rules
evidence: Sec. II-C/D: 'we will refer to u_hat_i as the nominal controller, i.e. how we would like to control our system ... In the following section we are going to provide a tool to keep the control u*_i safe when the linear inequality in (9) is not satisfied by the nominal controller', via a QP that minimally perturbs the nominal input.
method: Decentralised safety barrier certificates as a QP filter on each agent's nominal controller, extended with quasi-deadlock detection (acceleration/velocity/control thresholds) and a left/right direction-bias rotation of the nominal input to break head-on symmetry; bias of nearby humans is estimated online.
evaluation: Robotarium testbed, two robots swapping positions, four head-on configurations, plus 500 simulations comparing quasi-deadlock resolution against the original SBC formulation on arrival-time difference (60 s cap); mixed human-driven robot via joystick. Collision-freedom established by proof.
contribution: A direction-biased safety-barrier QP filter resolves head-on conflicts between robots and human-driven vehicles before either must come to a full stop, complying with local traffic conventions.
flag: Borderline E2: the 500-run baseline comparison measures arrival time and deadlock avoidance, not collision rate - collision-freedom is proven, never measured; the hardware demonstration is two robots and qualitative. Human driver is modelled as a benign peer whose bias is inferred, so (e) is not met despite the human-robot framing.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Driving Strategy for Avoidance of Chain Collisions and Its Safety Efficiency Analysis in Autonomous Vehicles
evidence: Abstract: 'we consider the problem of chain collision avoidance as a Markov Decision Process problem ... A reward function is being developed to deal with the challenge of multiple vehicle collision avoidance'; Sec. IV-D reports number of collisions per episode and an 88% success rate.
method: Chain-collision avoidance cast as an MDP with a hand-designed multi-vehicle collision reward and an LSTM/actor-critic perception network; policies trained with PPO, SAC and DDPG in Unity3D.
evaluation: Unity3D single- and multi-agent (4 vehicles) traffic, 5M steps / 24 h training; PPO vs SAC vs DDPG on collisions per episode, 88% success rate, rewards, episode length, value loss.
contribution: Casts chain-collision avoidance as an MDP with a multi-vehicle collision reward and compares three actor-critic algorithms on safety efficiency in single- and multi-agent Unity3D traffic.
flag: Weak for this review: safety lives in the training reward, so (a) explicitly fails and there is no runtime interception; the comparison is between RL algorithms rather than against a safety baseline or ablation, and most reported curves are training diagnostics. Maintainer may prefer exclude-E2.

title: Deliberative/Reactive Architecture of a Multirobot Patrol System Based on Supervisory Control Theory
evidence: Sec. II-A.3: 'By observing the plant events, the supervisor updates its states and enables or disables the controllable events and, therefore, its action on the plant can be considered reactive' - unsafe events requested by the deliberative layer are blocked before execution.
method: Hybrid deliberative/reactive architecture: modular supervisory-control-theory supervisors synthesised in Supremica disable unsafe controllable events; a deliberative heuristic layer chooses among the remaining enabled events.
evaluation: MATLAB plus V-REP, two robots and four patrol cells; four modes (Aleat, TCS aleat, TCS reg, TCS compl) compared on average/maximum cell idle time under sensing faults and battery discharge.
contribution: A supervisory-control reactive layer disables unsafe events for a two-robot patrol team while a deliberative heuristic layer minimises cell idle time under faults and battery discharge.
flag: Criterion (a) is clearly met (synthesised supervisor disables controllable events at runtime, including mutual exclusion over shared cells), but the only quantitative results are patrol idle times; safety is enforced by construction with no violation, collision or false-block rate reported, so the v1.5 evaluation floor fails. Worth keeping as a shielding-architecture citation.

title: Differentiable Model Predictive Safety for Heterogeneous Mobility at Urban Intersections
evidence: Sec. III-C, eq. (11): 'The final, safety-corrected action is given by u_t = clip(u~_t - eta*g_ato, U_i)' applied to the nominal action from the base RL policy, and 'the safety module not only corrects unsafe actions at runtime but also provides a rich, structured gradient signal'.
method: Encoder plus latent forward dynamics model unrolled H steps; differentiable safety critic max-pooled over the horizon (L-infinity risk); one backpropagated gradient step projects the RL policy's nominal action into a safer action.
evaluation: CARLA signal-free intersection with up to 10 AVs and 15 AMRs; baselines Vanilla/RS/AM-MAPPO plus ablations (no prediction, no gradient); total collisions 4.8% vs 18.5%, vehicle-robot 2.9%, success 81.6%, delay 14.2s vs AM-MAPPO's 18.2s; claimed small fraction of a 100ms control period on GPU.
contribution: DMPS backpropagates a differentiable safety critic through a learned latent dynamics rollout to correct each agent's action online, cutting mixed AV-robot intersection collisions well below action-masking baselines.
flag: Closest mechanism match in this batch (latent, non-generative world model plus runtime action correction over multi-agent state). Latency is only asserted - 'takes a small fraction of the 100ms control period' - never measured, and it runs on a GPU, so (d) and any latency/jitter claim are unverified; the corrector is co-trained with the policy.

title: Diffusion Models for Multi-target Adversarial Tracking
evidence: Sec. III: 'the goal of CADENCE is to estimate the joint trajectory of all agents p(tau_1..n | {d}_1..t)', using cross-attention across agents to generate joint multimodal track hypotheses.
method: CADENCE: cross-attention diffusion model generating joint multimodal trajectory hypotheses for multiple adversarial targets from sparse detections, with classifier-guided constraint sampling for motion and obstacle feasibility.
evaluation: Prison Escape (three detection rates) and Smuggler datasets plus new three-target sets; baselines VRNN, GrAMMI, GrAMMI w/o MI; ADE/minADE; constraint ablation cuts generated-track obstacle collisions 5%->0.64%.
contribution: Introduces a cross-attention diffusion tracker that reconstructs joint multi-target trajectories under sparse partial observability, improving displacement error over GrAMMI and enforcing motion constraints during sampling.
flag: protocol v1.6: included as world-model/predictor evidence on a predictive-accuracy metric with a baseline or ablation; not safety evidence, RQ5 capped at 2. Meets (b) but headline metrics are ADE/minADE accuracy; the only quantitative safety-shaped number is the obstacle-collision rate of generated hypotheses under the constraint-sampling ablation (5% vs 0.641%) - maintainer may count that and flip to include.

title: Direction Modulated Multi-agent Trajectory Prediction Based on Attention Mechanism
evidence: Abstract: "we propose DA-LSTM, a trajectory prediction method that integrates rule-based prior knowledge into neural network learning by cropping and filtering neighborhood information based on the relative relationship of 'agent orientation'".
method: A direction-based filtering rule prunes the Social-LSTM social tensor by neighbour orientation and visibility; the modulated tensor feeds an auto-encoder LSTM with a temporal attention mechanism.
evaluation: ETH and UCY pedestrian benchmarks, 8-frame observation and 12-frame prediction; comparators Vanilla-LSTM, Social-LSTM and a Dir-LSTM ablation; ADE/FDE only (DA-LSTM 0.34/0.45 on ETH); no safety metric.
contribution: Prunes the social tensor by neighbour orientation and visibility and adds temporal attention, lowering final displacement error on ETH and UCY relative to Social-LSTM while keeping interaction modelling non-generative.
flag: protocol v1.6: included as world-model/predictor evidence on a predictive-accuracy metric with a baseline or ablation; not safety evidence, RQ5 capped at 2. Criterion (b) is clearly met and the accuracy evaluation is sound (two benchmarks, three comparators including a Dir-LSTM ablation), but there is no quantitative safety metric at all - no collision, near-miss or hazard rate - so it fails the v1.5 evaluation floor. The maintainer may want an explicit rule for prediction-only (b) papers, since this is RQ1-relevant non-generative latent prediction over multi-agent state; also no latency, parameter count or hardware is reported.

title: Discovering Avoidable Planner Failures of Autonomous Vehicles using Counterfactual Analysis in Behaviorally Diverse Simulation
evidence: Sec. I/VI: 'Using large scale search, we generate, detect, and characterize dynamic scenarios leading to collisions' and 'we propose methods to distinguish between unavoidable and avoidable accidents', tested 'in complex multi-agent intersection scenarios'; Table II reports failure counts per policy set.
method: Scenario search over 50 behaviourally diverse RL traffic policies; collisions rewound by a 2 s reaction time and re-run under re-parameterised planner or a CMDP threat-function greedy-safe policy to classify avoidability.
evaluation: CARLA-free custom intersection simulator, 15,000 runs per scene (2 scenes); Diverse vs LessDiverse policy-set baseline; metrics = #failures and avoidable/unavoidable split (153 vs 100; 235 vs 23). No latency/hardware.
contribution: Counterfactual re-simulation after a rewind separates avoidable from unavoidable multi-agent collisions, turning collision search into planner-specific defect feedback.
flag: Offline test-generation, not runtime interception: the CMDP greedy-safe policy is a counterfactual replacement policy evaluated post-hoc, so (a) is not met. Avoidability rewind (2 s reaction time) is the closest thing to a time-to-irreversibility construct and may interest RQ2.

title: Distributed Collision-Free Control of MASs by Combining Reinforcement Learning With Filtered Position Barrier Certificates and Applications
evidence: Abstract: "The proposed FPBC is used in a Quadratic Program (QP)-based safety filter that enforces collision avoidance on the actions generated by a RL controller"; Sec. V-A2: "FPBC achieves zero constraint violations across all tested parameter sets, significantly outperforming the HOCBF method in terms of safety constraint satisfaction".
method: Filtered-position model reduces double-integrator collision avoidance to a first-order CBF (FPBC) used as a QP safety filter on single-agent-trained PPO actions, plus a three-case perturbation scheme for deadlock resolution.
evaluation: 2D/3D crossing simulations with 16-128 agents (i7-13700K, RTX 4060Ti); baselines HOCBF [19],[20] and with/without deadlock resolution; optimisation success rate (HOCBF down to 11.19%), constraint violations, minimum inter-agent distance; 4 UGV and 4 UAV experiments computed onboard with NOKOV motion capture.
contribution: A filtered-position barrier certificate makes a first-order QP filter sufficient to keep RL-driven multi-agent motion collision-free, with zero violations and far better feasibility than high-order CBFs.
flag: Closest match in the batch to a runtime safety filter evaluated on a hazard rate against a baseline, with a deadlock-resolution ablation and real hardware. No latency measurement despite onboard execution, so (d) is not met; UGV and UAV settings are both physical, so this is not cross-domain evaluation.

title: Distributed Hierarchical Shared Control for Flexible Multirobot Maneuver Through Dense Undetectable Obstacles
evidence: Sec. I/III-B: 'It is assumed that the obstacles can only be detected by humans but not by robots. Thus, the human operator needs to intervene to prevent collisions', with motion intervention to 'steer individual robots away from immediate danger' (Abstract).
method: Two-layer distributed shared control: intention-field networks convert operator inputs into virtual control signals for group management and motion intervention; a lower-layer blending law resolves human-versus-autonomous-formation conflicts, with IOS proof.
evaluation: 22-participant usability study, game-like teleoperation of a 5x5 robot formation, static and dynamic scenes, vs affine formation controller: collision cost 56.0 vs 77.2 (p<0.05); outdoor four-robot demo.
contribution: A distributed shared-control interface lets a few operators intervene in a large robot formation, significantly reducing collision cost versus affine formation teleoperation in a 22-participant study.
flag: Hazards are robot-obstacle rather than inter-agent, so (c) fails the primacy test; the intervention is weighted blending of human and autonomous inputs, not a veto; human overrides automation rather than automation deferring to the human.

title: Distributed Kinematic Control and Trajectory Scaling for Multi-Manipulator Systems in Presence of Human Operators
evidence: Sec. IV: 'Robots are asked to track the nominal trajectory as long as f > f_min; in the case the nominal trajectory would lead to f <= f_min, then the nominal parameter s_n(t) is scaled. Finally, if no scaling is found to meet the above constraint, the violation of the nominal path is allowed until the safety condition is recovered.'
method: Decentralised multi-manipulator work-cell where watcher robots track the operator and worker robots run a distributed observer of the cell state; a distance-and-derivative safety function drives time-scaling of the nominal cooperative trajectory, falling back to impedance path deformation.
evaluation: Single numerical simulation: 3 Comau Smart Six workers on mobile bases, 2 camera watchers, 1 operator, cooperative transport; plots show the safety function saturating at f_min during scaling and an impedance phase from t=36.4 s. No baseline, no aggregate metrics, no hardware.
contribution: Watcher robots feed a distributed safety function that time-scales a multi-manipulator cooperative trajectory, slowing rather than re-planning it to keep a human operator safe inside the cell.
flag: Trajectory scaling is a real runtime filter on the nominal trajectory (slow-to-halt, then path deformation), but validation is one simulation run with no baseline, no ablation and no aggregate safety metric, so it fails the v1.5 floor. Human is treated as an obstacle to be avoided, not an authority deferred to, so (e) is not met.

title: Distributed Sparse Bayesian Control Barrier Function and Its Application to Safe Persistent Exploration
evidence: Sec. V: 'SBCBF acts as a safety filter, minimally modifying the nominal control input' derived from persistent-coverage control; collision rate then measured in Secs. VI-B and VI-C.
method: Each robot trains a local sparse Bayesian classifier on its LiDAR data, exchanges relevance vectors, fuses them into a shared safety map, and enforces a distributed CBF-QP safety filter.
evaluation: Sim (4 robots, ten 60 s runs): collision and coverage rate vs centralized SBCBF, plus SVM/GP safety-map baselines; hardware: two TurtleBot3 with LiDAR, ten runs.
contribution: Distributed sparse Bayesian classifiers fused across a robot team give each agent a CBF safety filter over a shared learned safety map, cutting collisions versus a centralized variant.
flag: Hazards are static obstacles only - no inter-robot CBF - so (c) primacy is not met and inclusion rests on (a); compute reported as training time, no latency or platform figures.

title: Distributed barrier function-enabled human-in-the-loop control for multi-robot systems
evidence: Sec. I: safety 'is enforced using a computationally efficient implementation that leverages quadratic programs such that a pre-designed nominal controller is minimally modified to satisfy safety requirements'; Sec. III-F: 'umix,i = uHIL + unom,i ... will then be passed through the distributed QP (7) as the new nominal controller to obtain the final controller.'
method: Distributed CBF-induced QP, solved locally via an auxiliary consensus variable, merges collision, connectivity, arena and human-avoidance constraints into one through a smooth minimum approximation, plus a failure-region fix.
evaluation: Five Nexus 4WD robots, on-board Jetson TX2 or Intel NUC, ROS, vineyard lab; two human-in-the-loop scenarios; no baseline or ablation; positive barrier traces and nominal-vs-QP input difference.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; non-generative inference; edge deployment
contribution: A distributed CBF quadratic program folds collision, connectivity, arena and human-avoidance constraints into one and filters either a formation controller or live human commands on five vineyard robots.
flag: Strong on mechanism - runtime filter over a nominal controller, multi-robot, on-board Jetson TX2 - but the whole evaluation is qualitative barrier traces from two demonstration runs with no baseline, ablation or quantitative safety metric, so it sits below the v1.5 floor. The human-in-the-loop is command injection filtered for safety, not automation deferring to a person, so (e) and the human-handoff cell were not credited.

title: DoS Attack Detection and Resilient Control in Platoon of Smart Vehicles
evidence: "After detection of DoS attack over the communication network among vehicles in platoon by two incremental counters based on Algorithm 1, the amount of delay is estimated. Afterward, by applying Algorithm 2, the identified attacked vehicle is ceased or returned to consensus system again" (Sec. VI, Simulation Results).
method: DoS attack modelled as a fixed communication delay; two incremental counters detect and estimate it; a switched resilient controller isolates then re-admits the attacked vehicle, with Lyapunov-Krasovskii/LMI stability proof.
evaluation: One simulated 4-vehicle homogeneous platoon, third follower attacked, 10 s critical-zone bound; position/velocity trajectory plots only; no baseline, no ablation, no quantitative safety metric.
contribution: Detects DoS-induced delay in a vehicle platoon with incremental counters and isolates then re-admits the attacked vehicle through a switched resilient consensus controller with LMI stability conditions.
flag: Illustrative single case study only: no baseline or ablation and no quantitative safety metric, so the v1.5 evaluation floor fails. Criterion (a) borderline - the interception isolates a communication link, not a nominal action. Explicit 10 s critical delay beyond which the attacked agent cannot be retrieved may interest RQ2.

title: Drones in the Big City: Autonomous Collision Avoidance for Aerial Delivery Services
evidence: Sec. IV-C: 'UTSim calls SingleDrone() whenever an obstacle is within a drone detection radius. SingleDrone() checks if a collision is detected and the drone is not detouring', then halves velocity and sets a detour angle, terminating the detour when the relative-velocity projection clears.
method: Three geometric onboard avoidance strategies (SingleDrone, MultiDrone, SpeedDrone) that, on detecting a predicted collision inside the detection radius, override cruise with a velocity reduction and detour angle.
evaluation: Modified UTSim urban delivery simulation, fleets up to 200 drones, constant and Poisson arrivals; baselines DoNothing, Random, Rightward, two geometric SOTA; collision rate, successful trips; Markov-chain model.
contribution: Shows aviation-style and random detour rules increase collisions at urban drone-delivery densities, while geometric detours cut collision rates to 0-2% at the cost of fewer completed trips.
flag: Simulation plus Markov-chain modelling only, no hardware or latency figures; strongest evidence in this batch on the safety-versus-throughput trade-off (RQ5), with DoNothing as an explicit do-nothing baseline.

title: Dynamic Computational Resource Allocation for Ensuring Stability of Remote Edge-based Controlled Multi-agent Systems
evidence: Sec. III-B: 'rc(t) = K(tau_e - tau_rtt(t - tau_u(t)))... adjusts CPU shares to compensate for communication delays'; Sec. IV-B keeps round-trip time below the maximum allowable delay tau_max after 0.18-0.20 s delay injection.
method: Edge-offloaded centralized NMPC for multiple UAVs with agent-to-agent separation constraints; second-order polynomial regression predicts solver complexity and a delay-feedback law allocates Kubernetes CPU shares to bound round-trip time.
evaluation: Three-server k8s edge cluster, CNMPC for 1-5 UAVs at horizons 10 and 20; measured network, solver and round-trip delays against tau_max plus CPU shares; artificial delay injected; no baseline.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; latency/jitter aware; edge deployment
contribution: Dynamic CPU allocation driven by measured round-trip delay keeps an edge-offloaded multi-UAV NMPC inside its maximum allowable delay, tying computational resources directly to closed-loop stability.
flag: Best fit in this batch for the latency/jitter and edge-deployment cells, but no baseline or ablation and no safety outcome (no collision or separation-violation rate); the 'robots switch to fallback onboard actions' beyond tau_max is cited to prior work, not evaluated here.

title: Dynamic Data Integration for Resilience to Sensor Attacks in Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: Abstract: 'the proposed strategy reduces the effects of attacks not only on the affected agent, but also prevents the propagation of the attack over the remaining agents', using CUSUM detection on EKF residues in a six-robot formation.
method: Per-agent CUSUM test on extended-Kalman-filter residues detects sensor attacks; per-sensor confidence values give a convex-combination trusted measurement that is fed to the formation controller in real time.
evaluation: Six e-puck2 robots in leader-follower formation, two communication graphs; stealthy, odometry and camera attacks on one or several agents; normalised formation KPI with versus without mitigation; 0.1 s step.
contribution: Trust-weighted fusion of redundant sensors, driven by a CUSUM detector on EKF residues, keeps an attacked robot formation near nominal behaviour and stops attack propagation to neighbours.
flag: Criterion (a) fails on the strict reading: the runtime monitor overrides the measurement feeding the controller, not a nominal decision before execution. Included on (c) (cascading failure across agents, measured with and without mitigation). The safety metric is a normalised formation-deviation KPI rather than a collision or violation rate, and false-alarm rate is only used for threshold tuning - maintainer may want to check this against the floor.

title: Dynamic Distributed Coordination Schemes for Multi-Mobile Robot Systems Under Collision Avoidance Constraints
evidence: Problem 1 (Sec. III): "locally determine, at each time step t and for each agent i, a suitable command signal gi(t) that is the best approximation of ri(t) and such that its application does not lead to constraint violations" - the turn-based command governor supervises each agent's nominal reference at runtime.
method: Turn-based distributed command governor supervising nominal references of LTI closed-loop vehicles; non-convex collision-avoidance constraints recast as an MIQP, safe-area conditions for plug-and-play join/leave, token-based turn protocol.
evaluation: MATLAB/YALMIP/Gurobi simulations up to 18 agents in confined space; dynamic vs static coupling constraints compared on measured CPU time and exchanged packets; token protocol vs centralised minimal graph colouring over 2800 graphs; no collision or violation metric.
contribution: Extends the turn-based distributed command governor with non-convex collision-avoidance and safe-area conditions, enabling provably collision-free plug-and-play reconfiguration of mobile-robot formations.
flag: Genuine runtime interceptor (a reference/command governor between nominal reference and plant) with formal collision-free PnP theorems, but every measured outcome is computation or communication cost - CPU time, packet counts, graph-colouring error - plus illustrative patrolling/PnP scenarios, so the quantitative-safety-metric floor is not met. Worth a second look if the maintainer accepts formal results without a safety baseline; extends Tedesco et al. 2019 and the authors' preliminary study [33].

title: Dynamic Residual Safe Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Agent Safety-Critical Scenarios Decision-Making
evidence: Sec. III-C, Def. 2: 'pi_hybrid = pi_task + alpha(s)(pi_safe - pi_task)' where 'alpha(s) is the safety weighting factor. It is dynamically adjusted according to a real-time risk quantification function' using TTC and PET against a preset threshold tau_risk.
method: A lightweight 3-layer safety policy (27% of the task model's parameters) residually corrects the task policy's action, gated by TTC/PET risk; a multi-agent dynamic conflict-zone graph quantifies coupling risk; risk-aware prioritised replay rebalances data.
evaluation: SUMO scenario set built from Bench2Drive (LVEB, OPI, RPC, IJ), 5 seeds, GCN-based CDQN/CD3QN/CPPO baselines plus a DRS-PPO vs CPPO ablation; collision rate reduced 92.17% on average (zero in LVEB) with speed, acceleration and comfort metrics.
contribution: DRS-RL residually corrects a driving policy with a lightweight TTC/PET-gated safety policy over a multi-agent conflict-zone graph, cutting collisions by 92% in safety-critical multi-vehicle scenarios.
flag: (a) is borderline-strict: interception is a blended residual action rather than a veto, halt or defer, and the safety policy is co-trained with the task policy via weighted losses. 'Millisecond-level decision-making demands' is motivation only - no latency is measured, with parameter count (27%) used as the efficiency proxy.

title: E-CNMPC: Edge-Based Centralized Nonlinear Model Predictive Control for Multiagent Robotic Systems
evidence: Abstract: 'The data processing procedure for the time critical application of controlling the robots in a centralized manner, is offloaded to the edge machine ... while the latency remains bounded in desired values'; measured mean solver execution 100.6 ms and mean RTT 325-449 ms (Sec. III).
method: Centralized nonlinear MPC for a multi-robot swarm with hard inter-agent minimum-distance constraints, containerized and offloaded to an edge Kubernetes cluster to keep latency bounded.
evaluation: Four TurtleBots with Vicon and edge Kubernetes cluster; horizon (20/40/60) and tolerance ablations, two network setups; minimum inter-robot distance, solver time, uplink/downlink/RTT, CPU usage.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; latency/jitter aware; edge deployment
contribution: Demonstrates that offloading centralized nonlinear MPC for four ground robots to an edge Kubernetes cluster keeps inter-agent collision constraints satisfiable at horizons onboard computers cannot afford.
flag: Collision avoidance is a hard constraint inside the NMPC, so (a) and (c) are not met; proof-of-concept with no external baseline - safety evidence is min-distance traces plus the observation that a 20-step horizon made robots 'crash with each other'.

title: Ellipsoid Tether Model for Collision Avoidance in a Fleet of ROVs - Summary and Extension
evidence: Abstract: "we propose a guarantee ellipsoid model of the ROV's tether and its obstacles to perform a collision avoidance method, adapted for a fleet of ROVs"; Sec. VIII-A reports only illustrative runs and concedes "collisions can occurs (red ellipsoids in the videos) like in scenario exposed in Figures 9b".
method: Guaranteed ellipsoid enclosure of each ROV tether and obstacles; reactive repelling potential field, bypass paths and anchor-to-vehicle distance (leash) adjustment for entanglement-free fleet navigation.
evaluation: Matlab 2024a simulations with one to three ROVs and several obstacles, sampling time 1 s; qualitative trajectory figures and three videos; no baseline, no collision or violation rate, no timing.
contribution: A guaranteed ellipsoid tether model lets a fleet of tethered ROVs avoid entanglement using only attachment-point positions and tether length, demonstrated in qualitative Matlab scenarios.
flag: Qualitative demonstration only - no quantitative safety metric and no baseline or ablation, so the (c) primacy test cannot be assessed; the text itself reports collisions in plane-constrained and three-tether cases. Self-described "summary and extension" of the authors' earlier study [23], so check for duplication with that record.

title: EnterpriseAI: A Multi-Agent Autonomous System for Industrial Supervision and Trade Compliance with Rag-Based Regulatory Grounding
evidence: Sec. V: the deterministic governance engine 'functions as an intercepting layer that validates agent outputs against eleven predefined compliance and safety rules in real time'; if any rule is false 'the output is either blocked, modified, or escalated', and a sanctions match 'results in immediate transaction blocking'.
method: Eight LangGraph agents under a hierarchical supervisor with structure-aware RAG over regulatory PDFs; a deterministic eleven-rule boolean governance kernel intercepts every agent output to block, redact, escalate and hash-log it.
evaluation: 500 queries on local LLaMA-3-8B: 150 governance cases (100% sanctions detection, 97.3% PII redaction), hallucination 2.4% with RAG vs 15.8% without, 98% LOTO violation detection, 12 ms governance latency.
contribution: Multi-agent industrial-supervision and trade-compliance system whose deterministic eleven-rule governance kernel intercepts every LLM agent output in 12 ms, blocking, redacting or escalating unsafe and non-compliant recommendations.
flag: Strong (a)/(e) match and a rare measured 12 ms interception latency, plus a human-escalation rule. Weaknesses: governance numbers come from 150 self-designed cases with no comparator (only the with/without-RAG hallucination contrast is ablative), no adversarial prompt-injection testing, and the prose is garbled in places. Cross-domain evaluation is NOT claimable: industrial supervision here is log and document analysis, not a physical acting system.

title: Event-Triggered Control for Safety-Critical Systems With Unknown Dynamics
evidence: Sec. VI-C: 'the safe merging constraint between i and i-1 is not satisfied with the time-driven method ... The safe merging constraint for i and i-1 is guaranteed when using the event-driven approach.'
method: Adaptive affine dynamics updated from real-time sensor error states, high-order CBF/CLF constraints, and an event-triggering rule with a derived condition guaranteeing CBF satisfaction between QP solves.
evaluation: MATLAB: robot control, adaptive cruise control, traffic merging; vs time-driven CBF-QP; safe-set forward invariance, about 50% fewer QPs, each QP/LP under 0.01 s, 20/100 Hz sampling.
contribution: Event-triggered CBF control with adaptive affine dynamics keeps safety for multiagent systems with unknown dynamics while halving the number of quadratic programs versus time-driven solving.
flag: Borderline: the CBF-QP is the controller, not a filter on an upstream nominal decision, so strict (a) fails; safety evidence is forward-invariance plots against a time-driven baseline rather than a violation rate, so E2 is arguable.

title: Fast Decentralized Multi-Agent Collision Avoidance Based on Safe-Reachable Sets
evidence: Sec. IV-B: 'The makespan, defined as the time elapsed from the start of the process to the end, is used to compare the two methods... Both methods guarantee safety, but our SRS approach achieves an average improvement of 16.64% (size 10), 17.79% (size 20), and 15.58% (size 30) in the makespan.'
method: Safe-reachable sets give positions reachable collision-free under any admissible neighbour control; each agent solves an online convex program for the reachable point nearest its goal, with safety and convergence proofs.
evaluation: Single-integrator simulations, 3-30 agents, CVXPY on 2.3 GHz i7; baselines CBF- and BVC-based controllers; compared metrics average makespan (10 runs per size) and deadlock; safety only as barrier plots.
contribution: Distributed safe-reachable sets give provably collision-free single-integrator navigation that avoids the deadlocks of CBF controllers and cuts makespan by roughly 16% against buffered-Voronoi baselines.
flag: Collision avoidance is the controller's own objective, not a filter over a nominal decision, so (a) fails; the outcomes actually compared against baselines are makespan and deadlock, which is the explicit E1 planner clause, and (c)'s primacy test fails. It would also fail the E2 floor since no quantitative safety metric is reported against a baseline.

title: Fault-Resilience Role Engine for an Autonomous Cooperative Multi-Robot System using E-CARGO
evidence: Sec. IV: 'the Bayesian consensus algorithm can detect faults and call the central computer for a new role assignment' - detection triggers role re-planning rather than an execution-time veto; Table 1 reports only smoothness and reliability cost.
method: Extended E-CARGO role engine: centralised group role assignment plus decentralised factor-graph (Gaussian-process trajectory) Bayesian consensus that updates agent reliability and requests reassignment on fault.
evaluation: Python/GPMP2 simulation; Test 1 compares role-based against task-based collaboration on average jerk and reliability cost (three robots); Test 2 is one qualitative fault-recovery figure (four robots).
contribution: A role-based fault-resilience engine uses factor-graph Bayesian consensus among robots to flag unreliable agents and request central role reassignment during multi-robot path execution.
flag: Fails (a) strictly (fault detection triggers role reassignment, not an execution-time override) and fails (c) primacy (measured outcomes are jerk and reliability cost, no hazard rate); the fault-resilience test is a single qualitative figure, so it would also fail the E2 floor. A human 'part of the central unit to verify the re-evaluation process' is mentioned but never evaluated.

title: Fault-Tolerant Cooperative Driving at Signal-Free Intersections
evidence: Sec. I: 'vehicles around the failed vehicle may not have sufficient braking distance to stop, which may result in a chain collision between multiple vehicles'; Sec. V-D reports the average collision rate over 1000 simulations per parameter setting.
method: Eight-step rule-based fault-tolerant cooperative driving model that sizes required inter-vehicle safety distances against sudden vehicle breakdown and reschedules remaining vehicles after a failure.
evaluation: MATLAB signal-free intersection over arrival rates; conservative-driving baseline; delay, throughput, speed, headway; collision rate over 1000 runs; sensitivity to fault braking rate and detection lag.
contribution: Provides a fault-tolerant cooperative driving strategy for signal-free intersections that prevents chain collisions when one vehicle fails while cutting delay versus always-conservative driving.
flag: Safety distance is a rule inside the cooperative planner, not a runtime veto layer, and traffic efficiency is co-primary, so (c) is borderline; the detection-lag sensitivity (0.5-2 s estimate vs true 1.5 s) is the jitter-relevant part.

title: Finite-Horizon Shield for Path Planning Ensuring Safety/Co-Safety Specifications and Security Policies
evidence: Abstract/Sec. I: 'we propose an enforcement mechanism referred to as a finite-horizon shield. This mechanism modifies the path computed by the planner as small as possible to satisfy the safety/co-safety specifications and security policy under the leaked information'; 'A shield is attached to a system... It monitors the inputs and outputs of the system and modifies incorrect outputs to correct outputs.'
method: Shield takes a planner's pre-planned path and, once leaked information is revealed at runtime, computes a minimally modified path satisfying LTLf safety/co-safety specs and a hyperLTLf opacity policy via SMT.
evaluation: Grid path-planning simulations (15x15, horizon 25; 6x6 upward for timing), Z3 on 1.8 GHz quad-core; baseline security-aware planning; metrics computation time and optional-spec satisfaction count; safety holds by construction.
contribution: A finite-horizon shield minimally rewrites a planner's path at runtime so it still satisfies LTLf safety/co-safety specifications and a hyperLTLf opacity policy once leaked information is revealed.
flag: Textbook runtime shield - criterion (a) met in the strict sense and the shield-vs-replanning timing comparison speaks to RQ5 - but it is a single-robot path planner with no multi-agent, latency-budget or handoff aspect (E4 is arguable), and the only quantitative comparisons are computation time and optional-spec satisfaction, not a safety metric. Maintainer may still want it as a shielding/formal-methods baseline.

title: From Crowd Motion Prediction to Robot Navigation in Crowds
evidence: Sec. IV-A: a joint state prediction model f takes the joint states of n agents and predicts their future states, and Sec. I: 'We integrate the S-GAN as a dynamics model into a standard MPC architecture and deploy it on a self-balancing robot.'
method: S-GAN multi-agent trajectory prediction used as the dynamics model inside a sampling-based MPC, deployed on a self-balancing ballbot and compared with constant-velocity prediction.
evaluation: Gazebo/ORCA simulation plus 10-20 real trials per algorithm in three crowd conditions; baselines CV, CVN, S-GAN-1/20; ADE/FDE, min-distance Safety, time-to-goal; 10 Hz control loop.
contribution: Demonstrates that a state-of-the-art multi-agent motion predictor transfers in accuracy but not in navigation safety or efficiency, performing indistinguishably from constant-velocity prediction on a real crowd-navigation robot.
flag: Criterion (b) only: prediction sits inside the MPC cost, so no runtime interception; Safety (min distance) is co-primary with time efficiency, so (c) fails the primacy test.

title: Fuzzing Large Language Model Agents: A Taxonomy, Engineering Framework, and Evaluation Protocol
evidence: 'This paper presents a taxonomy and engineering framework for fuzz-testing LLM-based agents'; the study uses 'four scenarios, five seed tasks per scenario, five mutations per seed, three mutation strategies... 900 executed trajectories' against a single agent simulator, with multi-agent fuzzing listed only as an open problem (Abstract, Sec. 6.3, Sec. 3.5).
method: Taxonomy and engineering framework for agent fuzzing: structured perturbation of instructions, retrieved context, memory, tool parameters and environment feedback, with sandboxed execution, runtime logging, behavioural coverage feedback and risk scoring.
evaluation: 900 sandboxed trajectories over file-management, RAG, email and database scenarios; rule-based mutation baseline ASR 6.67% vs semantics-aware 38.00% and state-guided 62.67%; also UAR, TCR, RR, token cost.
contribution: Taxonomy, engineering workflow and metric protocol for trajectory-level fuzz testing of tool-using LLM agents, with a 900-trajectory pilot comparing rule-based, semantics-aware and state-guided mutation.
flag: Fails (c) on the primacy test: single-agent trajectory testing, multi-agent message fuzzing is only a taxonomy dimension and discussion item. 'Runtime monitoring' here is a test oracle inside a sandbox, not a mechanism that can override execution, so (a) fails. Also arguably E3 (taxonomy/protocol with extensive comparison tables of prior work). Author caveats that ASR values 'are not estimates of vulnerability rates for production systems' because the subject is a seeded agent simulator, not a real LLM agent.

title: GPU-Accelerated Resilient Control: Experimental Validation and Performance Benchmarking for Autonomous Systems
evidence: Sec. III-B: progressive fault injection during training 'encourages policies to develop inherent robustness rather than requiring separate fault detection modules' - robustness is learned offline and nothing intercepts actions at execution time.
method: FAROC: PPO multi-agent policies trained with progressive random agent-dropout fault injection (0-30%), then structured pruning to 50% sparsity and INT8 post-training quantisation for edge inference.
evaluation: Five-agent cooperative navigation, NVIDIA Quadro P4000, five seeds: success 84.7% vs 61.5% baseline at 20% fault rate, 2.8x faster recovery, inference 10.2 ms to 3.4 ms (294 Hz).
contribution: Trains multi-agent navigation policies with progressive fault injection and compresses them to 3.4 ms inference, improving task success under 20% agent failure by 23 points over a nominal baseline.
flag: No runtime interception at all - the paper explicitly substitutes training-time robustness for fault detection, so (a) fails; the measured outcome is task success and recovery under agent dropout, not a hazard, collision or violation rate, so (c) fails the primacy test and (d) is about the nominal controller, not a safety decision. Edge deployment is claimed but all timings are on a workstation GPU; headline incident statistics look loosely sourced.

title: Generating Adversarial Driving Scenarios in High-Fidelity Simulators
evidence: Abstract/Sec. VI: 'we propose to automate the process using Bayesian Optimization to generate adversarial self-driving scenarios ... and increase the risk of collision with simulated pedestrians and vehicles'; 'we measure the number of crashes and the magnitude of impact for each of these three methods'.
method: Bayesian optimisation with a Gaussian-process surrogate and expected improvement over a hierarchical parametrisation of NPC pedestrian/vehicle waypoint trajectories, minimising the ego policy's cost-to-go in CARLA; DAgger fine-tuning on found scenarios.
evaluation: CARLA, 200 function evaluations x 3 seeds, 3 scenario types; baselines random search and cross-entropy method; metrics min cost-to-go, crash count, impact magnitude (~1.4x higher than baselines). No latency/hardware.
contribution: Bayesian optimisation over NPC trajectory parameters finds high-impact crash scenarios for a driving policy faster than random search or CEM, and retraining on them reduces accidents.
flag: Multi-agent only nominally: the quantitative baseline comparisons use a single adversarial NPC (one pedestrian or one vehicle); the mixed pedestrian+vehicle multi-agent case (Sec. VI-C) is qualitative only. Offline test generation, no runtime mechanism.

title: Geometry-Based Cooperative Conflict Resolution for Multi-AAV Combining Heading and Speed Control
evidence: Sec. V-A: 'The first one is the safety rate alpha_safe, which is defined as the ratio of the minimum distance between the AAV and its neighbors during flight to its safety radius'; Sec. I: each AAV generates conflict-avoidance maneuvers that displace its nominal path when a conflict is predicted inside the look-ahead window tau.
method: Decentralised geometry-based conflict resolution: pairwise safe-separation constraints linearised by space mapping, right-side consensus rule, constraint decoupling, conflict-criticality ranking, optimisation minimising added heading/speed cost.
evaluation: Roundabout and two-circle scenarios with 6-40 AAVs vs eCCA and RVO; metrics minimum safety rate, max deviation, additional flight distance, conflict iterations; communication-delay robustness; criticality-selection ablation.
contribution: Decentralised geometric conflict resolution that holds 40 AAVs above safe separation with less deviation and additional flight distance than eCCA and RVO, and degrades gracefully under state-information delay.
flag: Reads as a reactive conflict-resolution planner rather than a filter over an external policy, so (a) is arguable; efficiency (additional consumption) is a co-primary objective; simulation only, no computation-time or hardware report.

title: Governed Agentic AI for Software Platforms: A Reference Architecture for Safe Autonomy at Scale
evidence: Guarded Execution Layer: 'Unauthorized or out-of-scope actions are blocked at this layer even if they pass earlier reasoning stages... blocked actions trigger escalation to human review', plus execution-time revalidation of preconditions (Sec. IV-D).
method: Four-layer governance control plane for enterprise LLM agents: intent validation, policy-aware planning, guarded execution via allow-listed adapters with execution-time precondition revalidation, telemetry/rollback, tiered bounded autonomy.
evaluation: Prototype, 1,000 agent action attempts (rollout/triage) with injected invalid actions; metrics policy-eval latency (median/P95), invalid-action blocking, human interventions per 100 actions vs Advisory tier; no numeric values reported.
contribution: Governance-first reference architecture that converts LLM agent outputs into proposals gated by deterministic policy evaluation, allow-listed execution and tiered human approval in enterprise software platforms.
flag: Metrics and an Advisory baseline are defined but NO numeric results are reported anywhere ('overhead on the order of tens to low hundreds of milliseconds', 'blocked the majority of invalid actions', 'decreased materially'); no tables. Authors state 'this paper focuses on a single governed agent for clarity' - multi-agent policy conflict is future work, so (c) fails. Architecture itself is a close conceptual match to the review's approval-gate framing if the maintainer wants it as background.

title: Guaranteed Obstacle Avoidance for Multi-Robot Operations With Limited Actuation: A Control Barrier Function Approach
evidence: Abstract: 'A decentralized supervisory controller is synthesized based on control barrier functions (CBF) that guarantees obstacle avoidance with limited actuation capability'; Sec. II-A: CBFs use 'a supervisory controller that keeps the system safe with minimum intervention' over the legacy controller.
method: Backup-strategy CBF: each agent forward-simulates a braking backup trajectory to certify an implicit control-invariant set, and a decentralized QP minimally modifies the nominal controller; broadcasting selects among multiple backup strategies.
evaluation: Robotarium hardware, 3 and 6 differential-drive robots patrolling, plus 17-dim quadrotor ROS/OSQP simulation; outcome reported is zero collisions and trajectory traces only, with no rates, baseline comparison or timings.
contribution: Decentralized backup-strategy control barrier functions let each robot override its nominal controller with a small QP, guaranteeing collision and obstacle avoidance under actuation limits without agent-to-agent communication.
flag: Architecturally a direct match (decentralized runtime safety filter with braking backup policies) and a plausible baseline the maintainer may want anyway, but the evaluation is a formal guarantee plus qualitative demonstration: no quantitative safety metric against a baseline or ablation, and no computation timings, so the v1.5 floor fails. Companion of the Koopman paper in this batch (doi:10.1109/lcsys.2020.3046159), which reuses this framework.

title: Guardrail-First Architecture for Multi-Agent Systems: Typed Rails as First-Class Connectors
evidence: Sec. III-C: 'A ComplianceType rail checks GDPR predicates before execution. If the predicate... is true, the call proceeds; otherwise, PolicyAction A replaces sensitive fields with masked placeholders'; Sec. IV-C reports the Safety Incident Rate falling from 0.128 to 0.068 (47%, p < 0.01).
method: Typed Rails as first-class architectural connectors on every agent-agent and agent-tool edge, each a tuple of type, predicate, evidence and policy action, enforced by a policy engine with a cryptographic evidence store.
evaluation: Controlled enterprise-style MAS, baseline versus GFA; Safety Incident Rate, Policy Recall (0.62 to 0.81), Task Success Rate (88 to 91%), 6.8% latency overhead, Time-to-Unsafe-Call survival (13.1 to 18.1 min); plus stakeholder interviews.
contribution: Embeds policy, capability and semantic guardrails into multi-agent architecture as typed connectors, cutting unsafe tool invocations by 47% with 6.8% latency overhead and full audit traceability.
flag: Evaluation is opaque: no task set, agent count, LLM, number of runs or trial protocol is reported anywhere, yet p-values and confidence intervals are given - treat the quantitative claims with caution. Time-to-Unsafe-Call survival analysis is the closest thing in this batch to a time-to-irreversibility measure and may be worth citing for RQ2 even though it measures hazard onset, not recoverability. Text reads as heavily machine-paraphrased.

title: HalluChain: Measuring and Controlling Cascade Hallucination Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines
evidence: Sec. IV-G: 'HalluFirewall stands at the point of every agent interaction in the pipeline where it blocks outputs from being used as inputs by the next agent'; Table IV reports linear-pipeline HPM@4 falling from 5.50-6.20 to 1.65-1.95, a 66-68% reduction.
method: Four-stage inter-agent verification gate: TF-IDF/logistic-regression confidence scoring, cosine-similarity consistency check against prior agent outputs, knowledge-base factual anchoring, then hedging/annotation sanitisation of high-risk claims.
evaluation: HaluEval, 2000 samples over medical/legal/financial/general, hallucinations injected at Agent 1; linear, parallel and hierarchical topologies; no-firewall baseline plus four-stage cumulative ablation; HPM@4 and processing overhead (340 ms per interface, +15% end-to-end on 4-core CPU).
contribution: Quantifies hallucination amplification across multi-agent LLM pipeline topologies with a propagation metric and blocks it with a four-stage inter-agent firewall at ~15% runtime cost.
flag: Reporting gaps: the LLM backend used for the agents is never stated, the HPM metric is self-defined, and the only baseline is no-firewall (no comparison with other defences). False halts are not measured end-to-end; only the stage-1 classifier's precision 0.82 / recall 0.78 is given. Four 'domains' are all textual, so cross-domain evaluation is not satisfied. Prose is noticeably machine-paraphrased.

title: Hallucination-Aware Collaborative Task Scheduling in Multiplex Industrial Networks With LLM-Driven Agents
evidence: 'Definition 10 (Verification node): A verifier at vi intercepts a[n exposure]... Verification blocks [the onward path]'; 'A verifier checks an agent's output before downstream agents' (Sec. V-A); blocked-error ratio is an audited metric.
method: Feedback-amplified linear-threshold cascade model on a multiplex agent network (task, communication, proximity, shared-LLM layers); NP-hard HACTS formulation; CLHAS heuristic placing verifiers (1-1/e greedy), assigning agents and routing messages by cascade risk.
evaluation: Semi-synthetic multiplex simulations plus 660 blinded API runs (two backbones, APS/OPS cases) vs DGBA, CATA, CFT-MN, single-agent and three ablations; cascade size -35.1%, success +8.6%, blocked-error ratio; scheduler p95 18.75 s cold, 8.21 ms/task cached.
contribution: Models hallucination as a feedback-amplified cascade on a multiplex agent network and schedules verifier placement, assignment and routing to cut cascade size 35% at measured scheduler latency.
flag: Best fit in this batch: verifier interception is evaluated as a cascade-risk mechanism with baselines, ablations and hierarchical bootstrap CIs. Verifier placement is a planning-time decision; only the verifier check itself is runtime, so (a) rests on Definition 10. Cached routing at 8.21 ms/task is the sub-15 ms figure relevant to RQ1 but on an i7-13700H CPU, not edge. Both case domains (APS manufacturing rescheduling, OPS microservice incidents) are logical/enterprise, so no cross-domain cell.

title: Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Autonomous Learning and Safe Cooperative Decision-Making
evidence: Sec. III: 'During execution, a safety correction layer projects any unsafe raw action onto the nearest feasible one, acting as a post-decision filter rather than replacing the policy'; the QP is 'solved online by OSQP (<0.5 ms/step, well within the 100 ms control cycle)'.
method: Dec-POMDP heterogeneous MARL (FS-MATD3) with dual safety: a training-stage cost penalty plus an execution-stage QP projection of unsafe actions, lexicographic collision>obstacle>boundary priority, and three-stage dropout/anomaly training.
evaluation: Simulated USV/UUV marine encirclement; reward and success-rate curves with across-run bands only; no baseline, no ablation, no violation count; safety QP timed at <0.5 ms/step inside a 100 ms cycle.
contribution: Heterogeneous USV/UUV safe MARL whose execution-stage QP projection filters unsafe actions in under 0.5 ms, backed by a training-stage safety cost and a dropout-anomaly curriculum.
flag: Textbook (a)+(d) match, including a rare sub-millisecond interception budget, but the evaluation is only the method's own reward/success-rate curves: no MATD3 baseline, no ablation of the projection layer, no safety-violation metric. Strong candidate to revisit if an extended version with comparisons appears.

title: Human Multi-Robot Safe Interaction: A Trajectory Scaling Approach Based on Safety Assessment
evidence: "Based on the value of this field, the cooperative task trajectory is properly modified so as to ensure a safe interaction while trying to preserve as much as possible the nominal task, which is instead completely aborted whenever the safety of the interaction cannot be guaranteed" (Abstract; scaling in Sec. IV-B, monitored stop in Sec. V-A).
method: Cumulative human multi-robot safety field drives a scaling parameter that slows the nominal cooperative trajectory to hold the index above a threshold, with monitored stop otherwise; centralised and distributed-observer implementations.
evaluation: Three-manipulator simulation plus two-Comau/UR10-Kinect cell at 2 ms exchange; baselines emergency stop and evasive action on execution/idle/concurrent-motion/path/average-safety-index; safety index computed in 6.8e-5 s.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; non-generative inference; latency/jitter aware
contribution: A cumulative safety field scales or aborts a cooperative multi-robot trajectory at runtime, keeping human safety above threshold while cutting idle and execution time against emergency-stop and evasive-action baselines.
flag: Closest batch match to RQ5: quantified throughput cost of an emergency-stop safeguard versus graded scaling. Human is an obstacle to be kept safe, not an operator the system defers to, so (e) is not met; hardware validation uses two manipulators and a standard real-time PC, not edge hardware.

title: Human(s) On The Loop Demand Aware Robot Scheduling: A Mixed Reality based User Study
evidence: Sec. III-B: "A paired T-test for the time when robots were heading towards a collision showed significantly lower times in Case 1 (t = -1.950, p < 0.050, Cohen's d = -0.571)", comparing human-on-the-loop scheduling with and without collision-cone visualisation.
method: Two mixed-reality user studies (8 + 8 participants) of human-on-the-loop demand-aware multi-robot task scheduling: single-robot vs autonomous-agent-assisted, and two-operator teleoperation with vs without collision-cone overlays.
evaluation: Mixed-reality warehouse, real and holographic robots; within-subject conditions (45 and 60 tasks); paired t-tests on reward, scheduling time, travel distance and time heading toward collision.
contribution: User studies show human schedulers gain reward when an autonomous agent assists, and that collision-cone overlays cut the time two teleoperated robots spend heading for collision without hurting demand-aware performance.
flag: BORDERLINE (e): a situation-awareness aid for a supervisor who is already in charge, with no deferral or takeover event; n=8 per study and several comparisons non-significant; multi-agent safety is one outcome among reward/time/distance, so (c) fails primacy.

title: Human-in-the-Loop Mixed-Initiative Control Under Temporal Tasks
evidence: Sec. IV-B: the mixed-initiative controller 'u = u_r(x, pi_s, pi_g) + kappa(x, O_t) u_h(t)' where O_t is the set of product states from which 'phi_hard can not be satisfied any more' and 'the function kappa is 0 on the boundary of undesired regions in O_t', ensuring 'the hard task phi_hard is respected at all times for all human inputs'.
method: LTL hard/soft task planning over a parameterised product automaton; Dijkstra identifies states from which the hard task is unsatisfiable, a smooth gain attenuates the operator's joystick input to zero near them, plus online plan adaptation and inverse RL of the operator's preference weight.
evaluation: Gazebo office case studies with a TIAGo robot and one TurtleBot hardware run; reports beta convergence (11.3 after 12 iterations; 1.58 after 15), plan-adaptation timelines and trajectories. No safety metric, no baseline or ablation; laptop 3.06 GHz CPU.
methods: temporal-logic; formal-methods; control-theory; shielding; human-factors; reinforcement-learning
contribution: A mixed-initiative controller gates operator inputs to zero exactly at the states from which a hard LTL task becomes unsatisfiable, keeping human takeover safe while learning the operator's preferences.
flag: Mechanism is highly relevant - O_t is an explicit time-to-irreversibility set and the kappa gate is a genuine runtime filter on human commands - but the case study is a demonstration: no safety metric, no baseline or ablation, so it fails the protocol v1.5 evaluation floor. Single robot plus one operator; worth keeping as a methodological citation even if excluded.

title: HyperCortex: Adaptive Enterprise AI Runtime for Policy-Governed Multi-Agent Workflow Execution
evidence: "The policy engine returns allow/requires-approval/deny; if it returns deny, it is a policy failure and passed to the replanner" before dispatch, and APPROVAL marks the task awaiting (Sec. V, Algorithm 2); "a plausible policy configuration would cost 129% more runtime while it would prevent nothing" (Sec. I).
method: HyperCortex: enterprise multi-agent workflow runtime; task DAG with bounded graph-mutation repair, saga-style compensation for committed irreversible effects, pre-dispatch allow/approval/deny policy gate, and seven validated plan invariants.
evaluation: Nine synthetic enterprise workflows, six injected failure classes, 120 seeds, 56,740 runs, local 3B models on a 2-core CPU; vs no-repair, retry, local repair, clairvoyant; policy-independent safety oracle.
contribution: A measurement methodology for policy-governed multi-agent workflow runtimes shows one policy configuration costs 129% more runtime while preventing nothing and one repair operator loses to a simpler baseline.
flag: Explicitly an evaluation vehicle - the mechanism is "not claimed as a novel mechanism". Human approval/escalation is counted as cost (540 escalations for one config), with no human study, so (e) is structural only. Strongest paper in the batch for RQ5 and for irreversibility accounting. Prose is garbled in several places (likely machine-generated text); re-read the tables before quoting any number.

title: I Know You Can't See Me: Dynamic Occlusion-Aware Safety Validation of Strategic Planners for Autonomous Vehicles Using Hypergames
evidence: Abstract: 'we develop a novel multi-agent dynamic occlusion risk (DOR) measure for assessing situational risk in dynamic occlusion scenarios'; Table I: occlusion-caused collisions rise from 2 on naturalistic data to 80 with the proposed injection method.
method: Hypergame-based dynamic occlusion risk measure plus planner-in-the-loop accelerated safety validation that injects occluding vehicles into naturalistic data to generate occlusion-caused collisions for strategic planners.
evaluation: Waterloo Multi-Agent intersection database (3.5k vehicles); baseline unaugmented naturalistic data; 80 versus 2 occlusion-caused collisions, 105,914 versus 1,534 scenarios, coverage, severity, 1.65 s mean occlusion-to-impact.
contribution: Defines a multi-agent dynamic occlusion risk measure and uses it to generate realistic occlusion-caused crash scenarios 40x more often than naturalistic data when validating strategic planners.
flag: Offline white-box test-generation and validation framework, not a runtime mechanism; the 'baseline' is unaugmented naturalistic data rather than a competing validation method. Occlusion-resolution-to-impact times (0.5-3.0 s vs 1.3-1.5 s driver reaction) are the handoff-relevant data.

title: Impact Study of Faulty Sensors on Flocking-Based Cooperative Control of Nonholonomic Robots
evidence: Abstract: 'Four carefully chosen evaluation metrics are used to quickly assess performance degradation caused by faulty sensors' (velocity mismatch, edges per agent, cohesion, gamma-agent distance); Sec. VI: 'Future impact studies will incorporate ... energy-efficiency metrics and safety metrics using surrogate safety measures.'
method: Fault-injection sensitivity study: a standard nonholonomic flocking controller in which a varying fraction of robots broadcast erroneous self-states with varying noise intensity; no mitigation mechanism is proposed.
evaluation: MATLAB, 50 agents; Exp.1 sweeps 0-100% faulty agents x noise 0-1.0, Exp.2 20-run aggregates; metrics velocity mismatch, edges/agent, cohesion, gamma-agent distance, binary success vs fault-free.
