contribution: Systematic fault-injection sweep quantifying how the density and intensity of faulty self-state sensors degrade flocking cohesion, connectivity and leader tracking in nonholonomic multi-robot teams.
flag: No safety mechanism and no safety metric: all outcomes are flocking quality, and the authors explicitly defer surrogate safety measures to future work, so it would also fail the E2 floor. Coordination-only study.

title: Improving Multi-Agent Motion Prediction with Heuristic Goals and Motion Refinement
evidence: Abstract: "We design our model using powerful attention mechanisms with GNNs to enhance agents interactions, heuristic proposals as preliminary plausible information and a motion refinement module", predicting multimodal futures for all relevant agents from HD map and past trajectories.
method: Transformer encoder over agent histories plus GCN actor-to-actor attention, HD-map and agent metadata, heuristic centerline goal proposals with GoICrop filtering, and a motion-refinement head for multimodal trajectory forecasting.
evaluation: Argoverse 2 forecasting val/test; baseline GANet plus internal variants; minADE 0.81, minFDE 1.42, brier-minFDE 2.04, 4.92M parameters; 946 ms per 128-scene batch on A100.
contribution: A lighter attention-plus-GNN forecaster with heuristic lane goals and motion refinement matches GANet-class accuracy on Argoverse 2 with fewer parameters and lower runtime.
flag: protocol v1.6: included as world-model/predictor evidence on a predictive-accuracy metric with a baseline or ablation; not safety evidence, RQ5 capped at 2. (b) is met, but every reported metric is displacement accuracy (minADE/minFDE/brier-minFDE/MR) with no safety outcome, so the v1.5 floor fails. Runtime is batch-128 A100 throughput rather than a latency budget, so (d) fails too.

title: IntNet: A Communication-Driven Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Cooperative Autonomous Driving
evidence: Abstract/Sec. III: an "observation prediction module ... enables agents to forecast subsequent policy outputs, which they can then share across a vehicle-to-vehicle network", processed by a Graph Attention Network; Sec. IV-B reports "test collision rates (%)" against IC3Net as agent count grows.
method: MARL with per-agent observation predictor (intent over horizon H), GAT message encoder and learned communication scheduler, trained end-to-end actor-critic; safety emerges from reward, no hard constraint.
evaluation: Highway-env urban scenarios (highway, 4-way intersection, merge) with human-driven vehicles; baselines no-comm, CommNet, IC3Net, MAGIC; arrival and collision rate, 3 seeds, 100 test episodes; scheduler ablation; no latency or hardware.
contribution: IntNet shares predicted intent over a scheduled vehicle-to-vehicle graph attention network, lowering multi-agent collision rates against communicative-MARL baselines while cutting communication by up to 60%.
flag: (a) not met: "safety to emerge naturally from coordinated learning, rather than relying on hard constraints" (Sec. I) - no runtime override and no latency measurement, so its value is as a graph world-model baseline, not an interceptor. Maintainer may read it as E1 under the protocol v1.2 coordination carve-out, since the mechanism is communication rather than a safety mechanism; collision rate is nonetheless a primary measured outcome against four baselines.

title: Integrated Path Planning and Safety Control for Multi-Robot Systems in Post-Disaster Environments
evidence: Sec. IV: "the real-time CBF-QP controller continuously replans trajectories to circumvent moving hazards while maintaining the prescribed task sequence"; Table II reports minimum inter-robot distance 0.15 +/- 0.02 m against a 0.15 m safety threshold.
method: LTL mission specifications mapped to zero- and finite-time CBF constraints; lasso reference paths from the product automaton tracked by a min-norm real-time QP enforcing safety and task progression.
evaluation: Five robots, MATLAB Robotarium post-disaster arena, 10 repeats; time-to-target and minimum inter-robot distance; only a dynamic-obstacle versus obstacle-free comparison, no method baseline.
contribution: Maps LTL mission specifications directly onto continuous-time barrier constraints solved as a real-time QP, keeping five Robotarium robots above a 0.15 m separation threshold while completing ordered rescue tasks.
flag: No method baseline or ablation - only a dynamic-versus-static environment comparison. CBF constraints sit inside the min-norm QP that generates the control (no nominal command is overridden), so criterion (a) fails. (c) primacy borderline: LTL task planning is co-primary and mission success is the headline.

title: Interface Design for Human-Machine Collaborations in Drone Management
evidence: Sec. VI-B: 'the role of the user changes from human-in-the-loop control to a strategic role in which human input is required for planning, prioritization, and analyzing the observed environment'; the UAV must fly reliably without the operator 'for a duration of up to 15 seconds' and safe-lands if communication fails.
method: Immersive VR ground-control interface for a UAV fleet with flight-monitoring, task-assignment and ML-annotated sensing views; onboard automation handles altitude, no-fly zones, conflict detection and safe landing.
evaluation: Two lab experiments (60 and 37 participants): NASA-TLX load versus event frequency by repeated-measures ANOVA, and disaster-event identification accuracy with versus without automated annotation; three field tests qualitative.
contribution: An immersive drone-management interface lets one operator task a fleet of automated UAVs with conflict detection and annotated sensing, reducing NASA-TLX load and raising event-identification accuracy.
flag: Criterion (e) is met and the 15-second communication-latency budget is relevant to RQ2/RQ3, but the only quantitative outcomes are NASA-TLX load and target-identification accuracy; the in-flight conflict detection and resolution is taken from the authors' earlier papers and never measured, so there is no quantitative safety metric.

title: Jury, Judge, and Executioner: Using LLMs to Steer Gamified Multi-Agent Decision-Making
evidence: 'a non-writing Agent Director audit all state changes through three gates: Jury (self-audit against persona and memory), Judge (rule, budget, and conflict checks), and Executioner (state write)... preventing hallucinated actions from ever reaching the environment' (Abstract).
method: Language-conditioned control loop separating proposal from execution: LLM policies emit one schema-valid intent under a legal-moves mask; a non-writing Director gates every intent (Jury/Judge/Executioner) with lease-based handshakes, conflict-free atomic commits and small/large policy escalation.
evaluation: D&D 5e one-shot with four agent roles, medians over 25 episodes vs FSM, policy-only and LLM-only ablations: success 76% vs 15-48%, violations 4.6 vs 12.4/100 turns, contradictions 3.5, entropy 2.32 bits, 980 tokens/decision, p95 latency 2.6 s.
contribution: Governance loop in which LLM agents may only propose intents while a non-writing director vetoes and commits them, halving rule violations and contradictions against FSM and policy-only ablations.
flag: Clean (a) and a proper ablation with violations/100 turns as the safety metric, plus explicit p50/p95 latency and token accounting (useful for RQ5). Domain is a single tabletop-game testbed with N=4 agents and 25 episodes, medians only, no CIs or significance tests, small venue; generalisation beyond the game is untested. The Policy-S -> Policy-L escalation on nack or high decoder entropy within one tick is the dual-speed/deferral element behind rq2=3.

title: KITNet: A Region-Attention-Activated Trajectory Predictor With Hierarchical Graph Neural Network in Dynamic-Mutant Multi-Agent System
evidence: Abstract: "KITNet employs a hierarchical Graph Neural Network (GNN) architecture to model intricate interaction dynamics" in a dynamic-mutant multi-agent system; Sec. V: the deployed detector-predictor-decider pipeline "exhibits an average end-to-end processing latency of 84.59 milliseconds ... well within the typical 100 ms (10 Hz) update rate of the ADV's onboard sensors".
method: Hierarchical GNN trajectory predictor with region-set-theory attention over behaviour modes and sinusoid/Bezier motion primitives; predictions feed a downstream decision module on an autonomous delivery vehicle.
evaluation: ETH/UCY, NGSIM, Argoverse 2 plus recorded campus data; minADE/minFDE versus Social-GAN, Social-STGCNN, TGR and others; onboard ADV pipeline latency 84.59 ms (about 80 ms/frame, five agents); no safety metric.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; non-generative inference; latency/jitter aware; edge deployment
contribution: A hierarchical GNN with region-attention activation forecasts heterogeneous agents for delivery robots and runs at 84.59 ms per frame inside an onboard detect-predict-decide navigation pipeline.
flag: protocol v1.6: included as world-model/predictor evidence on a predictive-accuracy metric with a baseline or ablation; not safety evidence, RQ5 capped at 2. Fails the v1.5 evaluation floor: only ADE/FDE accuracy and latency are measured, no collision or conflict rate, although the abstract claims "potential for significantly reducing conflict scenarios". Collision probability appears only in a motivating analytic scenario. Worth keeping as RQ1 evidence on onboard latency budgets for multi-agent graph prediction.

title: Knowledge-Informed Multi-Agent Trajectory Prediction at Signalized Intersections for Infrastructure-to-Everything
evidence: Sec. III-C: "we formulate the problem using dynamic graphs where nodes represent agents and edges encode geometric relationships" in a spatial-temporal-mode attention module over all detected vehicles; evaluation metrics are minADE, minFDE, MR, minJADE, minJFDE, minJMR only (Sec. IV).
method: Infrastructure-side multi-agent predictor: continuous traffic-signal encoder, maneuver-strategy awareness that prunes collision-infeasible joint strategies, spatial-temporal-mode graph attention; broadcasts trajectories for all detected vehicles.
evaluation: V2X-Seq and SinD; twelve SOTA baselines (V2X-Graph, HPNet, DenseTNT and others) plus component ablation; accuracy metrics only; 112 ms inference on A800 GPU; robustness tested to 0-500 ms delay.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; non-generative inference; latency/jitter aware
contribution: An infrastructure-to-everything scheme where roadside units predict and broadcast joint trajectories for every detected vehicle using signal-phase and maneuver-geometry priors, degrading gracefully to 400 ms delay.
flag: protocol v1.6: included as world-model/predictor evidence on a predictive-accuracy metric with a baseline or ablation; not safety evidence, RQ5 capped at 2. Evaluation floor fails: metrics are prediction accuracy only; the 0.96 m collision check exists inside the maneuver-strategy module, not as a measured outcome. The delay-robustness table (112 ms inference plus 0-500 ms communication delay on a roadside edge unit) is useful RQ2 background.

title: LLM-DiSC: LLM-enabled Distributed and Safe Coordination of Multi-Robot Systems using Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec. III-C Planner modifications: "we implement a modifier pi_m to verify and revise the generated planner. In this paper, we leverage CBF to characterize the collision risk and safeguard planner outputs."
method: LLM generates distributed multi-robot planners; a centralized refinement loop repairs them using simulation feedback and CBF risk evaluation; a CBF-based coordinator safeguards outputs during decentralized execution.
evaluation: 5 and 10 robots, single-integrator and unicycle, 40 runs per case; pass@k and collision-free success; baseline A*+Pure-Pursuit with the same CBF coordinator; ablation over o1-preview, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-r1.
contribution: Couples LLM-generated distributed planners with a CBF safeguard and simulation-feedback refinement, reaching 100 percent collision-free success for five robots and 75-to-100 percent for ten after 1.37 refinement iterations.
flag: Rare LLM-plus-CBF pairing that spans learned planning and runtime safety. Caveats: the safeguard also acts offline during planner refinement, so the purely runtime share of the benefit is not isolated; online compute is 7.85 s and offline 261.98 s, far from any latency budget; the conventional baseline is run once only (determinism argued).

title: Learning Differentiable and Safe Multi-Robot Control for Generalization to Novel Environments using Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec. I: 'CBF acts as a safety filter for unsafe actions' and CBF conditions are 'employed as constraints within a quadratic program to compute a safe control action by modifying a high-level controller... in a minimally invasive manner'; each robot solves the dCBF-QP online (Sec. IV).
method: A GNN parameterizes the CBF class-K function from each robot's local interaction graph and environment, and a differentiable CBF-QP layer allows end-to-end learning of decentralized safety filters under actuation limits.
evaluation: Unicycle multi-robot sims, 4-16 robots, 100 environment configurations with varied obstacle shapes; success weighted by path length vs grid-searched fixed class-K baselines; learned parameters copied to unseen 8-robot graphs.
contribution: Learning the CBF class-K function with a GNN over the local multi-robot graph makes safety filters transfer to unseen obstacle layouts and team sizes without per-environment retuning.
flag: Headline metric is SPL (success weighted by path length) rather than a collision or violation rate, so (c) primacy is borderline and inclusion rests on (a); simulation only, no latency or hardware. Closest paper in this batch to RQ4.

title: Learning World Transition Model for Socially Aware Robot Navigation
evidence: Sec. I: 'we propose a deep world transition model to predict the future observations of robots and the corresponding rewards', trained in 'a decentralized policy-sharing multi-agent simulation environment'.
method: Model-based RL for social navigation: a deep transition model over ego-motion-disentangled stacked local obstacle maps generates virtual rollouts used to train a laser-scan-to-steering policy.
evaluation: Gazebo, four policy-sharing agents, four social scenarios times 20 runs; baselines FDMCA and MNDS plus a no-world-model ablation; success rate, arriving time, ego and social score; real-robot runs qualitative.
contribution: A self-supervised world transition model over disentangled local obstacle maps lets model-based RL learn socially compliant crowd navigation from far less real interaction data.
flag: Included on (b), but the world model is used for training-time rollouts rather than runtime interception, the headline claim is sample efficiency, and multi-agent state enters only through policy-sharing peers; (c) would fail primacy (collision avoidance is one of several objectives). Real-robot evaluation is qualitative; quantitative comparison is Gazebo only.

title: Learning-Driven Layered Knowledge Construction with Structured Fine-Tuning and Human-in-the-Loop Reasoning for Multi-Robot SAR
evidence: Sec. IV-B-1: the Master LLM "evaluates structural completeness, semantic consistency and confidence" and the output is accepted, "re-evaluated by the global multimodal model, or escalated for human validation"; "If uncertainty persists, clarification queries are presented to a human operator."
method: Structured fine-tuning for schema-consistent geo-spatial descriptions; a Master LLM validates local-model output and escalates to a global multimodal model or human, distilling validated chain-of-thought back locally.
evaluation: Unity-simulated SAR scenes; custom vs default loss ablation (Object F1 0.873 to 0.926) plus Gemini similarity scoring; layered escalation assessed only through two qualitative case studies.
contribution: Layered multi-robot knowledge construction in which a lightweight local model handles routine scenes while a master router escalates uncertain ones to a global model or human and distils the result back.
flag: The escalation layer - the part that matters for RQ2/RQ3 - is evaluated only qualitatively: "we evaluate system behavior using representative scenarios rather than fixed benchmark metrics", two case studies. The only numbers are loss-function prediction quality, with no safety metric and no escalation-rate or routing baseline. Multi-agent aspect is largely nominal (per-scene descriptions, single-robot viewpoint), and the gate sits on knowledge construction rather than on action execution, so (a) is borderline.

title: Leveraging Cloud Computing to Make Autonomous Vehicles Safer
evidence: Sec. V: 'the system intercepts the invocation of the send to check for pending cloud requests ... if the timer was triggered, the message missed its deadline and is dropped', i.e. an explicit per-message deadline on the AV's safety-critical pipeline with fallback to local results.
method: Speculative execution of AV pipeline operators in the cloud with per-message deadlines and priorities, automatically falling back to onboard results when cloud replies miss their deadline.
evaluation: 5G field drive (median 68 ms, p99 3027 ms) and CARLA/Pylot scenarios at 11-24 m/s; Local-Orin and Cloud-A100 baselines; collision avoided/collided.
contribution: Shows AVs can safely exploit unreliable cloud compute by speculatively executing pipeline operators under per-message deadlines and falling back onboard, avoiding collisions that pure cloud execution incurs.
flag: Borderline (a): the deadline timer gates results at execution time, but it selects between computations rather than vetoing an action; safety outcome is a binary collision table over three CARLA scenarios, so evaluation is thin.

title: LightLLM-Enhanced Multi-Robot Collaboration with Human-in-the-Loop
evidence: Sec. III Level 3 - Execution Monitoring: 'If dmin < dsafe, execution halts. For instance, during execution, if two robots approach within 0.5 meters (dsafe = 1 meter), the system stops and requests human intervention to reroute one robot.'
method: Containerized TinyLlama-1.1B multi-robot planner with three-tier calibration: logistic-regression plan feasibility, conformal-prediction action reliability, and a physics-based execution monitor that halts motion and requests human intervention.
evaluation: ROS2/Gazebo TurtleBot3, 2-16 robots on an RTX 4090; baselines GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-Turbo, Llama-3.1-8B; success 89.6%, safety (collision-free) 94.8%, intervention 12.4%; per-tier ablation with false-positive rates 4.3-11.2%.
contribution: A three-tier calibrated lightweight-LLM pipeline for multi-robot coordination whose execution monitor halts motion and hands off to a human when confidence or safe-distance thresholds fail.
flag: Safety is one metric among success rate, speed and tokens, so (c) fails the primacy test; (a) and (e) carry it. Edge claim is architectural only ('less than 50MB per instance ... enabling deployment on resource-constrained edge devices') - all experiments run on an RTX 4090 workstation and no latency is reported for the safety check.

title: Lightweight Collision Avoidance for Resource-Constrained Robots
evidence: Sec. VII: 'It acts as the means of last resort in a pending collision by changing the robot's heading ... away from the collision'; the strategy works by 'blending a reference direction vector with a collision avoidance vector in real-time' (Sec. I).
method: Lightweight collision avoidance (LCA) as low-level motion control: blends the high-level reference direction vector with a sensor-derived avoidance vector using two gains, decentralized, range-and-bearing only, with a convergence proof for collision-free motion.
evaluation: MATLAB T-bone and ARGoS head-on/multi-robot simulations plus Khepera IV hardware (static obstacle, and 4 robots swapping positions), 5 runs per algorithm, compared with a modified RRT*; metrics mission time and distance travelled (LCA 47.1% less time, 22.5% less distance); no collision counts.
contribution: Decentralized last-resort collision-avoidance layer that blends a swarm robot's reference control with a sensor-based avoidance vector, cheap enough for resource-constrained robots and outperforming RRT* with moving obstacles.
flag: Genuine last-resort runtime filter over the reference control, so (a) holds, but the only quantitative outcomes versus the RRT* baseline are completion time and path length; collision avoidance itself is shown qualitatively and 'lightweight/real-time' is never quantified (no ms, Hz or CPU figures despite the resource-constrained framing).

title: LookOut: Diverse Multi-Future Prediction and Planning for Self-Driving
evidence: Sec. 3: futures are decoded by 'a deterministic function parameterized by a spatially-aware Graph Neural Network' from 'a set of continuous latent variables that capture latent scene dynamics' over a fully connected actor graph.
method: Implicit latent variable scene model with GNN decoder, a diverse latent sampler trained with a planning-aware diversity energy, a scenario scorer, and a contingency planner sharing one short-term action.
evaluation: ATG4D (over one million frames) open-loop forecasting plus closed-loop LiDAR simulation at 100 ms steps; CVAE/ILVM/diverse-forecasting baselines with PLT planner; collision rate, progress, progress-per-collision, jerk; four-way ablation.
contribution: LookOut learns a diverse set of scene-consistent multi-agent futures with a GNN latent model and plans contingent reactions, cutting closed-loop collisions while keeping route progress.
flag: Included on (b); (c) is borderline because collision rate shares headline status with progress and comfort, and the planner is a single-ego contingency planner rather than a safety interceptor. The latent model is generative (implicit latent variable model), so it does not address the non-generative-inference cell, and no inference-latency or hardware figures are given despite the 100 ms replanning interval. Strong RQ5 evidence on the safety-versus-conservatism trade-off.

title: MACS: Multi-Agent Adversarial Reinforcement Learning for Finding Diverse Critical Driving Scenarios
evidence: Sec. V-B-2: "We follow the collision rate, query time, and reward as metrics. The collision rate refers to the proportion of collision scenarios within the total generated scenario"; adversarial vehicles are trained "to induce collisions with the ego vehicle deliberately" (Fig. 1).
method: Multi-agent adversarial RL (MADDPG with hindsight experience replay and a maximum-entropy objective term) trains one to three adversary vehicles to induce ego collisions, producing diverse critical driving scenarios.
evaluation: SMARTS sumo/loop map, N=1,2,3 adversaries; baselines uniform sampling, MADDPG, VDARS, FAILMAKER-ADVRL, ablations MADDPG+HER and MADDPG+ET (-5.0% and -11.1%); collision rate, query time, reward; DBSCAN/TRACLUS diversity; RTX 3090.
contribution: MACS combines hindsight replay with an entropy term so multi-agent adversarial RL finds more and more diverse ego-collision scenarios than prior generators, and retraining the ego on them improves its robustness.
flag: BORDERLINE: hazard generation, not detection or interception. Collision rate measures the attack success of an offline test generator, so (c) passes the primacy test only literally; maintainer may well prefer exclude-E1. No runtime mechanism, latency or handoff aspect.

title: MADQN: A Decentralized and Lightweight Multi-AGV Coordination Framework with Hybrid Arbitration for Warehouse Automation
evidence: Sec. III-E: "the DQN-generated action undergoes immediate safety verification before execution"; Algorithm 1 sets "a_final <- wait {Rule-based safety override}" whenever CheckConflict returns true.
method: Each AGV runs a dueling DQN over a 3x3 local grid plus shared neighbour intentions; a rule-based arbitrator checks the intended action and overrides it with a wait on conflict.
evaluation: 3-5 AGVs in 15x11 and 20x20 grid worlds; baselines A*+time-windows and Dijkstra+time-windows; collisions, waiting time, path length; 44 versus 42 steps with zero collisions; >90 percent collision reduction across training.
contribution: Separates a DQN's long-horizon optimisation from a rule-based arbitrator that vetoes conflicting AGV actions before execution, reaching near-optimal 44-step paths with zero collisions at constant per-agent cost.
flag: Borderline E2: the "Pure MADQN" ablation claimed in the abstract is never reported in any table, and the A*/Dijkstra baselines also record zero collisions, so the arbitration mechanism's safety benefit is never actually isolated - the >90 percent collision reduction is early-versus-late training, not with-versus-without arbitration. Grid world only, 3-5 agents, and no measured latency despite the "lightweight" and O(1) claims.

title: MICA: Multi-Agent Industrial Coordination Assistant
evidence: Sec. III-C: "all agent outputs are audited by a dedicated safety checker that enforces rule-based assembly constraints and verifies responses against the KB ... thereby preventing unsafe recommendations from reaching the user"; Sec. V-E: "The safety checker still audits outputs and prevents unsafe advice."
method: An LLM router dispatches each query to five role-specialised RAG agents grounded in egocentric detection and a manual-derived knowledge base; a rule-based safety checker audits every output.
evaluation: 160 Gear8 queries over five task categories against four coordination topologies; task success, knowledge-base alignment, GPT-4o-judged safety score, 0.71 s average latency, 2.05 kJ per successful answer; ASF pre/post-adaptation study.
contribution: Industrial assistant that routes queries to five role-specialised LLM agents behind a rule-based safety checker, benchmarked against four coordination topologies on task success, knowledge alignment, latency and energy.
flag: Safety checker is a genuine output gate but is never ablated, and the only quantitative safety number is a GPT-4o judge score (MICA 4.94 vs 2.91-4.94 for the topologies). "Runs entirely on edge hardware" is contradicted by the conclusion that embedded edge deployment is future work; no device named, energy measured via NVML on a desktop GPU. Worker speech correction is human-in-the-loop, not automation deferring to a person, so (e) marked no.

title: MINDSTATE: Systematic Analysis of Belief Manipulation Vulnerabilities in Multi-Agent LLM Networks
evidence: Sec. III-C Memory Manipulation Vulnerabilities: 'the manipulation rate was 100% across all topics. Regardless of the topic, every instance of false memory injection was able to alter the belief of the system, revealing a critical and apparent vulnerability in LLM agent networks.'
method: MINDSTATE simulation platform: memory-aware GPT-3.5/GPT-4 agents on configurable network topologies, a drift detector over belief embeddings, controlled false-memory injection into targeted agents, and canonical social-model baselines.
evaluation: Simulated agent networks, three topics, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4; baselines DeGroot, voter, random walk, contagion with t-tests; 9-17 vs 20-50 convergence iterations; 100% manipulation success; manipulated-vs-control divergence.
contribution: MINDSTATE shows networked LLM agents reach consensus 2-5x faster than human social-dynamics models and that a single false-memory injection compromises the network within 3-6 iterations with 100% success.
flag: Vulnerability study only: no interception, monitor or defence is evaluated (safeguards appear only as future work); all results reported in figures without tables; undergraduate-conference venue, and the baseline models cover convergence speed rather than the manipulation metric.

title: Ma-Shield: A Collaborative Verification Framework for Secure Multi-Agent Instruction Inspection in Industrial Processes
evidence: 'Upon identifying hazardous instructions, it immediately interrupts the process flow and generates structured evaluations with actionable recommendations'; 'Through a detection-feedback-revision closed-loop, hazardous instructions are intercepted and corrected' (Sec. I, Sec. III-B).
method: MA-Shield: LLM safety inspector matching instructions against a predefined most-hazardous-operations library, counterfactual feasibility evaluator using process-engineering bounds, and a multi-dimensional cross-agent consistency verifier over subtask coverage, parameters and results.
evaluation: Wine-brewing industrial MAS testbed (doubao-1.5-lite, i5 laptop); 60 instructions (40 hazardous) vs rule-based baseline: accuracy 98.3% vs 75.0%, FPR 0% vs 15%, recall 97.5% vs 70%; feasibility recall 95%; consistency FNR 3.3%, FPR 5%.
contribution: Collaborative verification shield that intercepts hazardous industrial instructions before execution and checks feasibility and cross-agent logical consistency, lifting safety-screening accuracy 23.3 points over rule-based checks.
flag: (c) is borderline: the only baselined metric is screening of single user instructions (a single-input guardrail), while the genuinely cross-agent consistency module reports FNR/FPR with no baseline or ablation. Small datasets (60 instructions, 50 instruction pairs), one scenario, one small LLM, no repeated runs or CIs; 'temporal logic constraints' is asserted in the abstract but not formalised in the text. FPR 0% vs 15% is the useful RQ5 datum (false halts).

title: Magnetic Milli-Robot Swarm Platform: A Safety Barrier Certificate Enabled, Low-Cost Test Bed
evidence: Sec. II-C: 'Given an initial control input (u-hat) from any user provided nominal controller, the SBCs computes a new control input (u*) that provides three guarantees a) the outputs are collision-free, b) minimum modification to the original input only if the original control input leads to a collision.'
method: Safety barrier certificate QP wrapped around a nominal PID position controller for up to 16 magnetically actuated milli-robots; QP output discretised to zone commands with a random dither to break deadlock.
evaluation: ROS simulation (30 trials, N=5-20, with/without dither ablation) and 288 mm PCB testbed (16 robots, 18 trials); metrics normalised path length and deadlock-free success rate (100%); vision feedback 100-200 Hz.
contribution: Low-cost 288-DOF magnetic milli-robot testbed where safety barrier certificates minimally modify a nominal PID controller to keep up to 16 robots collision-free, with dithering to avoid deadlock.
flag: Criterion (a) clearly met - the SBC is a genuine runtime filter on the nominal controller - but the measured outcomes are deadlock-free success rate and normalised path length, not a safety metric; collision-freeness is asserted by the certificate and never counted. Primarily a hardware platform paper.

title: Measuring the impact of avionics faults with a set of safety metrics
evidence: Abstract: 'We compare three different variations of the crossing: (a) Chorus is absent (open loop), (b) Chorus is operational (closed loop), and (c) Chorus is operational, but one aircraft broadcasts a faulty ADS-B message with a +0.05 deg longitude error'; Table II records metric onset times and durations per condition.
method: Safety-assessment framework coupling an agent-based NAS model (ADS-B, CPDLC, NASA Chorus self-separation) with four pairwise hazard metrics: Loss of Separation, TCAS II, NASA Well Clear, and a new Critical Pair Identification based on time-to-NMAC after a blunder.
evaluation: One two-aircraft perpendicular crossing at 30000 ft, 350 kt, under three conditions (open loop, Chorus closed loop, closed loop with an injected ADS-B longitude fault); metrics min time-to-NMAC, violation onset and duration, relative distance; metrics run as post-processors; no repetitions.
contribution: Safety-assessment framework that quantifies how an injected ADS-B fault degrades self-separation between aircraft, using four hazard metrics including a new time-to-NMAC critical pair identification measure.
flag: The open-loop / closed-loop / faulted-closed-loop comparison with quantitative hazard metrics makes the floor arguable, but it is a single deterministic two-aircraft run that the authors themselves call an example ('a thorough demonstration of the framework's effectiveness is on going research'); the safeguard (NASA Chorus) is third-party and the metrics are post-hoc, so nothing intercepts at runtime. CPI's time-to-NMAC is RQ2-relevant.

title: Metamorphic Testing of Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Trace-Based Behavioral Oracle Framework
evidence: Seeded CCR faults are "(F4) delegation failure ... (F5) role confusion ... (F6) coordination deadlock" (Sec. IV-B-3) and MORPHAGENT "detects 82.0% of seeded behavioral faults, including 90.3% of coordination failures ... while maintaining a false positive rate of 6.1%" (Abstract).
method: MORPHAGENT: trace-based metamorphic testing with goal-preservation, coordination-consistency and tool-use-integrity relations checked over instrumented multi-agent traces via sentence-embedding similarity and communication-graph isomorphism.
evaluation: Four multi-agent benchmarks, three LLM backends, 96 faulty configurations, 2,840 source-followup pairs; vs Output-Only MT, LLM-as-Judge, Rule-Based Trace; FDR 82.0% vs 62.9% best baseline, FPR 6.1%.
contribution: Trace-level metamorphic relations supply a test oracle for multi-agent LLM systems, detecting 82% of seeded coordination, goal and tool-use faults at a 6.1% false-positive rate.
flag: Borderline on (c): faults are reliability/QA defects (deadlock, role confusion, tool misselection) rather than hazards, and testing is offline on source-followup pairs, not runtime interception. Threshold sweep moves FPR between 2.3% and 18.7%. Parts of the oracle call an LLM, so the non-generative gap cell was withheld.

title: Mitigating Emergency Stop Collisions in AGV Fleets in Case of Control Failure
evidence: Sec. VI Simulation Results: 'In the largest scenarios with 26 LoadRunners ... between 15% and 17.5% of the LoadRunners collide on average ... The results of the collision-avoiding algorithm are the lowest and are 0% regardless of the scenario.'
method: Extends centralized AGV fleet trajectory planning to predict emergency-stop roll-out collisions; three variants: delayed stop until a collision-free slot, collision-minimizing velocity profiles, explicit collision-avoiding replanning.
evaluation: Simulated LoadRunner fleets, three layouts, up to 45 AGVs; vs standard planner colliding robots 15-17.5% to 0%; throughput, planning runtime vs real-time limit (max 100 s).
contribution: Shows that anticipating emergency-stop collisions inside AGV fleet trajectory planning removes them entirely, at roughly half the throughput and planning runtimes far above the real-time limit.
flag: Mechanism is planner-level, so strict (a) fails; the delayed-emergency-stop variant does defer a stop at execution time but was discarded (>1 s delay needed in 27% of cases). (d) rests on planning runtime vs a real-time limit, not inference latency.

title: Modeling and Analysis of Bursty Delay Attacks in Cooperative Multi-Robot Systems
evidence: Sec. V-A(iv): "Collisions occur when delayed conflict-resolution messages cause multiple robots to target the same cell, leading to overlapping paths and redundant coverage" - but the reported outcomes are coverage excess (about 90 percent at 5 robots) and a 2-12 percent completion-time increase; collisions are never counted.
method: Formal model of a bursty delay insider attack (in-order and out-of-order message bursts) inside the ORMSTC distributed spanning-tree coverage algorithm, plus a self-adaptive backtracking recovery heuristic for stalled robots.
evaluation: ORMSTC on 16x16 and 50x50 grids, teams of 5-500 robots with one adversary, 20 iterations against the clean baseline; coverage efficiency, uncovered area, completion time; backtracking compared.
contribution: Models a stealthy bursty message-delay insider attack in cooperative multi-robot coverage and shows a single adversary degrades coverage and completion time, partly mitigated by self-adaptive backtracking.
flag: The subject is coordination efficiency and deadlock under a timing attack: collision occurrences are listed as a metric and asserted qualitatively but never quantified, and the measured outcomes are coverage excess and completion time, so (c) fails the primacy test. The backtracking mitigation is an in-algorithm recovery heuristic that by the authors' own statement does "not guarantee completeness or detect the attack". exclude-E2 is equally defensible.

title: Motion Planning with Adversary Avoidance Using Gaussian Process Classification
evidence: Abstract: 'a method for identifying these adversaries in real-time using Gaussian process classification is formulated. A method of real-time path replanning is then proposed and proven to avoid collisions with likely adversarial agents' (the proof is 'omitted for a future journal paper', Sec. IV).
method: Adversarial RRT-QX: a Gaussian-process classifier labels neighbouring agents adversarial from observed pursuit behaviour above threshold p_min; classified adversaries augment obstacle space and path cost, triggering kinodynamic replanning.
evaluation: 3-D urban-airspace simulations, varied agent counts, zero or one adversary; Table I: mean classifier probability 0.923 adversarial vs 0.196 independent; avoidance and false positives reported only qualitatively.
contribution: Adversarial RRT-QX pairs Gaussian-process classification of pursuing agents with cost-based kinodynamic replanning to dodge likely adversaries while avoiding the freezing-robot problem around benign traffic.
flag: The learned adversary detector would qualify under (c), but the only quantitative results are classifier probabilities: no collision or violation rate, no baseline or ablation, and the collision-avoidance proof is deferred to a journal version.

title: Multi-Agent Collision Avoidance Method Using Fuzzy Risk Estimation and Information Sharing in Unknown Environments
evidence: Sec. IV (Case 3): 'With the method enabled, the agents encountered an average of 0.33 collisions for 5 minute runs, average of 3.26 collisions for 15 minute runs and an average of 5.13 collisions for 30 minute runs. With the method disabled, the agents encountered an average of 14.73 collisions for 5 minute runs, average of 41.01... and an average of 81.86...'
method: Fuzzy rule base maps obstacle distance and velocity to safe/caution/risky, scaling speed and trajectory change; vehicles share GPS state and collectively build a virtual obstacle map.
evaluation: Unity simulation, five worker vehicles plus manager agent; ablation baseline with fuzzy logic and sharing disabled; mean collisions over 15 repeats of 5/15/30-minute runs; map completeness.
contribution: Fuzzy collision-risk estimation plus peer state sharing cuts average collisions among five warehouse vehicles from 81.9 to 5.1 over 30-minute runs while collectively mapping an unknown environment.
flag: Meets (c) on primacy - collisions are the measured outcome against a method-disabled ablation - but the risk estimator modulates speed and heading inside the navigation layer rather than vetoing a nominal decision, so (a) is not met and runtime_interceptor is 'no' (risk-triggered drastic deceleration is the closest thing). Simulation only; the ablation is the sole comparator, no external baseline.

title: Multi-Agent Driving Behavior Prediction across Different Scenarios with Self-Supervised Domain Knowledge
evidence: "we introduce a graph-neural-network-based framework for multi-agent interaction-aware trajectory prediction ... we propose to leverage human's prior knowledge such as the comprehension of pairwise relations between agents and pairwise context information extracted by self-supervised learning approaches" (Abstract and Sec. I).
method: Frenet-frame graph neural network for multi-agent trajectory prediction; hand-designed pairwise relational and context features as inductive bias, with self-supervised learning of the context representation.
evaluation: INTERACTION dataset, several road layouts; state-of-the-art prediction baselines plus one ablation; metrics mADE/mFDE only (about 24.9% mADE gain at 3 s) in overall, zero-shot and few-shot settings.
contribution: A Frenet-based graph network with self-supervised pairwise context features improves multi-agent trajectory prediction and its zero-shot and few-shot transfer to unseen traffic scenarios.
flag: protocol v1.6: included as world-model/predictor evidence on a predictive-accuracy metric with a baseline or ablation; not safety evidence, RQ5 capped at 2. Meets (b) but displacement error (mADE/mFDE) is the only measured outcome - no quantitative safety metric, so the v1.5 evaluation floor fails. Overlaps heavily with the queued LRA paper doi:10.1109/lra.2021.3104334 by the same first authors (same predictor, continual-learning extension).

title: Multi-Agent Safe Planning with Gaussian Processes
evidence: "the algorithm selects the action with the lowest probability of joint unsafety if the available action set is empty, or selects the action that optimizes the agent's objective Obj within the available action set" (Sec. V-D, overall algorithm); GPs are used "for estimating other agents' actions, which then enables us to increase the probability joint safety" (Sec. I).
method: Decentralised Gaussian-process planning: GPs model the individual safety/reward field and other agents' policies, and confidence bounds define individually safe and jointly safe action sets within which the objective is optimised.
evaluation: Mars-rover (HiRISE map, 10 runs x 20 episodes) and two-quadcopter simulations; baselines SafeMDP and naive/Bayesian/safe Q-agents; metrics safety (safe steps), episode reward, states visited; complexity bounds.
contribution: A decentralised Gaussian-process planner predicts other agents' actions and restricts each agent to individually and jointly safe actions, outperforming safe-RL baselines on safety in rover and quadcopter tasks.
flag: The safe-action set is computed inside the planner, so the strict runtime criterion (a) is not met (runtime_interceptor no). Two physical simulation domains only, so no cross-domain cell. Authors concede it "only avoids immediate jointly unsafe states" - directly relevant to RQ2 time-to-irreversibility; cross-domain enterprise claims (Dota, surgery) are discussion only.

title: Multi-Agent Variational Occlusion Inference Using People as Sensors
evidence: Abstract: 'we train a conditional variational autoencoder with a discrete latent space to learn a multimodal mapping from observed driver trajectories to an occupancy grid representation of the view ahead of the driver ... combining measurements from multiple observed drivers using evidential theory'; Sec. V: the pipeline 'runs on average at 56 Hz, which is real-time capable given that typical perception systems operate at 10 Hz'.
method: Discrete-latent conditional VAE maps observed driver trajectories to occupancy grids of the space they occlude; evidential theory fuses several drivers' inferences into the ego map.
evaluation: INTERACTION unsignalized-intersection data; baselines k-means PaS and GMM PaS; accuracy, MSE, image similarity over occluded cells including top-3 multimodal variants; 56 Hz runtime.
contribution: Treats multiple human drivers as sensors, using a discrete-latent CVAE and evidential fusion to infer multimodal occupancy of occluded regions in real time, beating prior people-as-sensors baselines.
flag: (d) rests only on a 56 Hz throughput claim against a 10 Hz perception requirement (no edge hardware, no latency budget), so it is borderline; metrics are occupancy accuracy with no downstream collision or hazard rate, so (c) fails primacy.

title: Multi-Partner Project: Safe, Secure and Dependable Multi-UAV Systems for Search and Rescue Operations
evidence: Sec. II-B: 'For each UAV, a corresponding ConSert model determines whether it can continue operating or if it must abort and return to the base, initiate an emergency landing or hold the position and wait until the critical situation is resolved', with a mission-level decider over all UAVs.
method: SESAME project integration: executable digital dependability identities (SafeDrones Markov reliability, SafeML/DeepKnowledge/SINADRA uncertainty, security EDDI spoofing detection) composed by runtime conditional safety certificates with a mission-level decider.
evaluation: Multi-UAV search-and-rescue scenarios, in-field and simulation: availability 91% vs 80% without SESAME in a single battery-fault scenario, SAR accuracy 99.8% after altitude change, ROS-spoofing safe landing shown as trajectory plots.
contribution: Project report integrating runtime conditional safety certificates over reliability, perception-uncertainty and security monitors so that multi-UAV search-and-rescue missions continue, hold, abort or land safely.
flag: Multi-partner project overview (E3-adjacent format); each headline number comes from one scripted scenario with assumed parameters and the spoofing mitigation is purely qualitative. ConSerts itself is a genuine runtime gate - worth chasing its primary reference [23].

title: Multi-Robot Cooperative Collision Avoidance with Conservatism Reduction
evidence: Sec. III: "The CA's conservatism is evaluated using proximity of the actual trajectory on the desired trajectory" - the only reported metrics (RMSE, MAE, standard deviation) measure trajectory proximity, not collision or violation rate; the safety constraint sits inside a unified tracking QP solved "in real-time" (Sec. II-E).
method: Binary approach/depart parameter embedded in a multi-robot CBF quadratic program that fuses tracking, control-effort and pairwise collision-avoidance objectives; Lagrange-multiplier solver.
evaluation: High-fidelity simulation replicating prior hardware models: 2 robots head-on, then antipodal circle swaps; baselines original CBF and authors' DV-SOATT; RMSE/MAE/SD of trajectory proximity; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Embeds a relative-velocity binary parameter in a multi-robot CBF-QP controller, cutting collision-avoidance conservatism while retaining formal safety, evaluated only by trajectory-proximity error.
flag: Fails (c) primacy test: the paper is about conservatism/efficiency and reports only trajectory-proximity error, with safety asserted as collision-free rather than measured. (a) also fails - the CBF is a constraint inside the unified controller QP, not a filter over a nominal command. Incremental extension of the authors' own DV-SOATT work [13]; 2-page conference paper.

title: Multi-Robot Coordination with Adversarial Perception
evidence: Sec. III: 'We conducted 16 real-time experiments to evaluate the framework in Fig. 2, excluding the adversary detection component'; Table I shows that as misclassification success rises from p=0 to p=0.95 the relative-position RMS grows 0.06->0.62 and sup||P_k||_2 grows 0.09->11.88, i.e. estimator and coordination degradation of the two-robot team.
method: Models adversarial misclassification/mislocalisation as intermittent and spurious measurements, fuses VIO with YOLOv7 detections in a Kalman filter for relative localisation, and quantifies observability-Gramian and peak-covariance degradation versus attack success rate.
evaluation: Two Tello-EDU quadrotors with Vicon ground truth over 16 real-time runs; attack-free Exp. 1 as control, severity sweep (11 runs) plus mixed misclassification+mislocalisation runs; RMS error, peak covariance, observability degradation; 35ms per iteration, rising to 41ms under overload attack.
contribution: A resilience-analysis framework quantifies how adversarial perception on one robot degrades observability and estimator stability of networked multi-robot coordination, validated on real quadrotors.
flag: Borderline (c): the measured outcome is estimator stability and observability degradation, not a collision or violation rate. The framework's adversary-detection block - the only interception element - is explicitly excluded from the experiments, and the 35/41ms loop latency is measured on a workstation PC, not on-board.

title: Multi-Robot MARL with Adaptive Safety Margins: Policy Relearning Triggered by Online Barrier-Function Interventions
evidence: Sec. VI: the CBF-QP filter runs 'at 10 Hz; CVXOPT solves each QP in less than 10 ms on a Raspberry Pi 4B' (6.8 ms mean, 9.2 ms worst case onboard), and TASRL cuts the intervention rate from 18.5% for the fixed-barrier baseline to 3.2% with no collisions in the physical trials.
method: CBF-QP filters each MARL action online; trigger-aware experience replay re-prioritises intervened transitions by TD error, barrier value and correction magnitude; adaptive safety margin tunes barrier gain from recent intervention rate via a proportional controller with hysteresis.
evaluation: Leader-follower formation, 7 simulation conditions over 10 runs: unprotected MAPPO, three fixed-CBF gains, TAER/ASM ablations; intervention rate, minimum distance, collisions, tracking error, completion. Plus 2 TurtleBot3 Burger robots, 3 trials, onboard QP timing on Raspberry Pi 4B, Wi-Fi latency < 5 ms.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; latency/jitter aware; edge deployment
contribution: Feeds online CBF intervention events back into MARL training through prioritised replay and an adaptive barrier margin, cutting interventions sixfold while keeping onboard QP solves under 10 ms.
flag: Best RQ1 evidence in this batch: measured sub-10 ms safety-filter solve times on edge hardware inside a 10 Hz budget, with real multi-robot hardware - though the interceptor is a CBF-QP, not a latent world model. Intervention rate doubles as a false-halt measure (RQ5). Physical evaluation is small and the authors say so: two robots, three trials per condition, 'not treated as confirmatory evidence'.

title: Multi-agent Heterogeneous Hybrid Safe Logistics Sorting System Based on Transformers
evidence: Sec. V-D 'Speed safe projection': 'Based on the Velocity Obstacle theory, unsafe actions are projected to the safe velocity region through linear programming, and the RL policy output is corrected in real time to avoid collisions caused by neural network prediction errors.'
method: Transformer central scheduler assigns tasks from global logistics state (CTCE) while MAPPO gives decentralised UAV/UGV path policies (CTDE); a velocity-obstacle linear-programming projection corrects unsafe policy outputs in real time.
evaluation: Isaac Sim/Isaac Lab warehouse with 3 UAVs and 3 UGVs repeated 30 times, plus a curriculum from 5 to 100 agents; only reward curves and qualitative trajectory/decision plots are reported - no collision rate, no baseline, no ablation.
contribution: A Transformer-scheduled MAPPO system for heterogeneous UAV/UGV logistics sorting adds a velocity-obstacle projection layer that corrects unsafe reinforcement-learning actions in real time.
flag: Mechanism genuinely meets (a), but the evaluation is a qualitative demonstration: 'three UAVs and three UGVs were randomly generated and repeated 30 times... all of which showed the optimal decision direction', with no safety metric, baseline or ablation. Edge-computing and real-time claims are unquantified. Worth revisiting if the authors publish an extended version.

title: Multi-agent coordination in high velocity UAVs conflict detection and resolution
evidence: Sec. 3.4: "The graph is temporarily constructed based on the instant UAVs states in each time step... CM turns the safe separation conditions into inequality constraints"; Sec. 4.1: "the solid line curves in Fig.7 are the preplanned paths... All agents return to their nominal paths after a short period of deviation. The minimum distance between every two agents is 0.22km"; Sec. 4.3 (64 UAVs, 600 s): "The original min. distance curve shows that during the flight, many UAVs would lose separation during the flight. All the conflicts are resolved by multi-agent cooperative coordination method".
method: Geometric relative-displacement conflict detection over per-timestep conflict graphs; local cooperative resolution solves a nonlinear program for heading changes weighted by agent priority subject to safe-separation and angular-rate constraints.
evaluation: MATLAB/Tomlab-SNOPT simulations: 8-UAV conflict, 3-UAV priority ablation (total heading cost 0.99-1.63 rad, min distance 0.21-0.22 km), 64 UAVs over 600 s versus uncoordinated separation curve.
contribution: Formulates multi-UAV conflict resolution as a priority-weighted nonlinear program over per-step conflict graphs, overriding preplanned headings only for conflict-relevant agents and restoring nominal paths, keeping separation in 64-UAV simulations.
flag: Two borderline calls for the maintainer. (a): the CDR layer does override nominal preplanned headings at each time step, but the override is itself a planner whose safe-separation condition appears as an inequality constraint, so a strict reading could deny (a). E2 floor: the only quantitative safety metric is minimum inter-agent distance, the no-coordination comparison appears only as an 'original min. distance' curve in Fig.9 with no numbers in the text and no competing algorithm (ORCA etc.) as baseline; the priority sweep in Table 1 is an ablation whose varied outcome is maneuver cost, not hazard rate, so the maintainer may prefer exclude-E2. No runtime/latency figures despite the real-time framing. time-to-irreversibility cell claimed on the time-window W feasibility argument (Sec. 3.3, 'insoluble situation because of UAVs dynamic constraints').

title: Multi-agent risk-aware constrained learning for network parameter optimization
evidence: Sec. V: "At the step-wise level, the action filter utilizes the safety critic's current cost estimate to perform instantaneous, high-frequency shielding", applied (Alg. 2-3) to the joint action from message passing before env.step; Theorem 2 proves non-propagation of violations along the coordination graph, and Fig. 4b/5a report average constraint violations against MAPPO and MAPPO-Lagrangian.
method: Graph-structured MARL for remote electrical tilt: CVaR safety critic on coordination-graph edges, message-passing joint action selection, then priority-ordered action filtering that steps each agent to the immediately safer tilt.
evaluation: Proprietary Okumura-Hata cellular simulator, 1000 UEs, five seeds; baselines MAPPO and MAPPO-Lagrangian; ablation over risk level alpha and filter threshold epsilon; average constraint violations and reward; Xeon CPUs, no latency.
contribution: A CVaR safety critic on a coordination graph with priority-ordered action filtering lets operators tune tail-risk tolerance, cutting interference-constraint violations while preserving network reward.
flag: Logical/enterprise-domain shielding over a multi-agent graph with a proven non-propagation property, the closest analogue in this batch to the review's own mechanism; the paper itself suggests transfer to driving and energy grids but evaluates only RET. (c) borderline: hazards are interference/SLA violations. No latency measurement, so no edge/jitter evidence.

title: Multi-robot obstacle avoidance in dynamic environments using opinion-driven CBFs
evidence: Sec. V-A: agents 'update their positions based on the computed control inputs that are modified by both the CBF constraints and the opinion dynamics'; CBF-only run reaches goals at 29 s, opinion-driven run at 24 s.
method: Nonlinear opinion dynamics with local and global attention heuristics augment decentralized CBF control so agents cooperatively escape deadlock and livelock while barrier constraints still modify commands.
evaluation: One 30 s simulation, four agents, two moving obstacles; CBF-only ablation vs opinion-augmented CBF: completion time 29 s vs 24 s, CBF-activation plots; safety only 'no collisions'.
contribution: Opinion dynamics with local and global attention sit on top of multi-robot CBFs, breaking the deadlocks barrier filters cause while leaving the safety constraint in force.
flag: Measured outcomes are deadlock and completion time, i.e. efficiency, with safety only qualitative ('no collisions') and no rate or baseline, so exclude-E1 is equally defensible; the CBF-activation vs completion-time contrast is still RQ5-relevant.

title: Multi-sensory Anti-collision Design for Autonomous Nano-swarm Exploration
evidence: Sec. III: "The exploration policy commands a straight trajectory until an obstacle or another nano-drone is revealed in one of the four surrounding zones. In this case, the navigation stops, and the drone reacts according to the strategy"; the ISCA module flags swarm agents inside a 65 cm safety distance (Sec. IV-A).
method: Onboard nano-drone anti-collision stack: four ToF zones plus a PULP-Dronet CNN collision probability on GAP8, and UWB ranging with Kalman filtering for intra-swarm distance, overriding the exploration state machine.
evaluation: In-field: 100 runs, three arenas, plus four-drone swarm (586 s); vs ToF-only baseline crash-free 20%->80%; ISCA 92.8%; 15.9 ms CNN, 1.6 Hz achieved vs >=8 Hz needed at 0.5 m/s.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; non-generative inference; latency/jitter aware; time-to-irreversibility; edge deployment
contribution: Fusing ToF ranging, a CNN collision predictor and UWB inter-drone ranging on a 27 g drone lifts crash-free swarm exploration from 20% to 80% and prevents 92.8% of intra-swarm conflicts.
flag: Strongest fit in the batch: an explicit edge latency budget (15.9 ms inference, 1.6 Hz achieved against >=8 Hz required at 0.5 m/s) tied to closing speed. Collision prediction is per-drone vision plus pairwise UWB, not a learned model over swarm state, so (b) is not met.

title: Multiagent Sensor Fusion for Connected & Autonomous Vehicles to Enhance Navigation Safety
evidence: Abstract/Sec. IV: 'The proposed statistical algorithm outputs a measure of similarity between local and world interpretations and identifies false negatives (if any) for the local agent'; results report the algorithm 'successfully corrected false negatives about 95-99% of times in case of 5 or more autonomous vehicle interactions'.
method: Each connected vehicle builds an EKF occupancy map, encodes it into a low-resolution DSRC super-frame, agents distributively fuse these into a world interpretation, and a statistical similarity test flags local false negatives and updates the kinematic model.
evaluation: SUMO+ROS co-simulation, 3-lane 2-mile highway, 50/100/200 vehicles, 5/10/20% faulty-sensor AVs, 50 Monte Carlo runs per cell; metric = % false negatives resolved (72-82% for 2-vehicle up to 95-99% for 5+ interactions); DSRC latency ~100 ms, 1 Hz map exchange.
contribution: Vehicles cross-check their own occupancy maps against a DSRC-fused multi-agent world interpretation, flagging missed-obstacle false negatives before they reach the planner.
flag: Weak evaluation floor: there is no no-fusion control condition; the only 'ablation' is grouping results by number of interacting AVs and by % faulty sensors, and no collision rate is reported. Detector informs the kinematic model upstream of planning rather than vetoing an action, so (a) is not met; 100 ms DSRC latency is asserted, never measured, so (d) not credited.

title: NSF-HRPT: Neural Semantic Field meets Hierarchical Risk Perception Tree for Safety-Critical Scenario Assessment
evidence: Sec. III-B (HRPT inference): "Risk Monitor: Root node's RiskValue and RiskMask are monitored for threshold violations, with risk source identification through hierarchical mask traversal"; Sec. IV-B reports accident AP/mTTA/AOLA above DSA, adaLEA and Liao et al.
method: Neural Semantic Field predicts BEV semantics, trajectories and probabilistic TTC from monocular video; a parallel quadtree risk tree aggregates per-entity multi-agent risk at inference; foundation-model priors bridge sim-to-real.
evaluation: CARLA SafeBench (800 scenarios) plus DAD and CCD dashcam datasets; baselines DSA, adaLEA, DSTA, Ustring, Liao et al.; AP, mTTA, AOLA; component ablations; two RTX 4090 GPUs; no latency reported.
contribution: Learns a neural semantic field of scene, motion and TTC distributions, then aggregates per-agent collision risk in a parallel quadtree for real-time multi-agent risk assessment.
flag: The risk monitor only warns and cannot override or halt, so (a) fails the strict runtime test (runtime_interceptor no). "Real-time" is claimed but no latency, throughput or edge measurement appears anywhere; experiments run on two RTX 4090s. Sim-to-real transfer is physical domain only, so no cross-domain cell.

title: Obstacle Avoidance Manager for UAVs Swarm
evidence: "when the distance between two or more UAVs is below an empiric safety threshold, UAVs velocities are changed base on the reduction factor, preventing collision when each UAV passes that point at a different time" (Sec. I; velocity control in Sec. III).
method: Two-layer obstacle-avoidance manager over preset swarm paths: a centralised velocity-obstacle layer scales each UAV's speed on proximity; a decentralised LiDAR layer re-plans with probabilistic roadmaps and A*.
evaluation: Gazebo/Hector-Quadrotor simulation: five UAVs on preset paths for the velocity layer, a single 16-plane-LiDAR UAV for re-planning; relative-distance versus velocity-factor traces only; no baseline, ablation or collision statistics.
contribution: A two-layer manager scales swarm UAV velocities when separation drops below threshold and re-plans around LiDAR-detected dynamic obstacles with PRM and A*, demonstrated in Gazebo.
flag: Qualitative simulation only - distance and velocity-factor traces, no baseline and no collision rate - so the v1.5 floor fails. The two layers are validated separately and the LiDAR layer with a single UAV; (a) is borderline, a speed-scaling navigation layer rather than a veto or halt.

title: On Provably Safe and Live Multirobot Coordination With Online Goal Posting
evidence: Abstract: 'we propose a centralized, loosely-coupled supervisory controller ... The approach responds to newly posed constraints and uncertainties during trajectory execution, ensuring at all times that planned robot trajectories remain kinodynamically feasible, that the fleet is in a safe state, and that there are no deadlocks or livelocks'; Sec. IV defines critical points and a stop lookahead used to 'filter changes of precedence orders that may result in a collision'.
method: Centralized supervisory coordinator revises precedence constraints and issues critical points online with a stop lookahead, adding blocking, deadlock and livelock avoidance, prevention and repair algorithms for asynchronously posted goals.
evaluation: Simulated heterogeneous fleets (10+ robots, warehouse and city roadmaps, injected communication delays); heuristics and strategies compared on mission-completion time and rate, deadlock occurrence (0% FCFS vs 100% IDs) and overhead.
contribution: A centralized supervisory coordinator that revises precedences and critical points during execution, with proofs and simulations of collision-free, deadlock- and livelock-free operation of heterogeneous fleets under asynchronous goal posting.
flag: Borderline. Collision freedom is proved (Theorem 1, 'collision checking is performed in all experiments') rather than measured against a baseline, and the measured outcomes are mission time/rate, deadlock rate and overhead - exactly what the protocol's coordination-planner carve-out calls E1. Included on (a) because the critical-point supervisor halts and defers executing trajectories at run time; maintainer may still judge E1.

title: Online Safety Under Multiple Constraints and Input Bounds Using gatekeeper: Theory and Applications
evidence: Sec. I: gatekeeper is 'a novel algorithmic component between the planner and the controller of the autonomous system'; 'The candidate is accepted if it remains within the known safe set. If so, it becomes the new committed trajectory to be tracked by the controller. Otherwise, the UAV continues to follow the previously committed trajectory.'
method: Each iteration stitches the nominal trajectory up to a switching time with a backup trajectory into a backup set and commits it only if it stays in the known safe set; optimisation is over a single scalar, with a runtime-computable suboptimality bound.
evaluation: Dubins formation flight, 3 agents, 24 engagement zones; baselines CBF-QP and IPOPT nonlinear trajectory optimisation; only gatekeeper shows no safety violations, deviation comparable to IPOPT, total compute 3.61s vs 9.49s (CBF-QP) and 302.65s (IPOPT).
contribution: gatekeeper recursively commits only trajectories provably completable by a backup manoeuvre, giving violation-free flight under multiple nonconvex constraints at a fraction of CBF-QP and nonlinear-optimisation cost.
flag: Clearest (a) in the batch and a natural interception baseline (switching time to backup is the deterministic analogue of time-to-irreversibility). Multi-agent only nominally: 'Inter-agent collision constraints are not considered', so (c) fails. Compute figures are run totals, not per-cycle deadlines, so (d) is not claimed. Formalises the authors' earlier gatekeeper paper - check the queue for that version.

title: ParkDiffusion++: Ego Intention Conditioned Joint Multi-Agent Trajectory Prediction for Automated Parking using Diffusion Models
evidence: Abstract/Sec. III: "we perform ego intention conditioned joint prediction, yielding socially consistent predictions of the surrounding agents for each possible ego intention"; Sec. VI-A-2 adds "OR denotes the overlap (collision) rate on the evaluated scene" as one metric among accuracy metrics.
method: Two-stage diffusion predictor: an ego intention tokeniser proposes discrete endpoint intentions, a conditional decoder predicts joint multi-agent scenes, and a frozen safety-guided denoiser plus counterfactual knowledge distillation refine training targets.
evaluation: Dragon Lake Parking and inD datasets; baselines include ParkDiffusion and an adapted random-joint variant; minADE/minFDE, f-ADE/f-FDE, miss rate, mAP and overlap (collision) rate; component ablations; no latency or hardware figures.
contribution: Jointly learns ego intention proposals and ego-conditioned multi-agent joint trajectories for automated parking, using a safety-guided denoiser and counterfactual distillation to improve accuracy and scene collision rate.
flag: The safety-guided denoiser is used only inside training (pretrained, frozen, non-differentiable targets), so (a) fails outright. Collision overlap rate is one metric among displacement-accuracy metrics and the paper's claim is prediction accuracy, so (c) fails the primacy test; included on (b) alone. Generative diffusion model, so it is a counter-example rather than evidence for the non-generative cell.

title: Passivity-Based Connectivity Maintenance of Teleoperated Multi-Robots Under DoS Attacks
evidence: Abstract/Sec. III: the paper augments a passivity-based teleoperation controller with 'a controller that stops the remote robots at safe distances from each other and from obstacles when a DoS attack starts' and one that 'restores the multi-robot connectivity before resuming normal teleoperation when a DoS attack stops'.
method: Distributed passivity-based teleoperation control that switches to a safe-stop controller when a DoS attack starts and to a connectivity-restoration controller when it ends; energy tanks enforce passivity.
evaluation: Simulated one-leader two-follower MRS teleoperated with a haptic device, 1 ms sampling; ablation without the connectivity controller (team disconnects); metrics inter-robot distance vs d_min, local Fiedler estimate, travel during attacks.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; latency/jitter aware; human handoff
contribution: Distributed passivity-based strategy that halts teleoperated multi-robots at safe separations during DoS attacks of arbitrary duration and restores connectivity before returning control to the operator.
flag: Borderline (a): the safe-stop is a switched control law triggered by lost packets, not a filter vetoing a nominal command. Evidence is one simulated 3-robot run with plot-read metrics and a single ablation; no hardware.

title: Persistent and Robust Execution of MAPF Schedules in Warehouses
evidence: Sec. IV-B2 (Execution): 'We only enqueue actions into a robot's command queue if i) the previous vertex ... is already enqueued or finished, and ii) all vertices associated with incoming Type 2 edges are finished'; and 'If a robot detects an unforeseen obstacle in its path, the robot stops autonomously, empties its command queue, and notifies the planner'.
method: An Action Dependency Graph built from any single-shot MAPF plan captures inter-robot action precedences; an execution monitor gates each robot's command queue on predecessor completion, so timing jitter cannot produce a collision, and commit cuts let re-planning overlap execution.
evaluation: Amazon HARMONIES warehouse simulator, 50 robots/600 shelves/8 stations, plus mixed-reality run with 6 physical iRobot Create2 + 6 simulated robots; baseline synchronous ALLSTOP-style execution; station utilisation 0.24 vs 0.09, zero collisions, 15 s mean re-plan, ODROID C1+/XU4 on-board controllers.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; latency/jitter aware; edge deployment
contribution: An action-dependency-graph execution monitor gates each robot's next action on its cross-robot predecessors, keeping MAPF plans collision-free under arbitrary timing jitter while tripling station utilisation over an all-stop baseline.
flag: Strongest runtime-gating example in this batch and a direct RQ5 datapoint (throughput gained over a conservative stop-everything safeguard). Note the baseline comparison is on station utilisation, not hazard rate: collisions are zero for both arms, so the safety metric is uncontested rather than improved; (c) fails the primacy test because the measured outcome is throughput.

title: Predicting Conflict Zones on Terrestrial Routes of Automated Guided Vehicles with Fuzzy Querying on Apache Kafka
evidence: Sec. V: "To avoid collisions between approaching AGVs, one of them has to reduce its speed or be stopped when the future distance (predicted based on the current location and time delays resulting from data acquisition and stream processing) is close"; Sec. VI: fuzzy queries "still operate at the level of tens of milliseconds, which is acceptable for real-time systems".
method: Fuzzy linguistic variable (collision/close/far) over predicted future inter-AGV distance, evaluated by fuzzy KSQL membership predicates on windowed joins of Kafka telemetry streams; threshold triggers slow-down or stop.
evaluation: Simulator on Formica-1 AGV data, Kafka on an i5 workstation; fuzzy vs crisp predicate baseline; tens-of-ms processing time, CPU <11%, memory, detection flexibility vs mu_min, 10-80 ms stream densities.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; non-generative inference; latency/jitter aware
contribution: Extends Kafka/ksqlDB with fuzzy predicates so AGV conflict zones are flagged earlier than crisp queries at tens-of-milliseconds latency and about 11% CPU, letting a fleet monitor slow or stop vehicles before collision.
flag: Collision prevention is asserted but never measured: no collision, near-miss or false-halt rate; the only safety-side comparison is the extra collision points detected by fuzzy vs crisp filtering (Fig. 7), so the E2 floor is met only narrowly. Enterprise stream stack over a physical fleet, but one domain only, so no cross-domain cell.

title: Preserving Agents Connectivity Amidst Static Obstacles: A Distributed Predictive Supervision Approach within Robot Operating System
evidence: Sec. I-B: the command governor 'is a nonlinear static device that ... is used to modify a nominal reference sequence in tracking control problems whenever its application results in a pointwise-in-time violation of set-membership constraints', here extended to collision, obstacle and connectivity constraints.
method: Distributed predictive command-governor supervision layer overrides each vehicle's nominal reference using future predictions, with online separating hyperplanes for obstacles and a reconfigurable minimum spanning tree for connectivity.
evaluation: ROS/Gazebo ASV formation (5 vehicles), with vs without scheme, static vs dynamic spanning tree; inter-vehicle distance vs 2 m constraint; Gurobi solve time distributed vs centralized; two-ASV pool experiment.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; latency/jitter aware; edge deployment
contribution: A distributed predictive command governor supervises a vehicle formation, overriding nominal references to keep collision, obstacle and connectivity constraints satisfied, with onboard solve times measured against the sampling period.
flag: True runtime reference governor on edge hardware with feasibility conditions, but coordination/connectivity is the primary objective and the with/without comparison shows constraint activation rather than a differentiated violation rate; stated extended version of the authors' earlier conference paper.

title: Preventing Wrong Work Item Retrieval in LLM-Based MCP Systems Through Multi-Agent Validation
evidence: Abstract: three agents (Executor, Validator, Refiner) 'intercept and validate every query before returning results'; Sec. I-C: 'When a query is ambiguous, the middleware detects this and asks for clarification rather than guessing.'
method: MCP validation middleware with Executor/Validator/Refiner agents: deterministic regex intent parsing, rule-based response validation, embedding-based ranking and session context tracking; ambiguous queries return a top-5 clarification request instead of a guess.
evaluation: 120 author-written queries against the production GitHub MCP server (microsoft/vscode): 0% hallucination, 43% disambiguation, 2ms validation overhead of 2322ms total; three baselines compared architecturally, not measured.
contribution: A deterministic validation middleware that intercepts every MCP tool result and asks the user to disambiguate rather than guess, adding 2 ms and returning no incorrect work items over 120 queries.
flag: Fails the v1.5 floor: the authors state 'direct apples-to-apples hallucination rate comparison with the baselines is not possible', so Table III compares architectural capabilities rather than measured rates, and the baseline failure mode is argued analytically (1/N). The 0% hallucination rate is partly definitional (disambiguations are excluded by definition; 48% of queries were unparsed and passed through unvalidated). Worth keeping for RQ1/RQ5: 2ms deterministic interception overhead on a real tool-calling path.

title: Probabilistic Multi-Robot Collision Avoidance Using Chance-Constrained Safety Barrier Certificates
evidence: Sec. 1: 'the proposed CC-SBC can be regarded as a probabilistic safety filter' that 'minimally modifies a given nominal controller'; Sec. 6: 'collision happens in all runs with the basic SBC ... our CC-SBC successfully navigates the robots without collision in every run'.
method: Chance-constrained safety barrier certificates turn probabilistic inter-robot collision conditions under Gaussian state-estimation uncertainty into deterministic quadratic constraints, solved per robot as a QCQP that minimally modifies the nominal controller.
evaluation: Simulation: 5 planar robots, asymmetric swap, 100 runs, Kalman-filter estimates (0.06 m error); vs basic SBC collisions in all runs vs none; minimum inter-robot distance stays above 0.6 m.
contribution: Chance-constrained safety barrier certificates make the standard SBC safety filter robust to state-estimation noise, eliminating collisions in a 5-robot swap where deterministic SBC collides in every run.
flag: Short conference paper; one scenario, simulation only, no runtime or hardware measurements.

title: Probabilistic Safety Certificate for Multi-agent Systems
evidence: Abstract/Sec. IV: 'We propose a probabilistic certificate for safety and performance specifications and use it to construct a distributed algorithm', with each agent solving a QP whose objective 'penalizes the derivation from the nominal controller policy'; Fig. 3: for the nominal controller 'the safety specification is violated several times', never for the proposed controller.
method: Probabilistic certificate uniting reachability and barrier-function invariance on long-term safe probability, evaluated myopically from each agent's local information, used as constraints in a per-agent QP over the nominal controller.
evaluation: Numerical simulation, 15 nonlinear agents, one unobservable; vs nominal controller: minimum pairwise distance never violated and safe probability stays above 1-epsilon; all agents reach goals.
contribution: A myopically evaluable probabilistic certificate lets distributed agents guarantee long-term global safety and performance even when no agent can evaluate the full safety condition.
flag: E2 borderline: one simulation run, only a nominal-controller baseline, and the authors state 'comparison with existing methods is not included in the simulation'. Low-latency onboard computation is motivation only, never measured.

title: Provably Safe Multi-Robot Coordination With Unreliable Communication
evidence: Sec. VII-A: 'The collision rate obtained using the algorithm proposed in [18] (which is uninformed of the channel model) is compared with the one obtained using our implementation of Algorithm 3 ... highlight the unsafety of the uninformed algorithm and validate the safety of the proposed solution.'
method: Centralized supervisor that continuously recomputes yielding precedences and critical points for potentially colliding robot pairs under second-order dynamics, using a known bound on transmission delay and packet loss to keep the probability of precedence violation under a threshold.
evaluation: Simulated fleets on two maps (110693 and 42748 critical sections analysed), 10 repetitions, injected delays and packet loss; baseline is the channel-unaware supervisor [18]; metric collision rate per critical section versus the analytic bound; Intel i7, Tc=1 s, Ti=0.03 s.
contribution: Centralized multi-robot coordination supervisor that keeps fleets provably collision-free under bounded message delay and packet loss, bounding the probability of unsafety by the communication channel model.
flag: (d) is communication delay and jitter awareness, not compute latency or edge hardware. Safety is proved first and the simulations confirm the bound rather than optimise it; deadlocks are offloaded to re-planning, so no false-halt/throughput accounting.

title: Quantifying Risk Propagation in Agentic AI Networks: A Simulation Framework and Singularity Index Approach
evidence: Sec. IV-B: 'Table 2 compares the predictive power of three metrics: SI, autocorrelation (ACF), and coefficient of variation (CV)' as early-warning indicators of cascading instability in coupled agentic AI networks, all reaching TPR = 1.0 in the transitional and unstable regimes.
method: Analytic N-agent risk-state difference equation (self-regulation, coupling, noise); spectral-radius stability test; Singularity Index with second-derivative acceleration detector for early warning.
evaluation: Synthetic simulation, 50-trial ensembles at coupling beta = 0.1/0.4/0.8; SI vs CV and ACF baselines on best true-positive rate; spectral radius and mean risk trajectories. No hardware or latency.
