contribution: Models cascading risk in coupled agentic AI networks as a linear-plus-noise process and validates a Singularity Index that flags approaching instability ahead of divergence.
flag: Borderline on the E2 floor: the only comparative table is degenerate (SI, CV and ACF all reach TPR = 1.0 at optimal threshold 0.0, no false-positive rate reported). Multi-agent only nominally - 'agents' are scalar risk states with no actions, tools or tasks. SI is a detector only; the paper defers control use to future work ('consider control mechanisms that use SI as a predictor of preventive interventions'). Maintainer may prefer exclude-E2.

title: ROS 2 Application to the Safety Monitoring of Collaborative Robots
evidence: Sec. III: "The fault detection event has been triggered, when the reconstruction residual was higher than a certain threshold"; Sec. II: if sensors disagree "the system can stop the cobot or take corrective action to avoid accidents".
method: Redundant fault detection for an EHA cobot: a Gazebo digital twin runs beside the monitored robot over ROS 2; a thresholded autoencoder residual on joint positions raises a fault alarm.
evaluation: Single Gazebo-vs-Gazebo case study: one synthetic joint-3 fault detected at 5.1 s from a ~1.2 rad residual. No baseline, ablation or rate metrics; real cobot left to future work.
contribution: Demonstrates a ROS 2 digital-twin residual monitor that flags a synthetic cobot joint fault within 0.1 s, but only as a single-fault proof of concept.
flag: Fails the v1.5 evaluation floor: one synthetic fault, no baseline or ablation and no rate metrics. Also a single-robot monitor with no multi-agent, sequential or handoff aspect, so exclude-E4 is arguable as a secondary ground.

title: RSFuzz: A Robustness-Guided Swarm Fuzzing Framework Based on Behavioral Constraints
evidence: Sec. IV-C: 'we used SWARMFLAWFINDER [7] as a baseline'; MA-Fuzzing 'boosting the detection rate by an impressive 126.2% while reducing the average time by 13.9% compared to SFF', and Table V: 'algorithm A1 collision rate surges from 10.03% to 67.39% as the swarm size increases (4-8)'.
method: STL robustness of behavioural constraints quantifies global swarm state; Katz centrality picks key drones; attack-drone placement is robustness-guided (SA-Fuzzing, MA-Fuzzing) to generate failure-triggering scenarios.
evaluation: Three swarm algorithms in simulation (4-20 drones), 2000 missions each; baseline SWARMFLAWFINDER plus component ablation; mission-failure/collision rate, detection success rate, detection time; Crazyflie 2.1+ real-world validation.
contribution: Robustness-guided swarm fuzzing uses STL behavioural-constraint robustness and Katz key-node selection to expose collision-causing logic flaws in multi-robot swarms faster than SWARMFLAWFINDER.
flag: Test-time hazard discovery, not a runtime interceptor: nothing overrides an action at execution time. Measured hazard rates belong to the system under test, so it fits the review as a hazard-generation/benchmark source (RQ4) rather than a safeguard baseline.

title: Reachability on Navigation for Multi-Robot Systems with Time-Varying Expanding Obstacle
evidence: Sec. IV-B, eq. (20): 'only robots assigned by the MIP to avoid someone switch to pairwise HJ avoidance; all others continue pursuing their reach-avoid objective', i.e. the per-timestep assignment overrides the nominal controller u_env at execution time.
method: Hamilton-Jacobi reach-avoid value function over a time-varying expanding-hazard set, plus pairwise HJ safety levels and per-timestep mixed-integer assignment of avoidance responsibility switching robots from nominal control to provably safe avoidance.
evaluation: Simulation, N=3-7 robots, 50 randomized episodes per team size; baselines ORCA and a CBF-QP safety filter; worst-case obstacle discriminator -0.035 +- 0.19 vs 0.085 and 0.683 at N=3.
contribution: Formulates multi-robot reach-avoid against hazards whose occupied region expands over time, combining HJ safety levels with mixed-integer avoidance assignment to keep teams of up to seven robots outside the shrinking safe set.
flag: Useful for RQ2: expanding hazards 'continuously shrink the safe region, imposing deadline-like constraints on motion planning', the closest thing in this batch to time-to-irreversibility. Caveats: the formal inter-robot collision guarantee holds only for N=3 (positive discriminator values appear for N>3, reported as near-boundary navigation); the headline metric is obstacle clearance, not inter-robot collision rate; HJ computation cost grows with N and no solve times are given.

title: Reactive and Safe Road User Simulations using Neural Barrier Certificates
evidence: "At the inference stage, the high-level controller selects a reference controller for different purposes ... and the CBF controller rectifies the reference control command to ensure system's safety while avoids diverging too much from the agents original purposes" (Sec. III, framework overview).
method: Hierarchical reactive road-user model: offline-learned high-level discrete decision picks an LQR reference controller; a jointly learned decentralised neural barrier certificate and CBF controller rectify that command pairwise over neighbours.
evaluation: Five real traffic datasets (NGSIM, HighD, RounD, SDD, VCI-DUT), 10-100 agents; baselines BC, PS-GAIL, RAIL, IDM, MPC; collision rate cut 53.8-97.7%; 0.01 s/step vs MPC 0.5 s (RTX 2080 Ti).
gap_cells: multi-agent state; non-generative inference; latency/jitter aware
contribution: Jointly learned decentralised neural barrier certificates rectify reference controls for heterogeneous road users, cutting collision rates 54-98% below imitation-learning and MPC baselines at 10 ms per step.
flag: (d) not coded: 10 ms per step is reported against MPC's 0.5 s ("cannot really be used online") but no explicit deadline and no edge hardware. The filter governs simulated traffic agents rather than an ego vehicle's safeguard; generalisation is to unseen densities (20 to 100 agents), not unseen hazard types.

title: Reasoning Graph Integrity: A Structural Framework for Detecting Poisoned Thought Processes in LLM Agents
evidence: Abstract / Sec. IV-B: the topology- and consensus-aware detector 'achieves an F1 score of 84.0 and an AUC of 0.937, consistently outperforming strong relational reasoning baselines such as the ARC framework' on poisoned multi-agent reasoning graphs.
method: Each agent's reasoning trace is modelled as a directed dependency graph; GNN message passing plus shared collaborative memory and a push-pull consensus update feed a binary integrity classifier with min-max adversarial training.
evaluation: Synthetic multi-agent reasoning dataset with injected edge/feature poisoning; baselines Isolation Forest, GAE, DGI, topology-aware GNN, ARC; accuracy/precision/recall/F1/AUC plus three-component ablation (F1 84.0 to 80.6 without topology consistency).
contribution: Detects poisoned LLM reasoning by modelling agent thought processes as dependency graphs and combining local topology consistency with cross-agent consensus over a shared memory.
flag: Detector only - no interception or override, so (a) is not met. (b) credited for latent GNN inference over multi-agent reasoning graphs, but it is representational classification, not forward prediction of multi-agent state; maintainer may want to drop (b). Authors concede external-validity limits: the dataset is synthetic because 'standard, labeled benchmarks for reasoning-level poisoning do not yet exist', and the gain over ARC is only 1.7 F1. No latency or deployment figures despite an O(KMd) complexity argument.

title: Reinforcement Learning-Based Dynamic Coverage Control of Multi-Rotor UAVs With Safety Priority
evidence: Sec. V-B: the shield is "a policy filter in the direct interaction of UAVs with the environment ... If the shield detects that the action violates safety constraints in the current state, it replaces the original action with a safe action and gives a penalty"; Fig. 6(c),(d) report connectivity rate and collision rate (ratio of safe steps) for MARLSP vs MADDPG and IQL.
method: MADDPG-style centralised-training/decentralised-execution MARL with a distributed discrete-time CBF shield (QP, velocity-compensated position) minimally correcting each UAV action for neighbour/obstacle avoidance and cluster connectivity.
evaluation: Dynamic coverage simulations (3-4 UAVs, 16-32 PoIs, obstacle variants, 100 random trials per scenario); baselines MADDPG, IQL, gradient-based law; coverage rate, steps, collision and connectivity rate; 4-UAV Pixhawk4/NOKOV flight demo; FLOPs analysis, no latency.
contribution: A distributed discrete-time CBF shield filters MARL actions for multi-UAV dynamic coverage, holding collision and connectivity rates safe where MADDPG and IQL repeatedly violate them.
flag: Strong (a) evidence: execution-time action replacement with a minimal-correction QP, applied in both learning and execution phases. Safety metrics are rates of safe steps shown as training curves rather than tabulated; the physical demo relies on a 44-camera motion-capture system, so it gives no edge-latency or onboard-compute evidence.

title: Relational Graph Learning for Crowd Navigation
evidence: "Our approach reasons about the relations between all agents based on their latent features and uses a Graph Convolutional Network to encode higher-order interactions in each agent's state representation, which is subsequently leveraged for state prediction and value estimation" (Abstract; model in Sec. III).
method: Model-based deep RL for crowd navigation: learned relational graph with a two-layer GCN over robot and human latent features yields a state-prediction model and value network for d-step tree lookahead.
evaluation: Simulated circle crossing with five humans, 500 test cases, five seeds; baseline LM-SARL-Linear plus RGL-Linear and one-step ablations; success, collision rate, extra time, average return; Pioneer robot demonstration.
contribution: A learned relational graph with GCN state prediction supports multi-step lookahead crowd navigation, raising success and lowering collisions versus LM-SARL while avoiding oscillation and freezing.
flag: Included on (b): latent prediction over a robot-plus-humans graph. (c) fails the primacy test - collision rate sits alongside efficiency metrics (extra time, return) in a navigation policy, and nothing intercepts an action at execution time. GNN computation cost is discussed only qualitatively; real-robot section is a demonstration without metrics.

title: Resilience of Multi-robot Systems to Physical Masquerade Attacks
evidence: Sec. IV: 'The key metric for evaluating the danger posed by physical masquerading attacks is the percentage of time that conventionally obtained MAPF solutions are vulnerable'; results show conventional MAPF 'predominantly (over 95% on average) vulnerable to the physical masquerade attack'.
method: Formalises physical masquerade attacks on multi-agent path finding; co-synthesises paths and an inter-agent observation plan so any deviation by a compromised robot must break a planned observation, encoded as an Exists/Forall SMT (EFSMT) problem solved with Z3/GUROBI.
evaluation: 100 random 8x8 grids plus 50 larger obstacle grids (ECBS as the conventional MAPF baseline) and 20 continuous-space instances; metrics = % instances vulnerable to Attack-MAPF (>90-95%) and # attack-proof plans synthesised; i7 CPUs, 20 min to 2 h solver budgets.
contribution: Crafting multi-robot plans so agents must observe each other at set times and places yields provable introspective monitoring against an insider robot masquerading as healthy.
flag: Resilience is obtained by offline plan synthesis: inter-agent observation gives a runtime detection guarantee but no override, halt or deferral is implemented or evaluated, so (a) is not met. Solver budgets are 20 min to 2 h and scalability is explicitly out of scope, so no real-time claim.

title: Risk-Adaptive CBF for Multi-Robot Coordination in Confined Tabletop Environments
evidence: Sec. IV-A: 'At each control step, the measured robot positions were sent to the controller, where nominal velocity commands were computed and modified by the CBF-QP safety filter before being transmitted to the robots for closed-loop motion control.'
method: Standard CBF-QP safety filter with an uncertainty-dependent inter-robot safety margin: required separation scales with relative-position uncertainty and an allowable collision-risk level, with slack variables so multiple pairwise constraints hold simultaneously.
evaluation: Real tabletop platform (90x90cm, under-table camera, fiducial localization); two-robot swap and three-robot crossing, 4 trials each vs fixed-margin CBF; success 0/4 vs 4/4, min inter-robot distance, goal error; no timing.
contribution: Replaces a fixed CBF safety margin with an uncertainty-scaled one, letting tabletop robots pass through narrow shared space where a conservative fixed-margin filter blocked all four trials.
flag: Borderline, included on (a) alone: the safety filter is explicit and runs on real robots, but the primary claim is reduced conservatism and deadlock rather than hazard rate, and RA-CBF's minimum inter-robot distance is actually smaller than the baseline's (0.213 vs 0.335 m). Only 4 trials per condition, no collision rate and no solver timing. Main value is as RQ5 evidence on false halts from over-conservative safeguards.

title: Risk-Aware Communication Link Pruning for Secure Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: "the Safety Memory is deployed alongside for runtime verification" with a retrieve-validate-execute path where "otherwise, full analysis is triggered" below the similarity thresholds (Sec. IV-B, Fig. 2); a locally compliant 3-hop chain raises non-compliance from 7.5% to 17.4% (Fig. 1).
method: RA-CLP alternates differentiable pruning of risk-amplifying communication edges with Safety Memory updates; embedding-similarity thresholds (0.85/0.60) reuse, adapt or escalate to full validation before each action executes.
evaluation: CyberSecEval-3, ToxicChat, Agent-Harm plus MMLU/GSM8K/HumanEval on GPT-4o and Claude 3.5; vs chain/tree/graph topologies, Llama-Guard 3, AGrail, Circuit Breakers, AgentBreeder; 4.13% non-compliance, 13-17% fewer tokens; pruning-only/memory-only ablation.
contribution: Joint communication-topology pruning and a reusable Safety Memory harden LLM agent clusters against topological risk propagation, reaching 4.13% non-compliance with 13-17% lower token cost than graph-based guardrail baselines.
flag: Topology learning is offline; the runtime interceptor is the Safety Memory validate-before-execute layer, so (a) rests on that component. Cost is accounted in completion tokens, not latency, so (d) is not met and latency/jitter was withheld. The 0.85/0.60 escalation thresholds make it a cost-aware selective-verification deferral - the closest thing in this batch to RQ2's sequential deferral, minus any timing model.

title: Risk-Aware Multi-Task Hybrid-Attention Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Decision-Making at Unsignalized Intersections
evidence: Algorithm 1 and Sec. III-D: the risk-aware local decision corrector screens conflict-zone pairs and "return[s] current planned action (no risky interactions)" when none is risky, otherwise returns a re-optimised action u*; Sec. IV: "RCMATQMIX-DP model achieves a success rate of 95.00% in Scenario 2, corresponding to a collision rate of only 5%" versus HAG-TRPO 78%, DRL-GNN 83%, MA-GA-DDPG 87%.
method: Multi-task hybrid-attention QMIX with diversity priority sampling plus a risk-aware local decision corrector that filters conflict-zone vehicles by arrival-time difference, ranks by time-to-conflict, and re-optimises actions over predicted rollouts.
evaluation: highway_env intersections, 4-8 CAVs with human vehicles; six MARL baselines plus corrector ablation; collision-free success rate, velocity, passing time; 15 ms mean compute versus 100 ms budget; Jetson mini-vehicle trials.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; non-generative inference; latency/jitter aware; time-to-irreversibility
contribution: A risk-aware corrector that screens intersection conflicts by time-to-conflict and overrides MARL actions, lifting collision-free success to 95-100% at 15 ms mean computation, for a small speed penalty.
flag: Best RQ5 evidence in this batch: the ablation quantifies both the safety gain (RCQMIX 86% versus QMIX 67% success) and the throughput cost (lower average velocity, about 5 s longer passing time). Corrector is rule-based, not learned; the MARL model runs on a central server while the mini-vehicles carry Jetson Orin Nanos.

title: Robust Autonomous Navigation in Dynamic Environments with a Modular Multi-Agent AI Architecture for Mobile Robots
evidence: "If the obstacle distance falls below the threshold (15cm), it overrides all commands and stops the robot instantly" (Sec. III, Safety Agent); the emergency-stop trigger time "was found to be 0.19 seconds" and is "unaffected by Wi-Fi latency or Decision Agent delays" (Sec. V-O).
method: Five-layer agentic architecture on an ESP8266 robot: OpenCV perception agent, LLM decision agent with rule-based fallback, independent ultrasonic safety agent holding override authority, control, monitoring agents and a Flask dashboard.
evaluation: 32 indoor/low-light/semi-outdoor runs; 92.4% detection accuracy over 150 frames, 9-13 FPS, 74-103 ms frame time, 0.19 s emergency stop, 28-41 ms motor command delay; no baseline, ablation or collision rate.
contribution: A low-cost mobile robot whose independent ultrasonic safety agent overrides LLM navigation commands within 0.19 s, presented as a system demonstration rather than a controlled comparison.
flag: Fails the v1.5 floor: the override is demonstrated, not measured - no baseline, no ablation, no collision or violation rate, only component accuracy and timing tables. Also an E4 candidate, since "multi-agent" means software modules on a single robot. Human override exists only as an unevaluated dashboard control.

title: Robust Collision-Avoidance Formation Navigation of Velocity and Input-Constrained Multirobot Systems
evidence: Abstract/Sec. V: 'a local quadratic optimization problem-based safe formation navigation controller is proposed for each robot' on top of the nominal controller; with the non-robust CBF method of [28] 'collision happens at t = 12.3 s', while the robust filter keeps the team safe.
method: Robust CBF conditions under bounded disturbance plus velocity and input constraints; a per-robot local QP filters a predefined-time-observer-based nominal formation navigation controller using relative position only.
evaluation: Simulation, leader plus five followers among obstacles; baselines potential-function controller and non-robust CBF [28]; minimum separation and collision time; QP solve 1.8-2.2 ms per robot on an i7-8700T.
contribution: Robust control-barrier conditions keep a disturbed, velocity- and input-constrained robot team collision-free where a standard CBF filter collides, at millisecond per-robot QP cost.
flag: Simulation only and a single scenario; the safety evidence is one collision event in a baseline rather than rates over repeated trials, so the v1.5 floor is met only narrowly.

title: Robust Consensus-Based Formation Control of Multi-Robot Systems with Guaranteed Safety
evidence: Sec. III-C: 'the control inputs for stability and safety of the robots comprise of the sliding-mode formation controller (26) and safety barrier constraints (37), which are manipulated according to quadratic programming', u*_i = argmin ||u_i - u_hat_i||^2.
method: Wheeled-robot dynamics reduced to disturbed double integrators; a distributed consensus sliding-mode leader-following controller supplies the nominal input, filtered by a pairwise CBF-QP for inter-robot and obstacle avoidance.
evaluation: One numerical simulation: four followers and a virtual leader on a directed graph with one static obstacle; barrier-function values and position/velocity error plots; no baseline, ablation or hazard rate.
contribution: Consensus sliding-mode formation control is filtered by pairwise barrier certificates in a QP, keeping disturbed wheeled-robot formations collision- and obstacle-free while formation errors converge.
flag: Single numerical simulation with barrier-value plots only: no baseline, ablation or quantitative hazard rate; the QP filter over a sliding-mode nominal controller is a textbook (a) instance if a method reference is wanted.

title: Robust, Flexible and Safe Cooperative Navigation for Multirobot Systems Under Disturbances and Input Saturation
evidence: Sec. I/III: safety requirements 'are guaranteed by applying distributed RCBF-QP framework' that is 'minimally invasive to the nominal control', with navigation achieved 'in the nominal situation, i.e. ui = ui_hat', i.e. the QP alters the nominal command only when constraints activate.
method: Robust CBF-QP filter over a saturated nominal consensus controller with disturbance observer; robust margin released over time and a switching topology drops unnecessary connectivity constraints.
evaluation: One numerical simulation, 6 robots and 4 obstacles; plots of distance to nearest obstacle, algebraic connectivity, observer error and bounded inputs; no baseline, ablation or rate metric.
contribution: A robust control-barrier QP keeps a disturbed, input-saturated robot team collision-free and connected while remaining minimally invasive to the nominal flocking controller.
flag: Runtime RCBF filter, but a single 6-robot simulation with no baseline, ablation or safety-rate metric fails the v1.5 floor; short workshop paper, likely superseded by the authors' journal work.

title: Runtime Verification on Hierarchical Properties of ROS-Based Robot Swarms
evidence: Sec. VI-B (EXP.3): 'In the simulator tool GAZEBO of ROS, we adjusted the direction of r3 so that it may collide with r2. The monitor then gave a violation when the distance of these two UAVs is less than the minimum distance limit minDis.'
method: RMoM hierarchical runtime verification for ROS swarms: monitoring interfaces over resource, communication, robot and swarm layers, a discrete-time three-valued MTL3-RMoM logic, a specification language, and algorithms generating central plus decentral monitors.
evaluation: Turtlebot hardware plus micros_swarm_framework/Gazebo 7-UAV scenarios; four qualitative violation demonstrations (memory, bogus shutdown node, UAV proximity, dead camera); quantitative results are only ROS communication and time overhead percentages (Table III), 100 ms window, 3.1 GHz CPU.
contribution: Hierarchical runtime verification framework for ROS robot swarms that automatically generates central and decentral monitors for timed, parameterised temporal properties spanning resource, communication, robot and swarm layers.
flag: Warning-only monitor: the paper states the monitoring process 'will not bring any influence and change to the execution', so (a) fails the strict runtime test; (c) is borderline because the only quantitative results are monitoring overhead, with hazard detection shown by single demonstrations. Same group as, and the predecessor of, doi:10.1631/fitee.2000203 in this batch.

title: SAFESTOP: Disturbance Handling in Prioritized Multi-robot Trajectory Planning
evidence: Abstract: 'The key idea is to maintain the paths and vary the motion of the affected robots, making them yield for others'; Sec. IV: 'The average delay per robot per run ... was 26.91 s with ALLSTOP and 15.29 s with SAFESTOP (-43% w.r.t. ALLSTOP)' and 3.51 vs 1.43 robots affected per run.
method: On a disturbance, SAFESTOP re-solves collision-free velocity profiles in distance-time space for affected robots over a 25 s horizon, making them yield instead of halting the fleet.
evaluation: 20,000 randomized disturbance runs in two scenarios against an ALLSTOP baseline (plus RMTRACK trends): affected robots 3.51 to 1.43 and 3.63 to 1.12, delays -43%/-55%, 0.35% fallback, 1.82 s planning.
contribution: SAFESTOP recovers from execution disturbances in prioritized multi-robot planning by making only affected robots yield rather than halting the fleet, cutting affected robots about 60% and average delay 43-55%.
flag: Collision-freedom comes from the prioritized planner's own constraints (so (a) fails the strict runtime test despite runtime overriding of executing plans) and every measured outcome is delay or affected-robot count, matching the coordination-planner E1 carve-out. Still worth noting for RQ5: ALLSTOP (halt-all) versus selective yield is a clean false-halt/throughput comparison, with a 0.35% fallback rate.

title: Safe Control Framework of Multi-Agent Systems From a Performance Enhancement Perspective
evidence: Sec. I: "This CBF constraint is integrated with quadratic programming (QPs) to filter nominal control inputs, which may be unsafe, in a minimally invasive manner, providing a safe control input"; Sec. V-A Eq. (19) applies u_nom when no neighbour is at risk and the QP output otherwise.
method: CBF-QP safety filter over nominal multi-agent controllers, with a feasible-hyperparameter notion and constrained Bayesian optimisation (expected improvement with constraints) tuning control gains and the CBF parameter for an LQR index.
evaluation: Two simulated tasks (4-agent destination swap, leader plus 4 followers formation); baselines random search, GA, CMA-ES; metrics LQR cost J and average feasibility rate over 5 trials of 100 evaluations; QP solve <0.001 s, EIC step ~0.6 s on a Xeon Gold CPU.
contribution: Shows a CBF-QP safety filter's hyperparameters govern multi-agent control cost, and tunes them by constrained Bayesian optimisation, outperforming random, GA and CMA-ES search.
flag: Borderline on the protocol v1.5 floor: headline metrics are LQR cost and hyperparameter feasibility rate against three search baselines, while collision avoidance itself appears only as inter-agent distance curves against Dsafe = 0.4, so the maintainer may downgrade to E2. (c) fails the primacy test (performance, not hazard rate). The reported <1 ms QP solve is incidental, not an explicit latency constraint, so (d) is not met.

title: Safe Edge Intelligent Control With Cross-Loop Constraints and Stability Guarantees
evidence: Sec. V: the edge safety agent "judges the safety of u_t^IMEC, deciding whether to switch to C^e(.)" and local safety agents "decide whether to activate the local safe controller (LSC)", with switching conditions derived for a bounded "end-to-end switching delay tau induced by sampling" and for packet loss; Sec. VI-B measures MPC at 594 ms vs IMEC at 0.41 ms per control period.
method: Cloud-trained lightweight multi-loop edge controller (feature-extractor network imitating constrained MPC, plus transfer learning and a saturation safeguard) under a two-level edge-end cooperative Simplex architecture switching to safe controllers.
evaluation: Semi-physical real-time simulations of a 6-loop linear positioning system and 6 coupled inverted pendulums with cross-loop constraints at 10 Hz; baselines MPC, IMEC-x, IMEC-xu, retrained IMEC-BL; MAE and execution-time distributions; EESA shown only via safety-region plots.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; non-generative inference; latency/jitter aware; edge deployment
methods: shielding; real-time-systems; networked-control; model-predictive-control; formal-methods; transfer-learning
contribution: Couples a learned millisecond-latency multi-loop edge controller with a two-level Simplex switching architecture that preserves stability and cross-loop constraints under network delay and packet loss.
flag: Most RQ1/RQ2-relevant paper in the batch - edge-side Simplex interception with explicit delay and packet-loss bounds and 0.41 ms inference - but EESA is validated only by visualising safety regions ("all the states during the simulation processes above are within the SRs"), while the quantitative baselines measure control MAE and execution time, so the safety-metric floor fails; maintainer may want to override. Note that "multi-agent" here means coupled control loops, and both case studies are physical, so no cross-domain evaluation.

title: Safe Fuzzy-CBF: A Monitoring Approach for Deep Reinforcement Learning Navigation Agents
evidence: 'when the barrier condition is violated, we solve a small quadratic program in the normalized control space to compute a safe corrective action... to generate safe actions to replace the original decisions' (Abstract / Note to Practitioners).
method: Safe Fuzzy-CBF: Takagi-Sugeno fuzzy rules extracted offline from 300 trajectory segments build a differentiable barrier over state-action-cost; online finite-difference derivative with Lipschitz correction triggers a QP that replaces unsafe RL actions.
evaluation: Three Safety-Gymnasium SafetyCar tasks plus MetaDrive, 500 test runs; baselines PPO-Lag, TRPO-Lag, CPPO-PID before/after monitoring; cumulative cost reduced up to 86.8%; barrier-gain gamma sweep ablation (cost 279->7.52).
contribution: Learned fuzzy control-barrier monitor that evaluates risk online and replaces unsafe RL navigation actions via a small QP, cutting accumulated cost up to 86.8% without degrading the policy.
flag: Explicitly single-agent: 'our method has demonstrated strong safety monitoring performance in single-agent scenarios... to extend it to multi-agent applications it is necessary to combine decentralized barrier function design with graph neural networks'. No measured per-step latency or hardware (real-time feasibility only argued qualitatively in Table I), so (d) not met. Value here is as a safety-filter baseline, not a multi-agent building block; maintainer may weigh E4.

title: Safe Human-Centric Shared Control for Consumer Service Robots in Smart Home Environments via Observer-Based ADP
evidence: 'a control barrier function is mathematically coupled with adaptive dynamic programming. This creates an asymmetric authority shield that actively filters unsafe commands without inducing algorithmic singularities' (Abstract); ablation 'Lacking Safety Filter' gives max intrusion depth 0.82 m and a safety violation vs 0.00 m fully integrated (Table II).
method: Observer-based ADP shared control for smart-home multi-robot networks: NN observer for unmeasured states, state-dependent bounded-rationality human model, CBF-QP authority shield filtering human commands, dynamic event-triggered communication with experience replay.
evaluation: Smart-living-room simulation with four robots under abrupt human panic inputs; triggering-strategy comparison (time-driven/fixed/dynamic: 6000/1850/820 samples, 86.3% packet reduction) and structural ablation (max intrusion 0.00 vs 0.82 m without the safety filter).
contribution: Event-triggered observer-based ADP shared control whose asymmetric authority shield filters kinematically unsafe human commands for consumer multi-robot networks while cutting Wi-Fi transmissions by 86.3%.
flag: Handoff direction is reversed: the automation overrides the non-expert human rather than deferring to a person, so (e) is a loose fit. Simulation only, no hardware; measured safety is barrier intrusion depth for the human-commanded leader, not inter-agent collisions, so (c) fails primacy. 'latency/jitter aware' claimed on the basis of dynamic event-triggered aperiodic/intermittent sampling, not compute timing. Prose is noticeably machine-polished; Table I/II numbers should be re-checked in the final version.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning-Based Motion Planning for Functional Mobile Robots Suffering Uncontrollable Mobile Robots
evidence: Abstract: 'A CBF-based shield is designed for every single functional AMR to ensure that the action of the functional AMR is safe, even if an uncontrollable AMR is pursuing the functional AMR'; Sec. V figures contrast the 'nominal action and safe action' of a robot.
method: Multi-agent TD3 policy with decentralized low-level CBF-based shields that regulate each functional robot's nominal action, with a proof of safety against an optimally pursuing uncontrollable robot.
evaluation: Gazebo warehouse, 3 then 10 AMRs (two uncontrollable), 100 tests; baselines no-shield and dynamic-obstacle-avoidance RL; safe-episode ratio and task time under 0.10 s delay; TurtleBot3 runs at 50 Hz.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; latency/jitter aware; edge deployment
contribution: Decentralized control-barrier shields over a multi-agent RL policy keep warehouse robots safe from a hijacked, actively pursuing robot, reaching 94-98% safe episodes against unshielded and reward-shaped baselines.
flag: Best fit in this batch: action-level override plus a genuinely adversarial multi-agent hazard (out-of-control robot) and a delay condition. (d) rests on the 50 Hz loop and the 0.10 s delay-robustness test rather than a latency-constrained design; no onboard compute figures.

title: Safe and Efficient Multi-Agent Collision Avoidance With Physics-Informed Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Sec. IV-C: 'After the actor network, we integrate a safety layer that addresses the problem through constrained optimization', finding 'a_safe as the action that is closest to a_i while satisfying the safety constraints'.
method: Physics-informed MARL combining potential-field regularisation of the critic loss with a post-actor MAMLS safety layer that Lagrangian-projects each agent's action onto multi-source, multi-level collision constraints.
evaluation: Webots e-puck simulation, 6/8/10 agents, 5 seeds; baselines APF, SAC, CSS, BICARL, BHDQN; success rate, minimum distance, travelled distance; two-module ablation; per-step runtime table; e-puck hardware trials.
contribution: Adds a closed-form multi-agent multi-level safety layer after the policy network, improving collision-free success rate and clearance over five RL and potential-field baselines at negligible per-step cost.
flag: Efficiency (travelled distance, training speed) shares top billing with safety; (d) not claimed - per-step runtime is reported but no explicit latency budget or edge hardware.

title: Safe and Efficient Resource Allocation in Multi-AI-Agent LLM Systems
evidence: "every group of AI agents overloaded the shared resource more often than a simple random policy calibrated to the system's capacity"; the random baseline hits 31.25% overload at (N=4,C=2) while small models overloaded 53.8% and large models 72.5% (Abstract; Sec. III).
method: El Farol Bar study of correlated LLM agent decisions under hard cloud capacity limits; compares personality prompts, epsilon-greedy action-level randomisation and raised sampling temperature as decorrelation mechanisms.
evaluation: 43 experiments, N in {3,4}, capacity in {1,2}, six models from three families, 154 agent instances, 100 feedback rounds; vs calibrated random policy p=C/N; overload rate 1.72-2.32x baseline.
contribution: Correlated reasoning among homogeneous LLM agents overloads shared cloud capacity far more often than a calibrated random policy, and larger models make the collective outcome worse.
flag: Three-page paper: results are narrated with no tables, protocol detail or confidence intervals, so the maintainer may judge the v1.5 floor only marginally met (baseline and quantitative overload rates are present). The proposed fix - epsilon-greedy randomisation of the final go/stay action (67.5% vs 100% overload) - does override the reasoned decision at execution time, but as decorrelation rather than a safety filter, which is why runtime_interceptor is no.

title: Safe and Scalable Multi-Agent Optimization for Autonomous Electric Taxi Dispatching via a Two-Stage Reinforcement Learning Framework
evidence: Sec. VII-C ablation: "the action filter pi plays a critical role in filtering invalid actions during execution", and with it removed "constraint violations remain severe even in later stages of training"; the Note to Practitioners reports ACAF "filters out 99.7% of infeasible actions and reduces energy violations to 0.4 per 10 hours" and a 38.7 percent drop in action conflict rate.
method: Two-stage MARL: a VDN value-decomposition action classifier filters energy-infeasible and conflicting actions for each agent, then a utility-prioritised model-based search maximises fleet utility inside the filtered feasible space.
evaluation: Simulated fleet of 200 electric taxis, 15 charging stations, scaled upward; baselines MADDPG, QMIX, IQL, MILP; energy, busy-state and order-conflict violation counts plus profit; two-stage ablation.
contribution: Decouples constraint handling from reward maximisation: a learned value-decomposition action filter vetoes infeasible or conflicting fleet actions at execution time, then utility search optimises within the feasible set.
flag: Clearest runtime action filter in this batch, with the filter ablated and violation counts against MARL and MILP baselines. Revenue is a co-headline with constraint satisfaction, so (c) primacy is arguable; the hazard is energy depletion and order/charger conflict rather than collision. Simulation only, and no latency, per-decision time or hardware figures despite the real-time framing.

title: Safe exploration: Addressing various uncertainty levels in human robot interactions
evidence: Sec. III-C 'A Projection to the Set of Safe Control': "Suppose there is a baseline control law u_R^o(t) for the robot R, which drives the robot to its goal without safety considerations. Then u_R^o(t) is mapped to the set of safe control U_S^R(t)"; Sec. III-B/V learn the humans' closed-loop behaviour by RLS in belief space and predict x_j(k+1) with an a priori MSEE bound.
method: Safe exploration algorithm: safety-index invariance defines a safe control set; online belief-space RLS estimation of human state uncertainty sizes the margin; nominal goal-seeking control is projected into that set.
evaluation: Single simulated human-vehicle interaction, human driven live via trackpad; SEA versus authors' prior SSA baseline; metrics relative distance (always >dmin=3), velocity smoothness, prediction-error bound. No latency/hardware.
contribution: Extends the safe set algorithm with online belief-space uncertainty estimation so a runtime projection of nominal control tightens or relaxes the safety margin with confidence, trading early conservatism for smoother motion.
flag: Criterion (a) is met cleanly (explicit projection of a safety-agnostic baseline controller), but evaluation is thin: one simulated scenario with one vehicle and one trackpad-driven human, compared only against the authors' own prior SSA; safety metric is a relative-distance profile, no collision/violation statistics, so the E2 floor is met only marginally. Multi-agent framing is nominal (N=2), hence (c) not credited. Authors state mobile-robot experiments are future work.

title: Safe multi-agent motion planning via filtered reinforcement learning
evidence: Sec. I: 'we develop a quadratic programming-based safety filter that ensures collective safety of a multi-agent system, while minimizing the deviation from the control input prescribed by a RL-based motion planner'; Sec. IV-A: computation 'below 0.1 s, which enable a real-time implementation at 10Hz'.
method: Single-agent RL policy (PPO) for target regulation plus a convex QP safety filter enforcing collective hard constraints (inter-agent and obstacle collision avoidance, state/input limits) on its actions.
evaluation: Six Crazyflie quadrotors (OptiTrack, 10 Hz waypoints) and simulation; 500 random configurations: no safety violations, 80.6% completion; vs unfiltered RL (collisions) and proportional baseline; under 0.1 s per iteration.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; non-generative inference; latency/jitter aware
contribution: A convex-QP safety filter makes a single-agent RL motion planner collectively safe for six quadrotors, enforcing hard collision constraints in real time at 10 Hz with moderate scaling cost.
flag: Strong candidate baseline for RQ1/RQ5; cost of filtering is deadlock in 19.4% of configurations and under 2% loitering; compute is an offboard Xeon workstation, not edge hardware.

title: SafeFlow: Attribution-Driven Adaptive Security Defense for Large Language Model Agents
evidence: "L2 performs three-tier cascaded verification before each tool" call and "if d = DENY" the call is blocked, with degradation levels mapping to L3 tool-permission bounds (Sec. III-D); "SafeFlow reduces UBR from 28.74% to 18.56% and ASR from 26.40% to 16.20% compared with SafeHarness" (Sec. IV-B).
method: SafeFlow embeds attribution-aware XGuard classifiers (0.6B L1 input filter, 8B L2 tool-call verifier) in the agent execution loop; confidence-aware adaptive degradation bounds tool permissions and feeds cross-layer attribution.
evaluation: Agent-SafetyBench (349 environments, 2,000 cases) under ReAct, Multi-Agent and Self-Evolving paradigms; vs unprotected, system-prompt, guardrail, LlamaFirewall, SafeHarness; UBR 18.56%, ASR 16.20%, TCR 93.08%; 6 ms L1, 50 ms L2.
contribution: An attribution-driven runtime guardrail blocks unsafe agent tool calls with confidence-graded degradation, cutting unsafe-behaviour and attack-success rates about ten points over lifecycle-defence baselines at 93% task completion.
flag: Latency is reported as overhead (6 ms/50 ms, +0.4-2.4 s end-to-end) with no deadline, so (d) was not claimed. Multi-agent is one of three execution paradigms rather than the focus. Compound attack class A5 (72.8% attribution accuracy) is the only compositional-hazard evidence. Fast-L1/slow-L2 cascade is machine-only; no human handoff.

title: SafeHierarchy: Benchmarking and Mitigating Hierarchy-Induced Harmful Compliance in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: Sec. VI: 'the Analysis layer strips authority cues and estimates causal dependence, while the Execution layer routes low-risk cases through a sanitized relay and high-risk cases through power-conditioned intervention' when risk R exceeds threshold tau=0.35, before the downstream agent acts.
method: Training-free inference-time defense on the relay pathway: strips French-Raven authority markers, re-queries the model counterfactually, scores authority reliance/persistence/task alignment, and above threshold triggers a rewrite, evidence or role-reset intervention arm.
evaluation: 300-case stratified benchmark on three backbones; baselines Instruction Hierarchy, Spotlighting, AgentDojo Input-Prompt; ASR 44.3% to 1.0% with bootstrap CIs and McNemar p=1.3e-7; TCR 99-100% on 100 benign tasks; no latency.
contribution: Shows hierarchical agent topologies themselves amplify harmful compliance (mean CAF 3.12), and that gating interventions on a counterfactual authority probe cuts attack success to 1% without taxing benign task completion.
flag: Strongest RQ5 evidence in this batch: explicit over-blocking versus utility trade-off against three published inference-time defenses, with TCR as the false-halt proxy. Costs an extra model query per relay but reports no latency or token overhead; text-only, single-turn, fixed topologies and heuristic risk weights (authors' own limitations). Benefit is uneven across backbones (only 2.6 pp on GPT-4.1).

title: SafeSeCA: Safe Action Decomposition for 3D Deformation of Large Soft-Linear Objects
evidence: Sec. IV-C and Conclusion: with ray masking plus an inverse-kinematics check 'all unsafe actions a_i_t are replaced for safe and viable actions', and 'the safe action set and viability check act on commanded velocities rather than simulation internals', so the layer could transfer unchanged to a real Panda.
method: Two sub-agents (translation, rotation) share one reward and sequential credit assignment; zonotope-based continuous ray masking plus an IK viability check map each raw action into the safe, kinematically feasible set.
evaluation: PyBullet FEM deformable-linear-object shaping with a Franka Panda; ablations DDPG-SA and action-replacement ReSeCA plus MultiAC6 baseline; safe-action proportion 1.0 vs 0.53, success 0.95 vs 0.41, seen and unseen goals.
contribution: Extends continuous zonotope action masking to multi-agent RL with a kinematic viability check, attaining a 1.0 safe-action rate and far higher success than action-replacement safeguards on deformable-object manipulation.
flag: Multi-agent only nominally: two sub-agents command one Franka gripper and there is no inter-agent hazard, so E4 is arguable (it survives on the sequential aspect). (a) is borderline - the mask is differentiable and trained with the policy (pre-emptive masking) even though the authors describe it as a transferable safety layer on commanded velocities. Value is mainly RQ5: a measured comparison of masking against action replacement.

title: Safety Barrier Certificates for Collisions-Free Multirobot Systems
evidence: Abstract: 'safety barrier certificates that ensure scalable and provably collision-free behaviors in multirobot systems by modifying the nominal controllers to formally satisfy safety constraints ... minimizing the difference between the actual and the nominal controllers subject to safety constraints'; Sec. VIII wraps them around nominal controllers 'explicitly designed to make the robots collide'.
method: Control-barrier-function QP that minimally modifies nominal multirobot controllers; centralized then decentralized with reduced neighbourhood, plus relaxed CBFs, a hybrid maximum-braking controller for QP feasibility and consistent perturbations for deadlock resolution.
evaluation: Position-swap and leader-follower simulations plus hardware with 8 and 5 Khepera III robots whose nominal controllers were designed to collide; ablation over nominal/relaxed/feasible certificates and centralized vs decentralized; metric inter-robot distance vs safety distance Ds; 60 robots >30 Hz centralized, >100 robots >100 Hz decentralized on a 2.6 GHz i5.
contribution: Foundational safety barrier certificates: a real-time QP that minimally modifies nominal multirobot controllers to guarantee collision-free behaviour, decentralised to neighbour-only computation with braking-based feasibility and deadlock resolution.
flag: Foundational SBC paper and the direct ancestor of doi:10.1109/lra.2020.2974713 in this batch. Safety is proved rather than counted: the quantitative safety evidence is minimum inter-robot distance against Ds across three certificate variants plus hardware runs with deliberately colliding nominal controllers. (d) rests on laptop-CPU update rates (>100 Hz), not edge hardware or an explicit deadline.

title: Safety for Time-Varying Parameterized Sets Using Control Barrier Function Methods
evidence: Sec. IV: 'The agents each minimally modify their nominal control input unom using the functions hj as described in algorithm 1', each agent i running a safe-set function with every other agent j.
method: Log-sum-exp overapproximations of convex ego and obstacle sets make the squared inter-set distance differentiable, giving smooth CBF constraints and safety-preserving inputs by convex optimization for parameterized sets.
evaluation: One demonstrative Python/JAX simulation, four polytope-bodied unicycle agents swapping goals; only reported metric is min_j h_ij remaining above zero; no baseline, ablation or timing.
contribution: Smooth CBF method keeps a whole time-varying parameterized convex body, not a single point, out of unsafe sets, giving differentiable set-distance safety filters for polytope-shaped agents.
flag: Theory paper: single 4-agent demonstration, no baseline or ablation and no hazard rate, so the v1.5 evaluation floor fails; the mechanism itself is a genuine runtime filter if wanted as a method reference.

title: Safety-Critical Control for Multi-Agent Collaborative Pursuit
evidence: Sec. III-B: 'we introduce a Minimum Intrusion Safety Strategy, formulating the problem as a QP challenge. This QP problem aims to minimize the discrepancy between the nominal control command, ud, and the actual control command, ui, under the constraint of CBF.'
method: Voronoi partitioning assigns evaders and yields a nominal pursuit input; a distributed zeroing-CBF quadratic program minimally modifies it online for obstacle and inter-agent collision avoidance.
evaluation: Single MATLAB scenario: 4 pursuers, 3 evaders, single integrators, 1m x 1m cluttered arena, 0.01s steps. No baseline or ablation; results are barrier-value, minimum-distance and velocity-CDF plots.
contribution: A minimally invasive QP-CBF layer over Voronoi-based pursuit assignment lets multiple pursuers capture multiple evaders in cluttered arenas while provably staying inside the safe set.
flag: Clear runtime safety filter over a nominal controller ((a) met) and genuinely multi-agent, but the only evaluation is one simulation run with no baseline, no ablation and no quantitative safety or capture rate - qualitative demonstration, so the v1.5 evaluation floor is not reached.

title: Safety-Critical Formation Tracking Control of Multi-Robot Systems via CLF-CBF-QP
evidence: Sec. IV three-stage fallback: Stage 2 is a safety-only QP that drops the CLF performance objective and "strictly enforces all safety constraints, guaranteeing forward invariance of the safe set", with Stage 3 minimally relaxing them to prevent controller failure.
method: Hierarchical-fallback CLF-HOCBF-QP: Stage 1 tracks a PD reference under safety constraints, Stage 2 drops performance to keep safety feasible, Stage 3 adds penalised slack avoiding QP infeasibility and deadlock.
evaluation: MATLAB quadprog, 10 double-integrator agents, V-formation tracking a 0.5 m/s leader, 0.05 s sampling; figures only; average solver time 5-10 ms per robot; no baseline or ablation.
contribution: A three-stage fallback CLF-HOCBF-QP that degrades from tracking to safety-only to penalised-slack modes, keeping ten-agent formation control feasible and collision-free at 5-10 ms solver time per robot.
flag: Fails the evaluation floor: safety distances and stage activation are shown only as figures, with no baseline or ablation, and the abstract's claim of computational efficiency "comparable to standard CLF-CBF-QP" is never measured. Still worth the maintainer's eye - the graceful-degradation fallback hierarchy (full performance / safety-only / minimal-violation) is structurally close to the dual-speed halt in RQ3, and the 5-10 ms per-robot solver time is RQ1-relevant.

title: Safety-Guaranteed Distributed Formation Control of Multi-Robot Systems Over Graphs With Rigid and Elastic Edges
evidence: Sec. II: 'given a nominal control input unom that encapsulates the primary control objective, the safe control input can be computed via u = arg min ||u - unom||^2' subject to CBF constraints; in Sec. IV-A the nominal input is a proportional go-to-goal controller.
method: Distributed CBF-QP filters each robot's nominal go-to-goal input to enforce LiDAR-based obstacle avoidance and graph formation constraints with rigid and elastic edges and dynamic distance tolerances.
evaluation: Single testbed trial, 4 TurtleBot3 Burger robots, VICON, ROS2, 50 Hz control loop and 5 Hz LiDAR; plots of minimum obstacle distance and per-edge distances; no baseline or ablation.
contribution: Encodes rigid and elastic formation edges together with obstacle avoidance as control-barrier constraints in a distributed QP that minimally modifies each robot's nominal command.
flag: Structurally a true CBF-QP safety filter, but one four-robot trial with no baseline or ablation and only qualitative safety claims; obstacles are static, hazard is inter-robot distance only.

title: Safety-Guaranteed Energy Management in Networked Multienergy Microgrids: A Multi-Actor Single-Critic Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach
evidence: Sec. III-D: "the model-based safety layer is invoked during both training and execution" and "the final action is projected onto the intersection of these intervals" by clipping; Sec. IV-C: the layer gives "zero observed violations and 100% safety accuracy" against 12,543 (penalty MADRL), 10,054 (Lagrangian constrained RL) and 1,250 (PI-SPPO) violations.
method: Multi-actor single-critic MARL with randomized ensembled double Q-learning critic for five-node networked multi-energy microgrids; analytic closed-form safety layer clips each action, with forward-looking hydrogen-chain bounds.
evaluation: Five-node N-MEMG simulation, 500 test days (12,000 steps); baselines MATD3, MADDPG, MASAC, Lagrangian CRL, penalty MADRL, PI-SPPO; violation counts, safety accuracy, daily normalised score; RTX 4080, no latency.
contribution: An analytic non-learned safety layer clips multi-agent RL actions to closed-form admissible intervals, including forward-looking bounds on inertial device chains, giving zero observed constraint violations.
flag: (c) is borderline: violations are mostly per-device and power-balance constraints rather than genuinely inter-agent hazards. The forward-looking bounds that "prevent delayed violations" over the horizon are the closest thing to time-to-irreversibility. No latency or edge measurement.

title: Scalable Safety Assurance in Multi-Agent Systems via Symmetry Reduction and Quotient Model Verification
evidence: Sec. III-A/IV: 'Safety requirements, such as collision avoidance and task achievement, are modeled as temporal logic requirements for formal verification'; after verification-guided retraining 'the per-cycle collision probability reduced from 0.028 to 0.002' and for 100 agents verification time fell 'from a stated 120 hours for the full system to 7.8 hours for the quotient model'.
method: Group behaviourally equivalent agents into equivalence classes, build a reduced quotient model, verify collision/temporal-logic properties by reachability on it, retrain only representative neural controllers, then update the whole fleet.
evaluation: Undocumented warehouse simulation with 50- and 100-agent fleets; comparator is full-system verification that was not run ('a stated 120 hours'); reports verification time, RAM 32GB->4.5GB, collision probability per cycle, task completion, accuracy/precision/recall. No verifier, simulator or seeds named.
contribution: Symmetry-reduced quotient verification with selective retraining of representative agents claims fleet-wide collision-avoidance assurance at a fraction of full multi-agent verification cost.
flag: Design-time verification plus retraining, no runtime interception. The headline measured outcome is verification speedup rather than a hazard rate against a real baseline, so (c) also fails the primacy test; figures are unlabelled and the baseline cost is asserted, not measured.

title: Scalable Safety-Critical Policy Evaluation with Accelerated Rare Event Sampling
evidence: Abstract/Sec. I: 'This paper proposes the Accelerated Policy Evaluation (APE) method, which simultaneously uncovers rare events and estimates the rare event probability in Markov decision processes' - offline pre-deployment estimation, no runtime mechanism.
method: Adaptive importance sampling for MDP policy evaluation: an environment adversary (conditional normalizing flow) plus a Gaussian-process value estimator learn the zero-variance sampling distribution.
evaluation: highway-env intersections (Int-v0/v1) and LunarLander; baselines APE-discrete, CEM-discrete, vanilla Monte Carlo; metrics bias, std, MSE, sampled rare-event rate; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Accelerated Policy Evaluation estimates rare crash probabilities for sequential RL policies with orders-of-magnitude fewer samples by learning an adversarial environment sampling distribution.
flag: Borderline: safety-critical but it is pre-deployment testing, not runtime interception; primary measured outcome is estimator bias/variance, not a hazard rate, and 'APE can handle more than two agents by treating all the other agents as part of the environment', so (c) primacy fails.

title: Self-Supervised Learning with Variational Autoencoders for Anomaly Detection in Autonomous Drone Fleets
evidence: Sec. IV: anomalies are per-UAV telemetry deviations ("real-time tracking of altitude, speed, battery level, and deviations of paths") and the measured outcome is detection quality - "best accuracy (94%), precision (92%), and recall (91%)" against One-Class SVM and DBSCAN; no inter-agent hazard rate is reported.
method: Isolation-Forest anomaly scoring on UAV telemetry with MDP trajectory prediction and DQN/crow-search path re-optimisation; Algorithm 1 flags a drone, replans its path and redirects it to the nearest landing zone if battery is low.
evaluation: Simulated smart-city multi-UAV corridors; baselines One-Class SVM and DBSCAN; accuracy, precision, recall, false-positive/negative rate, AUC-ROC ~0.91 vs ~0.87; claimed 20% collision-risk and 15% energy improvement unsupported by any table; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Isolation-Forest telemetry anomaly detection with MDP prediction and DQN re-routing for UAV fleets, reporting 94% detection accuracy against One-Class SVM and DBSCAN baselines.
flag: Single-agent telemetry guardrail - the "fleet" is nominal and no unsafe interaction between drones is measured, so (c) fails the primacy test. Low-quality and internally inconsistent: the title promises self-supervised VAEs but the method is Isolation Forest + MDP + DQN, and Sec. IV states "One Class SVM achieves the highest accuracy and lowest false positives" while the abstract claims the opposite. The landing-zone override exists only in pseudocode and is never evaluated, hence runtime_interceptor = no.

title: Sequential Cooperative Multi-Agent Online Learning and Adaptive Coordination Control in Dynamic and Uncertain Environments
evidence: Abstract and Sec. II-F: "The learned nominal inputs are then wrapped by a minimally invasive quadratic-program (QP) safety filter that enforces collision avoidance, formation/tracking constraints, and input saturation in real time".
method: Task graph activates ordered subtasks; agents run distributed online actor-critic with event-triggered neighbour messaging; a CBF/CLF QP safety filter plus adaptive disturbance compensation wraps the learned nominal input.
evaluation: 6/8/10 agents, three missions, 200 runs, dt=0.02 s; baselines fixed-gain, centralized MPC/DMPC, CTDE actor-critic, single-stage safe MARL; 94.7 percent success, zero violations; ablation without the QP filter.
contribution: Wraps distributed online actor-critic learning for ordered multi-robot missions in a minimally invasive CBF/CLF QP filter, reporting 94.7 percent task success and zero safety violations against four baselines with a filter ablation.
flag: Strongest evaluation in this batch: four baselines plus a "w/o QP safety filter" ablation over 200 runs. (c) primacy borderline because task success rate, not violation rate, is the headline number. The jitter relevance is communication staleness - a conservative margin eta capturing "neighbour motion between message updates" - not compute latency; simulation only, no hardware or solver timings reported. Author list and venue suggest limited peer review; the maintainer may want to sanity-check the numbers.

title: Stable, Safe, and Passive Teleoperation of Multi-Robot Systems
evidence: Remark 11 (Sec. III-E): 'Solving the QP (17) can be interpreted as filtering the desired control input given in (2) - comprised of a state feedback component, uc, and a human input, uh - to obtain v*', which is then integrated to form the input actually supplied to the multi-robot system.
method: Stability-safety-passivity filter: convex QP with control Lyapunov and integral control barrier functions minimally modifies the human teleoperation input to a multi-robot team before execution.
evaluation: One hardware demonstration, 6 DJI RoboMaster EP robots, Robohub; with- vs without-filter runs; qualitative unsafe-region violation plus CLF/CBF trajectory plots; no rates, no timings.
contribution: Unifies stability, safety and passivity as constraints in a single convex-QP filter that minimally modifies a human teleoperator's input to a multi-robot team at execution time.
flag: Genuine runtime input filter with a with/without-filter ablation, but evaluation is one qualitative 6-robot demonstration (no violation rate, no latency), so it fails the v1.5 floor.

title: Super-Ellipse Control Barrier Functions for Enhanced Obstacle Avoidance in Complex Multi-Agent Environments
evidence: Sec. III-B: "The median value for SE-CBF is approximately 0.45, with the interquartile range between 0.44 and 0.46... In contrast, the median value for CBF is around 0.385" for average minimum distance to obstacles and other robots, against a 0.3 m threshold.
method: Replaces the circular CBF safety set with a super-ellipse whose per-axis scalings and exponent n are tuned, so safety margins shrink or enlarge along different axes around non-uniform obstacles.
evaluation: ROS/Gazebo roundabout, 8 robots, 15 trials, identical initial states; baseline conventional circular CBF; metric average minimum distance (median 0.45 versus 0.385 m, threshold 0.3); plus qualitative 4-robot hardware trials.
contribution: Reshapes the CBF safety set as a tunable super-ellipse so robots exploit free space around irregular obstacles, holding a larger median minimum distance (0.45 versus 0.385 m) than a circular-CBF baseline at an eight-robot intersection.
flag: Method section defines only the barrier function - no QP, nominal input or controller formulation is given - so the runtime architecture is unstated and runtime_interceptor is marked no; (a) cannot be confirmed from the text. (c) primacy borderline: the stated motivation is reduced conservatism and path efficiency. The "obstacle avoidance success rate" that Sec. III names as the performance measure is never reported, the real-robot trials are purely qualitative, and control runs on an off-board PC.

title: Swarm Modeling With Dynamic Mode Decomposition
evidence: Abstract: 'a modified version of dynamic mode decomposition with control, called swarmDMD, is developed and tested on the canonical Vicsek swarm model ... to learn inter-agent interactions that give rise to the observed swarm behaviour.'
method: swarmDMD: dynamic mode decomposition with control adapted to swarms, learning a linear operator over inter-agent relative positions to reconstruct and briefly extrapolate swarm dynamics.
evaluation: Vicsek simulated swarms (standard and milling) across interaction radii; position, heading, polarisation and angular-momentum errors plus neighbour distributions versus ground truth; re-initialisation variant; no safety metric.
contribution: Shows data-driven dynamic mode decomposition can reconstruct homogeneous swarm dynamics from observation alone, with a short accurate prediction window trading accuracy against horizon.
flag: protocol v1.6: included as world-model/predictor evidence on a predictive-accuracy metric with a baseline or ablation; not safety evidence, RQ5 capped at 2. Fails the v1.5 evaluation floor: no quantitative safety metric and no safety mechanism anywhere - only reconstruction/prediction error on Vicsek data. Maintainer may prefer E1 since safety is never addressed.

title: Swarm-Steward: Scalable and Reliable Natural-Language Coordination of Autonomous Aerial and Ground Robots
evidence: "all actions must pass through deterministic tool boundaries and safety validation layers that enforce operational constraints, including geofencing, altitude limits, clearance requirements, and inter-robot separation. Actions can be previewed and optionally confirmed by the operator before dispatch" (Sec. I).
method: Swarm-Steward: hierarchical LLM multi-agent natural-language swarm control; query-only spatial/history agents, dual RAG over map features and telemetry, schema-constrained deterministic tools behind a safety gate plus operator preview/confirmation and abort.
evaluation: 280 prompts, 5-500 drones in simulation, 10,000-feature retrieval, 15-model replay, DJI Mini 4 Pro field trial; 92.9% prompt success, ~5.1 s latency; no safety metric or baseline.
contribution: Natural-language swarm control treats LLM outputs as proposals validated by a deterministic geofence/separation gate with operator preview, scaling to 500 drones at 92.9% prompt success.
flag: The safety gate and operator confirmation are asserted but never measured: reported metrics are prompt success, tokens and latency only - no violation rate, gate-rejection rate, near-miss count or safety baseline, so the v1.5 floor fails. (c) would also fail the primacy test (paper is about scalable coordination). UAV plus the earlier UGV deployment are both physical, so cross-domain does not apply. Still the best architecture exemplar in this batch for RQ3 (preview/confirm plus any-time abort) if the maintainer wants a non-evidential reference.

title: Synthesis of Minimum-Cost Shields for Multi-agent Systems
evidence: Sec. I: 'A shield is attached to a reactive system, monitors the behaviour of the system (i.e., its inputs and outputs), and corrects erroneous outputs instantaneously, but only if necessary and as infrequently as possible'; Fig. 2 shows the shield overriding each agent's intended action to prevent collision.
method: Shield synthesis for multi-agent systems from LTL global safety specifications, with interference cost functions, assumptions bounding runs of wrong outputs, and synthesis of cost-optimal and fair shields via reactive and Streett games (Slugs).
evaluation: Two case studies: 2-agent gridworld with charging station, and 3 UAVs on a warehouse mission in ROS/Gazebo; Table I reports input/output bits, game variables, reachable states and synthesis times for two values of the bound b; Intel i5 2.3 GHz; no hazard rate or baseline.
contribution: First shield synthesis for multi-agent systems with quantitative objectives, introducing interference cost and fairness so a runtime enforcer corrects agents' unsafe actions with minimal, fairly distributed interference.
flag: Canonical multi-agent shield formalism, strongly on-topic for (a) and conceptually for RQ5 (interference cost is the false-halt/intervention-cost idea), but the only quantitative results are synthesis times and state-space sizes - safety is correct-by-construction and never measured. Worth keeping as a method citation if the maintainer relaxes the v1.5 floor.

title: System Architecture for Digital Twin Based Collision Avoidance Through Private 5G Networks
evidence: Abstract: 'One approach to reduce this risk is to implement collision avoidance systems that intervene in the driving process, for example through warnings or speed reduction... For moving targets, wireless communication is required with high reliability, low latency and high data rates'; Sec. IV-C: RTT latency from 92 minutes of data, 5540 samples at 1 Hz, over a private 5G campus network with delay budget tau = 1/f + tau_rtt + tau_edge.
method: Forklift RTLS pose is streamed over private 5G to an edge-server digital twin that predicts collision events and returns warnings or dynamic speed reduction; centralized and decentralized flows analysed.
evaluation: Analytical efficiency comparison of global speed limit, zoning and dynamic speed reduction (drivable distance); 5G throughput model for n trucks; measured ICMP RTT on one forklift, 5540 samples.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; latency/jitter aware; edge deployment
contribution: A private-5G digital twin on an edge server predicts forklift collisions and returns warnings or dynamic speed reduction, with measured round-trip latency and throughput bounds for fleet-scale deployment.
flag: Closest paper in the batch to the latency/edge criterion (d) and the intervention is a genuine runtime speed-reduction/warning override, but it is an architecture and feasibility study: no measured collision, warning-accuracy or false-alarm metric, the efficiency comparison is analytical with an assumed 1% hazard incidence, and only one forklift was instrumented. Maintainer may want it as background for RQ1/RQ2 latency budgets.

title: Teleoperating Mobile Robots Via Vda 5050 - a First Middleware Evaluation Within Open Industrial Networks
evidence: Sec. I: "Teleoperation complements autonomy by providing a practical fallback for rare but safety- and throughput-critical edge cases such as blockages or navigation failures, where human intervention is required to maintain operational flow"; Sec. IV-C reports end-to-end uplink latency of roughly 11-30 ms across MQTT and Zenoh configurations over Open RAN.
method: VDA 5050 extension adding teleoperation instant actions (startTeleop/stopTeleop), an FMS teleoperation extension bridging WebSocket and MQTT with route-release policies, WebRTC video, plus an open-source VDA 5050 traffic generator.
evaluation: Software/hardware-in-the-loop Open5GS plus srsRAN Open RAN testbed (virtual radio and real 5G radio unit); MQTT versus Zenoh TCP/UDP/QUIC; end-to-end uplink latency and RLC-layer overhead; one simulated robot; no safety metric.
gap_cells: latency/jitter aware; edge deployment; human handoff
contribution: A VDA 5050 extension makes human teleoperation takeover a first-class part of fleet management, with measured end-to-end latency and protocol overhead for MQTT versus Zenoh over Open RAN.
flag: Topically strong for (e) and RQ3 but fails the evaluation floor: only latency, overhead and goodput are measured, with no safety outcome and no human-factors study (no participants). Multi-agent only nominally, since the evaluated scenario is a single simulated robot. The override is a human-initiated takeover channel, not an automated filter. Keep as latency-budget background for the handoff path.

title: The Model of Ship Navigation Risk Field for Risk Assessment of Icebreaker Convoy Operations
evidence: Sec. II: "the crews of the following ships can access the navigation risk in real time by comparing the current potential energy to the acceptable potential energy and making decisions based on this comparison"; the ship risk field "describes the ship-ship collision risk" within the convoy (Abstract).
method: Artificial-potential-field navigation risk field superposing a ship risk field (ship-ship collision) and a sea-ice risk field (stuck-in-channel risk) to derive minimum and maximum safe following distances for convoy ships.
evaluation: One 2018 Arctic convoy case (three ships, one day of AIS and ice data); minimum safe distance vs an existing safety-distance model (RMSE/MAE/MAPE <1.3%), maximum distance vs operator records.
contribution: Models icebreaker-convoy risk as superposed potential fields, giving following ships a real-time index bounding both collision and ice-entrapment risk that agrees with existing safe-distance models to within 1.3%.
flag: (c) is met on topic, but the only quantitative comparison is MAPE agreement with a prior safe-distance formula on a single convoy day; no collision, violation or alarm-rate outcome and no ablation. Advisory index for human crews, no runtime interception and no learned component. If the maintainer counts model-agreement as a baseline comparison this becomes a weak include.

title: The Safe Trusted Autonomy for Responsible Space Program
evidence: Sec. 4: "The RTA filter outputs an actual control signal uact that is either a) the unchanged desired control udes if it meets safety constraints, or b) a modified control command that ensures safety when necessary"; Sec. 6: trained controllers and "a majority of RTA configurations designed for spacecraft inspection have a maximum observed execution time well below 2 milliseconds on both the COTS and rad-tolerant processors".
method: Program integrating RL multi-satellite inspection control, switching and Active Set Invariance Filter run-time assurance over mission/collision constraints, and a human-autonomy interface exposing RTA settings and intervention timelines.
evaluation: Narrative summary of prior studies: RL-with/without-RTA ablations, discrete versus continuous CBFs, sub-2 ms RTA execution on COTS and rad-tolerant spacecraft processors, LINCS drone-lab integration; interface effectiveness left to future work.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; non-generative inference; latency/jitter aware; edge deployment; human handoff
methods: shielding; barrier-functions; reinforcement-learning; real-time-systems; human-factors; formal-methods
contribution: Programme retrospective integrating RL multi-satellite control, barrier-function run-time assurance executing under 2 ms on rad-tolerant processors, and an operator interface that explains when and why RTA intervened.
flag: Programme overview: every quantitative result is attributed to a cited paper and the interface is explicitly unevaluated ("detailed analysis of the effectiveness is left to future work"), so exclude-E2 fits equally. Highest-value signpost in this batch - it touches (a), (c), (d), (e) and RQ3's fast-halt/slow-explanation split; queue refs [25] (RTA-in-training ablation), [33] (secondary RTA) and [90] (spacecraft-processor timing) for separate screening.

title: Towards Efficient Distributed Collision Avoidance for Heterogeneous Mobile Robots
evidence: Sec. VII-C: 'Heter-CA achieves the lowest failure rate and collision rate compared with the baselines in real-world scenarios with dense obstacles'; Sec. VI-D: computation time 'directly impacts the response time... long computation time can output a delayed control command, resulting in unsafe control', measured in ms on a Raspberry Pi 3 on-board MCU (Sec. VII-A).
method: Each robot broadcasts size/pose/velocity, predicts neighbour trajectories and estimates static-obstacle extent from range finders, then picks collision-free linear/angular velocity inside its own motion constraints.
evaluation: Gazebo circle/group/warehouse scenarios (2-12 robots) plus 4 real TurtleBots on Raspberry Pi 3; baselines DWA, NH-ORCA, RL-Policy; success/failure/collision/stuck rate and ms computation time (10x faster).
gap_cells: multi-agent state; non-generative inference; latency/jitter aware; edge deployment
contribution: Heter-CA lets heterogeneous robots predict neighbour trajectories and obstacle extents on-board, cutting collision and failure rates while running 10x faster than DWA, NH-ORCA and RL baselines.
flag: Borderline (c) primacy: collision rate is reported against three baselines in sim and on hardware, but efficiency (success rate, makespan, 10x computation time) shares top billing in title and abstract. No interception layer - collision avoidance is the planner's own objective, so (a) fails. (d) has ms-level measurement on embedded hardware but no explicit deadline.

title: Trust-Adaptive Explainable Consensus and Permissioned Governance for Collaborative Embodied AI in Smart-Hospital IIoT Networks
evidence: Sec. IV-D: "Approved requests get proceeded directly to execution while denied requests get rejected and recorded. Those requests having significant conflicting recommendations, uncertainty, safety concerns or elevated risk levels get escalated to human oversight", with life-critical escalations on a 60-second clinician SLA.
method: Five governance agents (policy, privacy, clinical, risk, safety) score each request; trust-weighted consensus returns approve, deny or escalate-to-human; decisions and trust records go to a permissioned blockchain.
evaluation: Simulated smart-hospital workload of 1000 requests (600 data access, 400 physical actions), 10 repeats, versus RBAC, ABAC, blockchain and trust-based governance; 97 percent governance accuracy; component ablation.
gap_cells: multi-agent state; human handoff; cross-domain evaluation
contribution: Trust-weighted multi-agent approval gate for embodied hospital AI that approves, denies or escalates each physical action or data request to a clinician, with blockchain-auditable explanations.
flag: Magazine-format paper and a fully simulated prototype; the headline metric is governance accuracy against expected policy outcomes rather than a hazard rate, and the ablation is reported only as deltas in prose (adaptive trust worth about 2.1 percent). I claimed cross-domain evaluation because the same gate is measured on 400 physical device actions and 600 logical data-access requests - please confirm that reading, since both sit inside one simulated hospital.

title: Trust-Aware Runtime Verification for Autonomous LLM Agent Systems
evidence: Sec. V-A, Table I: TARV reaches 0.91 average violation-detection precision and 0.91 recall versus 0.62 / 0.66 for post-hoc filtering, and Sec. V-C reports reduced cascading-failure rate and higher task success across tool-oriented, collaborative and long-horizon multi-agent LLM tasks.
method: Middleware instrumentation layer intercepts agent actions, memory updates and inter-agent messages; parallel verification agents score action validity, constraint adherence, memory and communication coherence into a thresholded trust score.
evaluation: 150 tasks (ToolBench/CAMEL/AgentBench-derived), GPT-4-Turbo agents, 5 runs each; baselines no-verification, static prompt safeguards, post-hoc filtering; precision/recall, FPR, cascading-failure rate, success rate, per-step latency on one RTX A4000.
contribution: TARV monitors autonomous LLM agent execution through a non-intrusive middleware, computing multi-dimensional trust signals that detect runtime violations earlier and more precisely than post-hoc filtering.
flag: Fails the strict runtime criterion (a) by the paper's own statement: 'Importantly, TARV does not attempt to enforce corrective actions directly' - it only emits trust diagnostics for higher-level controllers, human operators or self-healing layers. Unresolved tension: cascading-failure reduction and higher success rates are claimed despite no enforcement path, so the causal mechanism is unexplained. False-positive rate is asserted as 'low' in prose but no number is given.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Model-Based Offline Reinforcement Learning for Automated Driving
evidence: Abstract: 'A trained action-conditioned stochastic dynamics model captures distinctively different future evolutions of the traffic scene', rolled out during planning under partial observability (Sec. III).
method: UMBRELLA: model-based offline RL that plans in MPC over an action-conditioned stochastic latent dynamics model of the multi-agent traffic scene under partial observability.
evaluation: NGSIM I-80 and CARLA intersection (ID, OOD, adversarial; 60 scenarios each); baselines BC, BC-VAE, MBOP, NMP, MPUR; ablations without ensemble/value; success rate; RTX 3090 runtime.
contribution: Adds a stochastic multi-agent dynamics model and partial observability to model-based offline RL planning, raising collision-free success rates over MBOP and imitation baselines in dense traffic.
flag: (c) fails primacy: success rate is the collision-free episode rate, but the primary claim is offline-RL method quality; the dynamics model is generative and sits inside the planner, not a runtime filter.

title: Using Control Barrier Functions for Constrained Reinforcement Learning in Backward Chained Behavior Trees
evidence: Sec. I: "By filtering out unsafe actions using CBFs, we can enable RL with safety guarantees"; Sec. IV adds that "the mask should be applied during both training and inference time, especially when having continuous state spaces".
method: Backward-chained behaviour tree decomposes the mission; per-subtask RL policies are constrained by CBFs derived from action-condition constraints, enforced as an invalid-action mask at both training and inference.
evaluation: Unity/MLAgents, one double-integrator agent, randomized geometry, 5000 episodes; baselines single-policy RL and BTRL-Penalty reward shaping; ACC violation rate 0.088 to 0.014, success 0.912 to 0.986, fewer steps.
